A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have company this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is currently orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#6325. How 4 states voted on election-related ballot measures

More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.

Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:

Voters in Maryland on Tuesday approved an amendment to the state’s constitution that will make it easier for the state’s Democrat-controlled legislature to redraw the congressional map for the 2028 elections.

The outcome was a victory for Democrats, who could potentially eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held seat – the 1st District on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, represented by Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of the hard-line conservative House Freedom Caucus.

The Old Line State emerged as a bright spot in Democrats’ plan to counter the redistricting wars initiated by President Donald Trump and turbocharged by the spring Supreme Court ruling that diluted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and set off a slew of Republican-led map-remaking across the South.

But those GOP-led efforts appeared to backfire this week, with Democrats holding many of the redrawn seats in states such as Texas, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina.

Still, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told reporters Wednesday that he was “ready to engage” with the legislature on a new map, citing the threat of further redistricting in Republican states.

“Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states, to go after places like Mississippi and South Carolina and Indiana,” Moore said, according to video posted by WBAL-TV 11 News.

Following an unsuccessful attempt to redraw the Maryland map in February, Moore called a special August legislative session during which state lawmakers voted to put the redistricting amendment, known as Question 3, on the November ballot.

The move faced immediate legal challenges from Republicans. Two Maryland courts ruled to block the measure from appearing on the ballot, finding that lawmakers had missed the legally imposed deadline to refer the ballot measure. The state’s Supreme Court, though, allowed the redistricting amendment to go before the voters, with changes to the ballot text.

State and national Democrats campaigned heavily for Question 3 as some public polling pointed to skepticism among voters. Former President Barack Obama even appeared in an ad urging voters to approve it.

Voters in the Show-Me State overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map that sought to dismantle a safely Democratic seat in the Kansas City area.

Missouri Republicans enacted the new lines in 2025, aiming to give them an advantage in seven of the state’s eight House districts, including the 5th District held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver II.

A protracted legal and political tussle over the map ensued.

The group People Not Politicians Missouri started a citizen petition to put the adoption of the map to a statewide vote. While the petition effort was pending, the state held its August primaries under the new lines. But in September, the state Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 map could not be used in the general election because of the pending ballot measure and ordered state officials to hold November’s election under the previous boundaries, first enacted in 2022.

Attempts to challenge the ruling in federal court ultimately proved unsuccessful, with the U.S. Supreme Court issuing an order that reinstated the 2022 map.

Groups on both sides of the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, reportedly spent millions to persuade voters. But St. Louis Public Radio reported last week that while opponents of the 2025 map were actively campaigning against it, organized efforts in favor of Proposition A appeared “nearly nonexistent.”

Republican efforts to try again and enact a new congressional map for 2028 could be complicated by a constitutional amendment, approved by voters Tuesday, that curtails the power of state legislators to override the result of a voter-approved initiative.

Voters in Massachusetts opted this week not to join states such as California and Washington and adopt a nonpartisan primary system.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, would have replaced the state’s partisan primaries with an open primary under which all candidates would appear on the same ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to the general election.

The outcome was a victory for the chorus of labor unions and progressive groups, including the Working Families Party, that opposed the measure. Holding so-called jungle primaries, the groups argued, could make it harder for candidates without financial resources or high name recognition to run for office.

A bipartisan coalition that included the NAACP of New England and Republican former Gov. Charlie Baker supported the measure, arguing that open primaries would give voters more choice and create more competitive elections in a state dominated by Democrats.

Alaskans weighed in this year for the second time as many cycles on a ballot measure to revert to partisan primaries and repeal the state's top-four ranked choice voting system.

With over 70 percent of the vote in, The Associated Press had yet to call the ballot initiative, known as Measure 2, which would also roll back certain campaign finance disclosure requirements. As of Thursday evening, the “no” side, which supports keeping the current election system, was narrowly ahead. The state has until Nov. 18 to finish counting outstanding ballots.

Under Alaska’s voting system, all candidates run on the same ballot during the primary. Then the top four candidates, regardless of party, advance to the general election, which is decided by ranked choice voting if no one takes a majority of the vote.

In 2024, Alaska voters narrowly voted to keep the current system in place.

National Republicans, though, have largely opposed ranked choice voting, including Trump, who has characterized Alaska’s voting system as a “scam.”

The state’s use of open primaries and the top-four ranked choice system has drawn fresh scrutiny this year.  Outside groups spent big sums trying to boost underdog candidates during the Senate primary in an effort to hurt the front-runners. And several candidates in the Senate, House and governor’s races dropped out before the deadline to finalize the general election ballot, again trying to prevent splitting votes with their party front-runners.

Then last week, the Senate race was upended by a New York Times investigation that revealed operatives aligned with the Senate campaign of Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate with a similar name to GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan in an attempt to stack the ballot with two Republicans with the same first and last names. The revelations have fueled an ongoing debate in the state about whether ranked choice voting encourages this kind of alleged campaign chicanery.

“We would not be having this conversation at all if we didn’t have a thing in place called ranked choice voting,” Mike Dunleavy, Alaska's outgoing Republican governor, told Fox News last week.

Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the revelations, as has the Justice Department. The DOJ also sought to block the certification of the Senate result if the incumbent Sullivan loses. Last weekend, a federal court dismissed the lawsuit.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states that currently use ranked choice voting in regular federal elections, along with the District of Columbia.

Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#6324. Unusual warmth has reached the seafloor off Canada’s Pacific coast – and scientists may know why

A seafloor sensor off Vancouver Island logged its highest temperature since monitoring began in 2009, and researchers say El Niño may be behind the spike.

El Niño is usually described as a warming of the surface waters in the tropical Pacific.

This fall, sensors off Canada’s west coast recorded unusually warm water hundreds of feet below the surface.

One seafloor sensor logged its highest temperature since monitoring began there in 2009. The scientists who operate the sensor said the warm pulse is consistent with a strong El Niño.

The sensors are operated by Ocean Networks Canada, an ocean-monitoring initiative of the University of Victoria.

The readings were announced by the organization itself this week. They have not yet been published as a study.

The record was set at a site called Barkley Canyon Upper Slope, off Vancouver Island. A sensor rests on the seafloor there, about 1,300 feet (400 meters) down. That depth is roughly a quarter of a mile.

On November 8, the water at this site reached 46.8°F (8.21°C).

Jay Cullen is the interim president and chief executive of Ocean Networks Canada.

“We’re seeing significant warming not just at the surface, but hundreds of meters below it,” Cullen said.

The November 8 reading was 4.5°F (2.49°C) above the long-term average for the site. It was also 1.6°F (0.89°C) warmer than the previous record, which was set in 2019.

The water has cooled since then, but normal temperatures have not returned. In mid-November, it was still about 2.9°F (1.6°C) warmer than average.

Warm water has been found at other sites too. The Barkley Canyon sensor is one part of a much larger network. Roughly 530 miles (850 kilometers) of seafloor cable connect its five main research sites.

One of those sites is Clayoquot Slope, which lies more than 3,900 feet (1,200 meters) down. Temperatures well above average are being recorded there as well.

Since late summer, sites between 1,300 and 4,100 feet (400 and 1,250 meters) deep have logged record seasonal temperatures.

The deepest site is the exception. At Cascadia Basin, about 8,700 feet (2,650 meters) down, temperatures remain within their usual range.

El Niño was declared by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in June.

On November 12, the agency’s Climate Prediction Center said El Niño was still strengthening.

A strong or very strong event was judged likely to continue into early 2027. The chance of that was put at more than 79%.

How can El Niño affect waters off Canada’s Pacific coast?

Steve Mihaly is a senior scientist at Ocean Networks Canada. According to Mihaly, the energy of a strong El Niño travels north from the equatorial Pacific.

It moves as waves that follow the coastline, and oceanographers call them coastal trapped waves.

Sea level has also been above normal since the warm water arrived. The rise was recorded by tide gauges at Bamfield and Tofino, two communities on Vancouver Island.

Pressure recorders on the seafloor picked it up as well. By mid-November, sea level was about 10 inches (25 centimeters) above normal. Local wind and atmospheric effects were accounted for first.

The scientists then attributed about 6 inches (15 centimeters) of the rise to the waves.

At Barkley Canyon Upper Slope, the water temperature began climbing sharply in late October and reached a record on November 8.

Mihaly said northwest winds persisted into the fall, pushing warmer surface water offshore and drawing colder water upward.

This process, known as upwelling, helped mask the warming at depth.

A second network, called VENUS, is run by Ocean Networks Canada in the Salish Sea.

These sheltered waters are shared by British Columbia and Washington State. The VENUS sensors reach depths of about 980 feet (300 meters).

Temperatures in the Strait of Georgia, which is part of that sea, have been above average throughout 2026.

Jordan Watson is the science director of Ocean Networks Canada.

“Since the start of 2026, the VENUS observatory has shown temperatures consistently higher than we’ve previously observed,” Watson said. “And this was before any El Niño effects started to appear.”

Watson described the area as known for migrating salmon, spawning herring, and marine mammals.

Warming from El Niño could add to the already high temperatures there. That would put more stress on marine ecosystems, the organization said.

So far, only temperatures and sea levels have been reported by the scientists. No effects on marine life have been reported yet.

The record is also a short one. Monitoring at Barkley Canyon began in 2009, so it covers less than two decades.

The scientists were not certain about the cause either. They said the warming likely marks the arrival of El Niño’s effects on Canada’s Pacific coast.

Cullen noted that conditions will be monitored closely over the coming months.

A new tool is also being planned by Ocean Networks Canada and CIOOS Pacific, a regional ocean-data group. It will track ocean conditions across the region.

The seafloor data will be combined with measurements from other groups around the Salish Sea.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada and the University of Washington are among them. More details will be shared later this year, the partners said.

Live and long-term readings can be viewed on Ocean Networks Canada’s data dashboard.

#6323. Ancient Egyptians Revered Cats as Sacred. Then 131 Skulls Revealed What Really Happened to Them.

Fractured skulls, healed wounds, and signs of strangling suggest sacred cats lived—and died—brutally.

Not every Egyptian necropolis was meant for humans. Across Egypt, the cemeteries of Bubastis in the eastern Nile Delta, the Bubasteion in northern Saqqara, and Speos Artemidos near Beni Hassan, along with others in Giza and the Dakhla Oasis, were meant for animals, especially cats. Cats were seen as the earthly embodiment of the feline goddess Bastet. Yet although they were often mummified as votive offerings, their treatment did not always match their status.

Early archaeologists usually ignored animal mummies in favor of human mummies, which were often showcased at theatrical unwrapping parties. Some animal mummies were used as ship ballast for the journey home after an expedition, while others were powdered for questionable medicine, burned for fuel, or ground into fertilizer. During the 19th and early 20th centuries, however, some animal mummies were unwrapped (without a party) so that their skeletal remains could inform studies of Egyptian fauna. Many of these skulls remain in museum collections in Egypt and abroad. Zooarchaeologist Wim Van Neer of the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences and his research team studied one such collection: 131 exceptionally well-preserved skulls of small cats from Beni Hassan, now housed at the Natural History Museum in Vienna. Their goal was to find out how the cats lived before they died.

“Attention was also paid to the presence of pathologies and marks on the skulls, which could provide information about the conditions in which the cats were kept and their cause of death,” Van Neer and his colleagues wrote in their study, recently published in the Journal of Archaeological Science. In addition to carbon and nitrogen isotope analysis to determine diet, “characteristics such as dental abnormalities, infectious or metabolic disorders and trauma were recorded.”

Most of the skulls turned out to be from domestic cats (Felis catus), with several jungle cats (Felis chaus) among them. Many of the animals apparently suffered from conditions such as gum disease and infections, and some skulls had puncture marks and fractures that could indicate fights between cats. How the cats met their end, however, was more disturbing. Evidence suggests that cats were deliberately killed so they could be turned into offerings to Bastet. Fourteen of the skulls show traumatic injuries, including blunt-force and sharp-force trauma. Sharp-force trauma is thought to have possibly killed the humans who were sacrificed to join First Dynasty pharaohs in the afterlife. Beyond fight wounds, some injuries were inflicted long enough before death to show signs of healing, which suggests that the animals may have endured physical violence from humans while still alive.

When Van Neer and his team took a closer look at one skull, they found marks consistent with blows from a sharp metal weapon. Wounds on some of the other skulls were thought to have been made by strikes from a heavy wooden implement. The cats’ treatment before death also seems to have been deplorable. Although no ancient records describe how the cats were kept, the researchers inferred that they were probably held in crowded enclosures. This could explain the fights, as well as the attacks on domestic cats by jungle cats, which were caught in marshlands or along the banks of the Nile when Egypt was lusher than it is today. Isotope analysis showed that the jungle cats’ diet clearly differed from that of the domestic cats, further suggesting that this species was unlikely to have been bred in captivity.

Even among the wild-caught jungle cats, six of the seven skulls came from animals with conditions similar to those of their domestic relatives. This was probably a sign that all of the cats, the overwhelming majority of which were adults, were kept in conditions that caused illness and injury before death. Radiocarbon dating revealed when they died.

Cats are generally thought to have first been domesticated in the Fertile Crescent of the Near East roughly 10,000 years ago, although some recent genetic studies suggest it happened later, in Egypt or elsewhere in North Africa. In Egypt, the earliest clear evidence of domestic cats dates to the Middle Kingdom (c. 2000–1700 B.C.E.). However, demand for mummified cat offerings was greatest much later, in the Late and Ptolemaic Periods. Older feline mummies do exist, and one of the nine dated skulls goes back to the Third Intermediate Period. The other eight, however, date to between 380 and 40 B.C.E., from the end of the Late Period into the Ptolemaic era.

As for how the cats were killed, blunt- or sharp-force trauma appears to have been the main cause of death. Some cats were strangled, but a blow to the head was apparently the more common method. “Skull fractures were the most common cause of death, whereas evidence of strangulation occurred less frequently,” the researchers said. “Our observations of traumatic lesions on the skulls provide evidence of fatal injuries, as well as cases of animals that survived violent interactions with humans.”

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. She lurks right outside New York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

#6322. Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

#6321. Howler monkey droppings hold clues about the fragmented forests they live in

In southern Mexico, the mix of gut bacteria in howler monkeys varied with forest patch size, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.

Howler monkeys can survive in small patches of forest.

A study in southern Mexico found that the mix of bacteria in their guts varied with the size of those patches, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.

Researchers found these patterns in droppings from adult male mantled howler monkeys.

Repeating that sampling could help conservationists track changes over time without capturing the animals.

The study was led by Tabor Whitney while she was a doctoral student at Northwestern University. She worked with primate researchers at Universidad Veracruzana in Mexico.

The work was carried out in the Los Tuxtlas Biosphere Reserve in the state of Veracruz. About 60% of the original forest cover in the reserve has been lost. The remaining forest is broken into patches among pastures, farm fields, and towns.

The 10 study patches ranged from about 5 acres to nearly 500 acres (2 to 199 hectares). Farmland or pasture bordered every one of them.

Whitney and field assistants followed adult male howlers in October and November, during the 2022 rainy season. When a male defecated, the fresh droppings were collected from the ground with sterile sticks.

The team tested the droppings for three things. The first was the bacteria in them. The second was the fatty acids that those bacteria produce. The third was the breakdown products of stress hormones.

The trees in every patch were also measured. Across patches, average trunk width ranged from about 10 to 16 inches (25 to 42 centimeters).

Biologists call the community of microbes in an animal’s gut its microbiome.

“An awesome takeaway of the study is the knowledge the gut microbiome is the most sensitive to ecological change,” Whitney said.

Gut bacteria were analyzed in 41 samples from 32 males. Monkeys from different patches carried different mixes of bacteria.

These differences were linked to all four measures of a patch’s size and layout. Its area and its distance from other forest were among those measures. All seven measures of the trees growing in the patch were linked to the differences too.

Plant fiber is digested by some of the bacteria involved. One such group is Prevotella, and monkeys in larger patches carried more of it.

A different group of bacteria was most common where trees were small. The same was true where few rows of trees linked a patch to other forest.

Only one forest measure predicted the diversity of bacteria carried by a monkey. That measure was trunk thickness. Less variety was found in monkeys from patches with thicker-trunked trees.

The authors suggested that monkeys in mature forest may eat a narrower diet. Fewer kinds of microbes may be taken in as a result.

The team also tested distances to the nearest houses and roads. Neither distance predicted any of the three health measures in the main analysis.

Stress hormone levels were measured in 36 males. They didn’t differ clearly from patch to patch. One pattern, however, was the reverse of what the team had predicted.

Males in larger patches tended to have higher hormone levels, not lower ones.

Higher levels were also found in patches with more fig trees. Figs are a central part of the howler diet.

The authors explained the result in social terms. Several howler groups are supported by larger patches. More than one group may be attracted to the same place by fig trees.

Hormone levels could be raised by competition during encounters with rival groups, not by food shortage. Ordinary demands such as reproduction and fighting infection are also known to raise these hormones.

A monkey with a high level is therefore not necessarily in trouble.

Plant fiber is fermented by gut bacteria, and small fatty acids are released in the process.

Those acids are used by the animal for energy. These acids also help maintain the gut lining and the immune system.

No difference between patches was found in the amounts of these acids. Instead, the team’s attention was drawn to the balance between propionate and butyrate, two of the acids.

A surplus of propionate over butyrate has been proposed as a sign of an unbalanced gut. That pattern has been documented both in people and in wild primates that are short of food.

More propionate than butyrate was present in the droppings from all 10 patches.

In four of the 10 forest patches, the ratio of propionate to butyrate was about 2.6 or higher.

Human studies have linked that threshold to gut disorders. Whether it signals a health problem in howler monkeys remains unknown.

The authors wrote that a reduction in butyrate-producing bacteria may be indicated by the pattern. The reduction may extend across the whole landscape.

The researchers also raised the possibility of long-term effects on the monkeys’ gut lining and immune function.

Howlers in southern Mexico suffered a mass die-off in 2024. Up to 31% of some local populations died from the combined effects of extreme heat, drought, and habitat degradation.

Baseline health records are needed if early warning signs of decline are to be detected, the authors wrote.

Two conservation priorities were recommended by the authors. Patches of mature, varied forest should be protected and enlarged. Rows of trees and wooded strips along rivers should keep those patches connected.

The researchers also suggested that a wider variety of trees be planted, including fruiting species. Howlers would then be able to move through the canopy in search of food and mates.

Permission from local landowners was needed before the team could reach the monkeys.

“Landowners we’ve spoken with are really open to these conversations,” Whitney said.

“They’ve said they love seeing the monkeys, and if they can help them travel on the trees, they’re very interested in it.”

She said the same sampling could be repeated every five or 10 years. Changes could then be compared over time, and the effect of conservation work could be checked.

Every sample came from an adult male. All of the samples were collected in a single rainy season.

Female and young howlers have different energy and hormone demands. The results therefore can’t be assumed to apply to them.

The gut bacteria samples were also limited and unevenly distributed across patches. Some patches supplied one sample, while others supplied as many as 12.

The team identified which bacteria were present. What those bacteria were doing inside the monkeys was not measured.

The study found links between forest features and gut bacteria.

Further research could test whether changes to the forest lead to changes in the monkeys’ gut bacteria.

The authors also noted that forests across Los Tuxtlas may be too uniformly degraded.

That could explain why the fatty acids varied so little. Comparisons with other landscapes are needed, they wrote.

Future research could pair repeated sampling with long-term records of the monkeys’ behavior. Such work could test whether these signals change as the forest does.

The team is now preparing a study comparing the gut bacteria of male and female howlers.

The full study was published in the journal Animal Conservation.

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

#6319. Why Do Helmets Still Fail to Stop Concussions? Scientists May Have Been Fighting the Wrong Force All Along.

A WWII physicist said twisting hits were the real danger. Sensors in 203 athletes’ mouths say otherwise.

An estimated 3.8 million sports-related concussions occur in the U.S. each year. They’re so common that you might assume they’re not as serious as other injuries—but in fact, these mild traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) can often be more dangerous. While tendons, muscle, and bone heal good as new, repeated and sustained concussions—a typical occurrence in many athletic endeavors—can lead to dementia and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), an aggressive degenerative brain disease.

Although helmets have grown safer over the years in certain sports, concussions are still commonplace. That’s especially true in football, even after the high-profile introduction of the Guardian Cap for NFL preseason practices in 2022 and then in regular-season games in 2024. This suggests that there’s something about concussions, specifically the relationship of linear and rotational acceleration and the brain, that scientists still don’t understand.

During World War II, Scottish physicist A.H.S. Holbourn argued that rotational acceleration (think of an uppercut to the jaw) was more dangerous than linear acceleration (a straight-on, direct hit whose force goes through the center of the head). His theory was that rotation was worse because it stretches and strains brain tissue by moving different parts at different speeds. Scientists have focused on protecting against rotation ever since.

However, a new Stanford Medicine-led study suggests that linear acceleration, not rotation, may be the better predictor of concussion. The research comes from the lab of bioengineer David Camarillo, who’s spent more than a decade studying concussions and helmet safety. By analyzing unprecedentedly accurate impact data from motion-sensing mouthguards worn by 203 athletes across seven different sports, Camarillo and his team discovered that Holbourn’s initial assumptions weren’t correct. The results of their study were published in the journal Annals of Biomedical Engineering.

“Holbourn’s reasoning was based just on mechanics; it wasn’t biology,” David Camarillo, senior author of the study, said in a press statement. “The question we started out with many years ago was, ‘What are the forces required to cause concussion?’ If we understand the nature of those forces and the limits of the human brain, then it might be possible to prevent concussions.”

Previous studies relied on helmet-mounted sensors, but the authors note that those sensors are often inaccurate because helmets tend to move around a lot. Across the mouthguard-enabled data set, the researchers analyzed 3,851 impacts, of which 47 were verified as concussions. In their mathematical models comparing the data, peak linear acceleration was the single most predictive factor in whether a hit eventually produced a concussion. Camarillo and his team haven’t pinned down a mechanism for this result, but they suspect one of two culprits: the brain striking the inside of the skull, or cavitation, in which sudden pressure changes form tiny bubbles that then collapse.

If these results hold up in future studies, they could have profound implications for helmet safety and design. The mouthguard data showed that a hit producing 100 g of linear acceleration (100 times the acceleration of gravity) carries a 50 percent risk of concussion. That’s far lower than the often-cited 192 g threshold from earlier helmet-sensor studies. At 150 g, a hit that older data would have considered below the danger line, concussion risk tops 99 percent.

“Why are there so many concussions even when people are wearing helmets?” Camarillo asked. “Part of the answer could be in this paper, which is that the linear accelerations that we previously thought were safe, we now see are much more dangerous.”

In a way, the new results offer a bit of hope that helmets do have room for improvement, and with a greater focus on addressing linear acceleration, concussions could significantly drop in the coming years and decades. One Stanford-developed technology is a helmet with liquid-filled pads that reduces peak linear acceleration and knocks nearly 20 percentage points off the chances of concussion on high-impact hits versus standard football helmets.

“If linear acceleration is its own distinct mechanism of concussion and it’s very common, then we’ve been missing a lot,” Camarillo said. “We haven’t tried as hard to optimize for this variable. It gives me some hope that there’s a new opportunity for preventing concussions.”

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

#6318. Foster bill would bolster tech use to monitor AI financial risks

A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.

The draft bill, from Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond quickly to cybersecurity and other threats.

The bill is designed to help regulators keep pace with new risks "driven largely by the development of state-of-the-art AI models," according to a summary.

The legislation is intended to help regulators provide financing to banks during crises and wind down failing banks. The model software would reduce the amount of manual compliance work that smaller financial institutions would have to do by providing standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and transmit the information to regulators, according to a Foster spokesperson.

“With advances in AI creating new cybersecurity threats and financial risks, it's more important than ever that we modernize the way we monitor the health of our financial institutions,” Foster said in a statement. “We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.”

Foster, who has a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leader on AI issues on the Financial Services panel, is in line to become chair of the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year.

He has been mulling a challenge to ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., to chair the full committee in the new Congress. But Foster is now “leaning toward not running,” a person familiar with his thinking said.

Waters already has a confirmed challenger in Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., who on Thursday circulated a "Dear Colleague" letter seeking the support of House Democrats for his bid.

Casten touted his “career at the intersection of business, science and public policy." Before entering Congress, he worked in clean energy and co-founded a company that converted industrial waste energy into usable power.

In his letter, Casten cited the need to lower housing and insurance costs, protect consumers from fraud, address risks posed by cryptocurrency and prediction markets and guard against the next financial crisis. He also promised to hold the Trump administration accountable for ethical lapses.

He's got a tough road ahead of him, however. Every Financial Services Democrat except Casten, Foster and Rep. Sam Liccardo of California signed an Oct. 21 letter to House Democrats in support of Waters. That show of support came after Casten made it known he was interested and it was clear that Foster had been considering his own bid.

Although Foster may not compete for the chairmanship, he has recently talked to Waters about changing how the committee operates.

“He wants a variety of members to play a role in legislation brought up in committee,” the source familiar with his thinking said. He’s also seeking more input on witnesses who testify at subcommittee hearings.

The draft bill he released on Thursday covers a topic that Foster is likely to pursue throughout the 120th Congress. He often asks the most questions about the use of AI in financial services at hearings and offers the most amendments related to the issue at markups.

Under the bill, model software would be developed for banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, AI risk monitoring and other activities.

The software must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, according to the summary. It would be tested using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than actual customer accounts. Regulators would not take financial or supervisory actions during the study.

The software developed during the study would not have to be adopted; rather, it “should be viewed as a starting point for further modernization,” the summary says.

All software models would have to be published within one year of enactment of the bill and a final report assessing feasibility, costs and savings, competition and other criteria, would be due to Congress within two years.

#6317. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

#6316. Archaeologists Found a Castaway Camp on an Island at the End of the World. Did a Legendary Sailor Build It?

The island behind a Jules Verne classic was hiding a shipwreck mystery.

While hunting penguins for oil (yes, people really do that) in 1873, famed Argentine sailor Luis Piedra Buena wrecked his schooner brig Espora off the southern tip of South America. He and his crew regrouped on a deserted beach, spent about two months building a new cutter, the Luisito, and sailed safely to Chile to tell their tale. Now, researchers believe they may have found pieces of a shipwreck and the remains of a “castaway camp” possibly tied to Piedra Buena on Isla de los Estados, an island “at the end of the world.”

In a new study published in the journal Antiquity, lead author Nicolás Ciarlo of Spain’s University of Cádiz and his colleagues describe how their research into the maritime history of the island, which lies across the Strait of Le Maire from the tip of Tierra del Fuego, led them to a castaway camp. They believe the camp may link the island’s Lacroix Inlet in Franklin Bay to the more than 150-year-old survival story.

Isla de los Estados is probably best known for a lighthouse that inspired Jules Verne’s novel The Lighthouse at the End of the World. The island forms the easternmost point of Argentina’s Tierra del Fuego Province, and from the 17th century onward it lay along a key sailing route.

By 1870, the Argentine government had granted the island to Piedra Buena. Although he never established a settlement there, he sailed past it countless times while pursuing his interests throughout Patagonia. Then disaster struck. “During a campaign for exploiting penguins for oil, he and his crew lost the schooner brig Espora,” according to the study.

The crew survived, built a cutter, and sailed to Punta Arenas, Chile. There, Piedra Buena described the time they had spent at Lacroix Inlet, although experts have long doubted that he identified the location correctly.

To test his account, the research team visited Lacroix Inlet in January 2026 with help from the Argentine Navy. There, they found the “remains of a shipwreck and a temporary camp” on a wind-battered stretch of coast at the base of a cliff, exposed to strong southwesterly storms. The “possible castaway camp” sat near a stream.

“Although there is still no common agreement, Piedra Buena’s account and other documentary evidence suggest that this bay is likely the place where the Espora sank,” the authors wrote. “The location and material culture of the temporary occupation at Lacroix Inlet point to a connection between this site and the nearby shipwreck remains and thus, possibly with the Espora and her crew.”

At the camp, which the team described as a “short-term occupation,” they found glass beads, buttons, and a bottle, along with nautical items such as a deck prism and a rudder hinge. Elsewhere in the inlet lay the remains of three wooden hulls, including timber that may have been used to build a structure. All the wood likely came from ships’ hulls, but it’s unclear whether it all came from the same vessel.

The team called the finds “novel data” on the history of seafaring around the island. Their preliminary assessment points to at least one shipwreck that led to a temporary settlement. “The identity of the vessel/s and the castaways’ trajectories are the subject of ongoing inquiry,” they wrote, adding that a thorough study of the timbers may provide definitive answers.

Some artifacts are especially telling. “The deck glass located on the surface is one of the most revealing artifacts,” Ciarlo told Discover Magazine. “To assess the identity of the Espora—as it happens with other shipwreck sites—is like putting together a puzzle. It does not rely on a unique proof, but on a critical analysis and merging of multiple lines of evidence.”

Still, questions remain. In the study, the authors acknowledged that they found no trace of the site where the Luisito was built, and it’s unclear whether the Espora was ever completely taken apart. They wrote that more work is needed at the camp and on the shipwrecks in the weather-beaten inlet.

“As archaeologists,” Ciarlo said, according to Phys.org, “being in this isolated and wild place allowed us to taste what a small group of castaways saw and felt about 150 years ago.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. Jeremy Bentham, the "godless" philosopher who founded modern utilitarianism, had severe dental and jaw problems, a CT scan of his skull reveals.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6314. Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

Former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous New York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

“Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”

West Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and New Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey said.

Rockefeller was born in New York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

He returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

In West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he said of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness."

He had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

Rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

Rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

Rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

But defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

Despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension plans.

In 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him said the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

He believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the issues. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

He viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

But industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

“The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he said on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

He had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller announced he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

Rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance plan, he said, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”

"These are people," Rockefeller said, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice."

The amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

Rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

Rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.

#6312. Stone Age children left fingerprints on ancient art projects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Clay figurines hint at hands-on learning in the Levant

Stone Age hunter-gatherer children from the Levant may have helped make small clay sculptures of birds, gazelle, humans and more (some shown).

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

Fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, says archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

The archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

This evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, says archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.

#6309. Trump names Stephen Miller his chief of staff ahead of Dem takeover

President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Stephen Miller, the architect of the hard-line immigration and deportation program voters rejected this week, will become White House chief of staff.

Susie Wiles will depart that post and move to the Trump political organization, which appears to be in full operation, even after the president's last midterm election. Miller has been deputy chief of staff, overseeing the Trump administration's domestic policy.

Miller’s first day will be Monday, Trump said in a social media post.

Trump dubbed Miller “one of my most trusted advisors” and said Wiles, who also oversaw his 2024 presidential campaign, “has done an outstanding job.”

Wiles, who Trump recently announced had won a battle with breast cancer, said in a X post that “serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding she was “proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

The chief-of-staff change came three days after Republicans were demolished in Trump’s final midterm election, with House Democrats on pace for the largest majority in over a decade and at least a 54-seat Senate majority come January.

Trump addressed the personnel move as he departed the White House Friday for an event and weekend in Florida — though he ignored a question about his recent declaration that Wiles would be sticking around.

“I wanted to make a change,” he said in a roughly three-minute exchange with reporters before he walked to Marine One. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”

Trump in recent days had become open to working with Democrats after the new Congress is seated on Jan. 3, even after railing against what he called the party’s “bad” policy during an October-long campaign rally blitz.

“Look, I mean, I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “But I have the power of the veto. So if we don't like what they're doing… They've already called and they want to talk about things. And that's fine.”

Trump summoned Thursday's press pool into the Oval Office for an executive order signing. On his desk was a red baseball cap with "VETO" across the front in large white lettering.

Miller has worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to several GOP lawmakers, including former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who became attorney general in Trump's first administration.

But making the hard-line Miller his White House chief of staff even before congressional Democrats get organized likely will draw the ire of the incoming majority.

Virginia Rep. Donald S. Beyer Jr. was among the first Democratic lawmakers to slam Trump’s decision.

“Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller doubles down on the politics of hatred, lawlessness, and failure that the American people soundly rejected three days ago,” Beyer said in a statement. "Miller embodies the worst elements of the Trump presidency. His promotion shows that Trump has learned nothing from his electoral debacle and has no intention of even trying to work constructively with the next Congress.”

Many congressional Democrats — leaders, returning incumbents and members-elect — want to investigate Trump, his inner circle and family members while also pursuing a legislative agenda aimed at paring the cost of living.

To that end, as chief of staff, Democrat-run committees calling Miller to testify is highly unlikely since he could continue to claim executive privilege. That allows senior White House aides to withhold many internal West Wing communications, documents, and presidential-related conversations and actions, from lawmakers.

In public comments and television interviews, Miller has accused Democrats of being aligned with figures and candidates who “hate” Americans, and once said the party is “unworthy of power.”

“So the Democrats have become a party of freaks, weirdos, losers and crazies,” Miller said during a July appearance on Fox News. “But you can’t laugh it off because it’s deadly serious. When you give these people power, everything you know and love in this world falls apart. You have chaos, corruption, decay, violence, poverty.”
