#6307. Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Asteroid defense is the mission’s top priority, but there’s also fascinating science to be done.

The Hera spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera captured this black-and-white image of Didymos and Dimorphos from about 60 kilometers away. The photo shows the far side of Didymos compared to the DART impact.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

On November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

The cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.)

Hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so quickly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

Juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

“Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” says planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always showed the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” says planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

#6306. The Sky Today on Tuesday, November 17: Spotlight on the Pleiades

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Early this evening brighter targets are best, as the Moon doesn’t set until late. Ready for viewing as the winter constellations start to dominate earlier each day is the Pleiades, an open cluster cataloged as M45.

Known since antiquity and readily visible to the naked eye, the Pleiades contains several bright stars arranged in a tiny dipperlike shape. Located in northwestern Taurus, the cluster is sometimes mistaken for the Little Dipper, although that asterism is much larger and lies in the northern sky, anchored at the end of its handle by Polaris, the North Star. The Pleiades shines with a collective magnitude of 1.6 and spans roughly 110’ — a huge swath of sky. It lies above the sideways V-shape of Taurus’ face as the Bull rises in the east this evening, and is already 30° high by 7:30 P.M. local time. How many stars can you make out with the naked eye? Most observers see six or seven.

Once you’ve taken in the cluster without any optical aid, zoom in with binoculars or a finder scope. (Any higher magnification and you won’t see most of the cluster at once, but instead be limited to a smaller portion.) Many more stars will now pop into your field of view. If you do opt for high magnification, look for a faint grayish haze around the stars — this is nearby dust reflecting the stars’ light, and requires clear, dark conditions to make out.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight, with the best meteor viewing overnight into the early-morning hours of November 18, as the Moon sets around midnight and the radiant rises higher. Keep reading for more detail below on how to observe the shower.

Sunrise: 6:47 A.M.Sunset: 4:42 P.M.Moonrise: 12:56 P.M.Moonset: —Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (57%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

The peak of the Leonid meteor shower, caused by the dusty debris of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is best seen early on the morning of the 18th, after the Moon has set and the shower’s radiant rises high in the hours before dawn.

Two hours before sunrise, Leo is high in the southeast, with bright Jupiter and Mars joining the curved shape of the Sickle asterism. The Leonids’ radiant is located just inside the cuved blade’s inner edge, near 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Leonis to the upper left (north) of Mars and Jupiter. The two planets appear roughly side by side in the sky around this time, with ruddy Mars at left and more golden-yellow Jupiter at right. Regulus sits just to their lower left.

To catch the most meteors, you’ll actually want to look a little ways away from Leo, about 40° to 60° to the left or right of the constellation. This is where meteors with the longest trains will also occur. Although this shower isn’t particularly strong, you can expect to see roughly a half-dozen or more Leonid meteors per hour. The Leonid shower produces some of the fastest-moving meteors we experience all year, streaking through the sky at some 44 miles (70 kilometers) per second.

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to correct an error in the speed of the meteors.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) officially announced its decision to revoke the United States' measles elimination status on Nov. 17, 2026. The week prior, the Wall Street Journal reported that the PAHO had reached that decision.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6301. The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A new study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman says. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their new role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao says.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

The hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao says.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

J. Xiao et al. Stimulus-specific recruitment of human amygdala neurons predicts episodic memory encoding success. Nature Neuroscience. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41593-026-02493-9

K.L. Wahlstrom et al. Direct electrical stimulation of the human amygdala enhances recognition memory for objects but not scenes. Communications Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s42003-026-10270-4

#6300. Nov. 17, 1966: A phenomenal Leonid meteor storm

On Nov. 17, 1966, the Leonids put on one of the greatest meteor shows in recorded history, during which eyewitnesses reported a sky that seemed to “rain shooting stars.” Observers in North America witnessed a peak of thousands of meteors per minute; Kitt Peak National Observatory reported 40 meteors per second. This peak occurred around 12:00 Universal Time, and lasted for about 15 to 20 minutes. As the requisite rate of 1,000 meteors per hour was not just met but superseded dozens of times over, the event was firmly classified as a true meteor storm.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of our DNA," geneticist Turi King examines how DNA was used to reveal the ultimate fate of the last members of the House of Romanov.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In 1917, the Russian Revolution was in full swing. Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, and he and his family were exiled to a remote Siberian town. There were plans to get the family to the U.K., but King George V (Nicholas' first cousin) and the British government withdrew their offer of asylum over concerns of the ramifications.

After the Russian Provisional Government was overthrown by the more extreme Bolsheviks in October 1917, Nicholas, his wife, their children and several members of the family's staff were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, where, in July 1918, they were executed. Their bodies were hidden and remained lost to time ‪for nearly a century —‬ until modern technology, with some help from the British royal family, unraveled the fascinating story of their disappearance.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World" (Pegasus Books, 2026), author Turi King, director of the Center for Evolution at the University of Bath, looks back at the incredible story of how DNA was used to solve a major mystery of modern history: What happened to the last members of the House of Romanov?

I was sitting in a lecture theatre at Cambridge University in 1994 when one of my lecturers, Erika Hagelberg, spoke about a new study she had just been involved in. It was the first major case to combine both mitochondrial DNA and DNA fingerprinting to identify human remains: those of the Russian imperial family.

But first I need to take you back to Russia in 1917 and the abdication of the tsar following the Russian Revolution.

The Russian royal family, the Romanovs, had been the reigning imperial dynasty since 1617, and three centuries later, Tsar Nicholas II was on the throne. Nicholas was the cousin of George V, king of the United Kingdom, their mothers being sisters, and had married George's cousin Princess Alix (Alexandra) of Hesse, who was apparently Queen Victoria's favourite grandchild. Nicholas and Alix had five children, four daughters (Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia) and a son, Alexei.

The tsar and his wife were not well liked by the Russian population and political unrest culminated in the revolution of 1917, when Nicholas was forced to abdicate. The family were kept under house arrest and in 1918 they were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg with the royal physician, Dr Botkin, and three of their staff. On the night of 16 July, the family, their doctor and staff were herded into the cellar together and executed. Their bodies were then taken to a secret location and placed in a hastily dug communal grave, doused in sulphuric acid in an attempt to disfigure them and hinder identification, and then covered over, the location of the grave being lost for more than 70 years.

The Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, 1919.

Ironically, the new Russian government had wanted to get the Romanovs out of Russia due to the risk of their becoming a rallying point, but a plan to grant asylum to the Romanovs in the U.K. because of their links with the British royal family fell through, owing to a reluctance on the part of George V to grant it. Yet those links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial in their identification.

Fast-forward to 1991, when several skeletons were found in a shallow grave some 20 miles from Yekaterinburg. Many of the bones were badly damaged but it was possible to determine, based on examination of the skeletal remains, that there were nine individuals — two short of the 11 killed that night. The faces of the skulls were badly damaged in all of the skeletons, all of them showing evidence of violence either in the form of bullet holes or bayonet wounds or both. Before the genetic study, Russian forensic scientists had used numerous techniques alongside historical data to tentatively identify the remains as some of the members of the Russian royal family, their doctor and servants.

These included examining the bones, to determine approximate age and sex, and some of the teeth, the expensive dental work, incorporating gold, platinum and porcelain, indicating that certain remains must belong to members of an aristocratic family. The team worked out that the two missing individuals would have been two of the children, one of the daughters (while it was hard to determine which one it would be, given how close in age they were, it was thought that it was either Maria or Anastasia) and the son, Prince Alexei.

The Russian chief forensic medical examiner then contacted a team in the U.K., which included Erika, to see if genetic evidence could be used to confirm the identification. The U.K. team used the amelogenin genetic sex test, now part of standard forensic DNA testing, which confirmed the sex of the skeletons (four male and five female bodies), while an early form of DNA profiling showed that there was a family group here — two parents and three children — and four unrelated individuals. So far, so good.

Next, they needed to prove that this was the Russian royal family, and they did this using mitochondrial DNA analysis. As you'll remember, mitochondrial DNA is passed down by a mother to all her children, male and female, but only daughters can pass it on — so if female-line family members of Tsar Nicholas and Tsarina Alexandra could be found and would agree to give a DNA test, their mitochondrial DNA should match that of their royal ancestors. It just so happened that the late Prince Philip, husband of the late Queen Elizabeth, was related to the tsarina through the female line: she was his great-aunt, his maternal grandmother being the sister of the tsarina. He kindly gave a DNA sample.

The testing that they did was standard for the time in that they looked at two regions known as hypervariable regions 1 and 2 (HVR1 and HVR2). You'll remember that mitochondrial DNA has 37 rather crucial genes on it where any "typo" that occurs as the DNA is being copied could have serious consequences if the mutation is deleterious. By contrast, in those parts of the mitochondrial genome that don't code for anything, such as these two hypervariable regions, mutations can occur more freely without necessarily causing issues, meaning that these regions contain much more genetic variation. These are the sections of mitochondrial DNA that scientists began analysing for identification purposes. While it's not as precise as DNA profiling because many thousands of people will all have the same mitochondrial DNA type, it can be very helpful in a case such as this.

Prince Philip's DNA was eventually used to confirm the identities of the lost Romanov family.

When the team sequenced these two regions, Prince Philip's mitochondrial DNA was found to match that of the putative remains of the tsarina and her daughters. Next they found two living female-line relatives of the tsar, descended from his maternal grandmother: a great-great-niece, Princess Xenia Cheremeteff Sfiris, and a first cousin twice removed, James Carnegie, 3rd Duke of Fife. The mitochondrial DNA from these two matched each other perfectly, and they, in turn, matched that of the tsar, except at one base where there was both a match and a mismatch.

This is because the tsar had what's known as a heteroplasmy at this position: some of the mitochondrial DNA sequences showed a T and others showed a C, his maternal relatives showing a T. Heteroplasmy is known to take place primarily through mutations occurring when the DNA is copied to make new cells in a person's lifetime, but it can be inherited from a maternal ancestor with heteroplasmy. Extremely rarely, it can come from paternal mitochondrial DNA making it into the cell. So the fact that heteroplasmy existed in the DNA sample didn't negate the match, and the probability that these were the Romanovs was still between 70 to 1 through to 840,000 to 1 in favour. But, it did sow some seeds of doubt. Incidentally, we now know that heteroplasmy is fairly common, with potentially over half of the human population having at least one heteroplasmy, albeit at a low percentage in terms of their mitochondrial DNA carrying it.

So, to be doubly sure, in 1996 the remains of the tsar's brother, Georgij, who had died in 1899, were exhumed and he was found to have exactly the same mitochondrial heteroplasmy. Given the very low chance of two people having this particular heteroplasmy if they weren't related, this pointed to the mitochondrial DNA data the researchers obtained being 130,000,000 times more likely if these were the Romanovs than if they were an unrelated family.

The case was solved in terms of identifying the tsar, tsarina and three of their daughters, but the mystery still remained as to what had happened to the two other children. In the scientific paper reporting the results, the authors conjectured that possibly the two children had been buried separately, or that they could have survived the massacre. Incidentally, there was a woman living in the U.S. who claimed to be Anastasia, saying she had managed to escape being executed, and so the fact that two of the children were missing from the Romanov family group only fuelled the idea that maybe she truly was the missing princess.

Then, in 2007, a group of amateur archaeologists, digging a mere 70 metres away from the previously discovered mass grave, came across more human remains. Skeletal evidence showed that they were the remains of two bodies, a young woman aged 15-19 and a probable male aged 12-15. DNA analysis was brought to bear and again showed that the two individuals were siblings and related to the Romanovs already identified. As an extra DNA test, Y-chromosome testing was carried out, the Y chromosome being passed from father to son, to confirm that the Y chromosome of the newly found male skeleton was indeed male and that it matched the Y chromosome of the tsar. This also then matched male-line relatives — a second cousin once removed of the tsar (third cousin of Alexei) through Tsar Nicholas I. The missing Romanov children had been found.

From an award-winning expert on DNA, discover the myth-busting book that opens a dazzling window into the world of modern genetics.

Fascinating, compassionate, and entirely captivating, The Secrets of Our DNA is the essential book that explains how genetics has changed and transformed the world around us.

Turi King is renowned for presenting complex findings on DNA and genetic science in an accessible and compelling way and she has won awards for her public engagement in science. Turi is the director of the Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath. She is an honorary fellow of the British Science Association, a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London, a member of the Chartered Society of Forensic Sciences, and a member of the International Society of Forensic Geneticists. She is well known for her academic work leading the identification of Richard III; advising on the case of Mary Jane Kelly (the last victim of Jack the Ripper); leading the project on sequencing Hitler’s genome; as well as her media work co-presenting BBC’s DNA Family Secrets.

#6297. Lucid Dreaming Was Once a Rare Gift. Now Scientists Say They Can Help You Learn It.

Researchers built dreamlike virtual worlds to teach people how to realize they’re dreaming—and it worked.

Some people don’t just dream. They often realize they’re dreaming and can even control the dreamworld, from giving themselves powers that defy the laws of physics to escaping a nightmare by waking themselves up. Lucid dreamers can go on adventures most of us can only dream about (pun intended). But is it possible to train yourself to do the same?

Dreams can happen during any stage of sleep, but they usually occur during REM sleep. When dreamers suddenly become aware that they’re dreaming, they’re in a lucid state. However, people who frequently have lucid dreams are rare. Researchers from the University of Trento in Rovereto, Italy, wanted to find out whether standard exercises, meditation, and virtual reality could teach people to have lucid dreams. Participants in the experimental group practiced open monitoring meditation, which is meant to sharpen sensory awareness and perception through nonjudgmental observation. They then did VR training that took them into virtual worlds full of bizarre, dreamlike scenarios. For comparison, a control group used VR that had nothing to do with dreaming, while a third group did only the standard training, without VR.

All participants started with the same baseline training, which they did while awake to practice dream recall and reality checks. They were told to keep a dream diary, noting each morning whether they remembered any dreams and, if so, what the dreams were about. Participants were also told to do reality checks, such as pinching themselves, to test whether they were awake or dreaming. They did these checks whenever they ran into something strange or simply thought of something strange. On top of that, phone alarms went off every hour for 12 hours each day to prompt more checks. The idea was that the habit would eventually carry over into their dreams. On top of this training, the experimental group did open monitoring meditation sessions in the lab to prepare for their VR training. During these sessions, participants observed their breathing, bodily sensations, thoughts, and emotions without reacting to them. Each session also included a guided exploration of an environment designed to look like a scene from a dream.

“Through repetition, [reality checks] are intended to become habitual and to transfer into dreams via ‘dream residue,’ where they may be triggered by dream signs that are unusual, surprising, or incongruent events, and thereby precipitate insight into the dream state,” the researchers wrote in their study, recently published in Frontiers in Psychology.

To build these scenes, the researchers created LucidDreamingVR, a program inspired by Tibetan dream yoga. Unlike the VR control group, whose content had nothing to do with dreaming, the experimental group completed eight sessions that grew steadily more elaborate, taking participants from recognizing a dream to controlling one. The early tasks taught them to spot dream signs: the virtual surroundings would suddenly shift, cueing a reality check, much as an odd detail might inside a dream. Later sessions drew on dream yoga techniques to let participants rehearse what they might do once they became lucid. With a single spoken command, they could fly, leap to incredible heights or, like Alice after tumbling down the rabbit hole, grow and shrink at will.

The researchers counted both lucid and semi-lucid dreams as “lucid-like” dreams. By the end of the experiment, 11 of the 13 participants who had trained with LucidDreamingVR had reported at least one lucid-like dream. By contrast, eight of 13 people in the control group without VR and only four of 12 in the VR control group reported one. Nearly 12% of the dreams the experimental group remembered were lucid-like, compared with about 3% for the control group without VR and about 1% for the VR control group. Surprisingly, the LucidDreamingVR group remembered the fewest dreams overall, so they also reported the fewest ordinary, non-lucid dreams. These results suggest that combining open monitoring meditation with dream-themed VR may increase lucid dreaming. However, because neither control group meditated, the study can’t show which part of the training mattered more.

“[Our] findings support the use of immersive environments as…cognitive-enhancement tools,” the researchers said. “Future work should combine VR-based rehearsal with objective sleep verification, factorial designs, and waking cognitive measures to clarify mechanism, specificity, and transfer.”

Elizabeth Rayne is a creature who writes. Her work has appeared in Popular Mechanics, Ars Technica, SYFY WIRE, Space.com, Live Science, Den of Geek, Forbidden Futures and Collective Tales. You’ll find our roundup of sales below. Manufacturers selling directly from their own sites come first. Retailers follow, along with the brand promotions they’re carrying.

#6295. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds

The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).

Illustrated by Danielle Dufault, © Danielle Dufault, 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

More than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

This chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston says. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

G.F. Funston et al. Fruit-eating adaptations in a Late Cretaceous oviraptorosaur (Theropoda). Nature Communications. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-78343-w

#6294. This week: Lame duck kicks off with Hegseth impeachment effort

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”

Departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

"We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the new Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

“One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., said in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.

Think that cows are the king of flatulence? There's another animal that likely blows the competition away.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Flatology, the study of flatulence, sounds more like a joke than a serious scientific discipline. But studying farts actually helps biologists understand an animal's diet and digestion.

We know that a host of creatures ‪—​​ from whales, to snakes, to sloths ‪— pass gas. But do we know which animal is the top tooter? Experts told Live Science the answer is blowing in the wind.

"Getting quantitative measurements for farts per animal is pretty difficult," Nick Caruso, a data scientist and co-author of '"Does It Fart?: The Definitive Field Guide to Animal Flatulence'' (Quercus Publishing, 2017), told Live Science in an email.

What we can do is hypothesize using the data we do have. Expelled gas is made partially of methane, so comparing methane emissions produced by different species may provide a clue. However, this method does have limitations, experts pointed out.

Researchers measure the methane animals produce by placing them inside respiration chambers, then inserting a capsule into the stomach that releases a tracer gas while strapping them with a harness that samples their breath. Alternatively, they capture their breath at stations where they feed or are milked.

Research points to livestock, especially cows, as major methane emitters. A recent report puts their total methane emissions at 117 teragrams per year. (One teragram is equal to 1 billion kilograms, or 2.2 billion pounds.) A buildup of cow-generated methane gas even caused a dairy shed in Germany to explode. However, contrary to what many people believe, the "overwhelming majority" of methane emissions from livestock is released through burping, not flatulence, Ermias Kebreab, a professor of animal science at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science in an email.

The reason comes down to where in the gut the gas is made. Herbivores can't break down plant material on their own; they rely on microbes in their guts to ferment it, and that fermentation releases gases such as methane and carbon dioxide, Dr. Marcus Clauss, head of research and co-director of the Clinic for Zoo Animals, Exotic Pets and Wildlife at the University of Zurich, told Live Science in an email. Some of this gas is absorbed into the bloodstream and exhaled. The rest tends to leave by the nearest exit ‪—‬ animals that ferment their food toward the front of the digestive tract mostly burp it out, while those that ferment it toward the back mostly pass it as wind, Clauss explained.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Cows and other ruminants ‪(such as buffalo, sheep, goats and camels)‬ ferment their food in a chamber called the rumen, located near the front of the digestive system, so most of the methane they produce is through belching, Matthew Hayek, an associate professor of environmental studies at New York University, told Live Science in an email.

So if it's not cows, which animal is the top farter based on their methane emissions? The best candidates are hindgut fermenters ‪—‬ herbivores that digest plant matter in the large intestine (the hindgut). Meat eaters, by contrast, typically produce far less methane than herbivores do, Clauss said.

Are cows really the top contender for animal farts?

One possible contender are termites, which break down wood and grass in their hindguts. Their global population is estimated to be around 27 quadrillion (that's 15 zeros) individuals, and they collectively emit 10 teragrams of methane per year.

But, per individual, the title might go to horses. According to a 2019 report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, horses have the highest methane emissions among hindgut fermenters — around 40 pounds (18 kg) of methane per horse each year.

However, Clauss is skeptical. "The ranking of horse as highest is only because it has been measured," he told Live Science in an email. "But there are so many hindgut fermenters not measured, like rhino ... Who knows?"

If we consider methane emissions per unit of bodyweight, the nutria (Myocastor coypus) ‪—‬ an herbivorous, semiaquatic rodent ‪—‬ would have higher methane emissions than the horse, Clauss said.

Clauss also questioned the accuracy of using methane emissions data as an indicator of flatulence. "There is some methane in flatulence, but most likely the majority of methane produced by an animal is exhaled, i.e. it goes via blood to the lungs," he said.

So until scientists figure out how to measure animal farts, any ranking remains speculative. For now, scientists have developed ways to track intestinal gas in people, including swallowable electronic capsules that measure gases inside the gut and clip-on underwear sensors that detect hydrogen in farts.

Methane is a particularly potent greenhouse gas when released into the atmosphere, and the quantities that large herds of cows and other ruminants emit through burping are enough to contribute to climate change. Indeed, scientists are experimenting with ways to reduce methane emissions from cattle — for example, by adding seaweed to their diet.

But animal flatulence is not a major contributor to global methane increases, Hayek said.

Even methane emissions from termite flatulence, while large, do not have an impact, Stefan Arndt, a professor of physiological and ecosystem ecology at the University of Melbourne in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "A large proportion of that methane is then consumed by methanotrophic bacteria in the soil," he said. These bacteria use methane as an energy source, thereby reducing the net methane emissions from termites substantially.

"Their emissions are part of the natural cycle of methane that has always been there for millennia," Arndt added. "The increasing methane concentrations in the atmosphere that are leading to climate change are caused by humans."

#6291. Can robots save Earth orbit?

There are likely fewer satellites in Earth orbit right now than there will be at any point for the rest of your life.

It’s a sobering thought. The threats from our ever-more-crowded skies are well documented: light pollution from megaconstellations, aluminum oxide accumulating in the upper atmosphere as satellites burn up on reentry, and the possibility of a chain reaction of collisions and debris that could render entire orbital regions unusable for generations — to name a few. So what can we do?

One possible solution lies in the emerging satellite-servicing industry — also known as in-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing (ISAM). Satellites can be refueled, repaired, and repositioned — extending their operational lives and reducing the need to launch replacements. The technology has been demonstrated and the industry is expanding.

But unlocking the potential of this technology will also require a sea change in how space is regulated, experts say. “Servicing needs to go hand in hand with regulation to be effective,” says Jonas Bahlmann, a doctoral researcher at the University of Luxembourg who studies space sustainability. Some regulations may need to be eased or eliminated, and others created in order to incentivize the industry to tackle the problem. If done right, new regulations could create a win-win — slowing the crowding in Earth orbit while boosting the bottom line of the launch providers, but it’s a problem without easy answers.

The first spacecraft to undergo repair in space was NASA’s Skylab space station, launched on May 14, 1973. During launch, the station lost its micrometeoroid shield. Designed to protect the spacecraft from impacts, the shield also shaded Skylab from the Sun. Without the shield, the craft wasn’t habitable for human occupants as internal temperatures could become unbearably high.

On May 25, 1973, NASA sent up the station’s first crew with newly designed hardware to replace the shield. Across a series of spacewalks, the crew installed the nylon and Mylar parasol, successfully completing the first on-orbit repair.

Brian Weeden, who directs commercial space research at the Aerospace Corporation’s Center for Space Policy and Strategy, says over the decades since, ISAM has gone through three distinct waves.

The first wave rode the space shuttle. Astronauts on a shuttle mission serviced the Solar Maximum Mission in 1984 and, across five shuttle missions between 1993 and 2009, repaired and upgraded the Hubble Space Telescope. Initially, Weeden tells Astronomy, the shuttle was seen “as a vehicle you could reuse; you could do servicing of satellites and [these] kinds of things.” Ultimately “that never really panned out,” he concludes. Each shuttle launch cost $1 billion, two orbiters were lost in the Challenger and Columbia disasters, and the entire program was eventually retired in 2011.

The second wave, which began in the mid-2000s, swapped astronauts for robots. DARPA’s Orbital Express mission showed spacecraft could service each other autonomously. In 2007, the mission’s servicing satellite ASTRO transferred hydrazine fuel and installed a battery for its counterpart satellite NEXTSat while the two were in low-Earth orbit (LEO). Several other experiments followed, like NASA’s Robotic Refueling Missions on the International Space Station (ISS), which demonstrated refueling of satellites not designed for servicing and advanced cryogenic fuel storage across its three phases beginning in 2011. Still, these second-wave missions were more technology demonstrations than a business model.

“But then about 10 years ago, you started to see this … third wave of real interest,” Weeden says. These new missions draw on three basic servicing tasks — refueling a satellite, repositioning its orbit, and repairing or upgrading its hardware.

Virginia-based aerospace and defense contractor Northrop Grumman became the first commercial firm to service a satellite when its Mission Extension Vehicle-1 (MEV-1) launched in 2019 to extend the life of an aging communications satellite in geosynchronous Earth orbit (GEO). Rather than transferring propellant, MEV-1 docked directly to the satellite and became its new thruster. MEV-2 followed, docking in 2021 with a similar communications satellite.

In March 2021, Astroscale — a satellite-servicing company headquartered in Tokyo — launched ELSA-d, a mission aimed in the other direction: moving a spacecraft lower to speed its reentry for debris removal. ELSA-d demonstrated that a robotic spacecraft could capture an object in orbit, the core capability any debris-removal service depends on. The mission was aborted early due to thruster issues before it could attempt to capture an uncontrolled, tumbling object.

That same year, Orbit Fab, a satellite-refueling company based in Lafayette, Colorado, launched Tanker-001 Tenzing: a technology demonstration that they call the first commercial fuel depot in orbit. Tenzing is a small, 77-pound (35 kilograms), microwave-sized satellite that houses a full tank of storable high-test peroxide fuel and Orbit Fab’s proprietary refueling interface, which is known as the Rapidly Attachable Fluid Transfer Interface (RAFTI). Tenzing has not been used to refuel any satellites, but is one step on Orbit Fab’s journey to make in-orbit refueling routine. The company is targeting 2026 for its first refueling missions and envisions an architecture where shuttles deliver fuel from depots like Tenzing to customers in orbit.

In September 2025, NASA contracted Katalyst Space Technologies, a small robotic-servicing company based in Flagstaff, Arizona, to send its LINK spacecraft to rendezvous with the aging Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and reposition the X-ray telescope into a higher, safer orbit. The mission launched in July 2026. Unfortunately, the craft experienced control issues after launch, and on Aug. 19, NASA announced the mission would not attempt to capture Swift.

Perhaps the most capable example of a third wave ISAM spacecraft is Northrop Grumman’s Mission Robotic Vehicle (MRV). Launched on July 21 of this year, the spacecraft is billed as a next-generation on-orbit servicing vehicle. It features robotic arms, developed with DARPA funding, that can inspect a malfunctioning satellite, swap components, and install upgrades. It also carries three Mission Extension Pods (MEP) that it can attach to satellites as cheaper alternatives to a full MEV. Once the first three MEPs are deployed, replacements will launch and rendezvous with MRV. A built-in standardized refueling port will ensure MRV can sustain its mission for at least a decade. The spacecraft will arrive in geosynchronous orbit in 2027 to perform its first demonstrations.

Unlike the two waves of on-orbit servicing before it, Weeden says this one hasn’t lost steam. Where earlier eras produced isolated demonstrations, this wave has laid the foundation for an industry that may soon see companies competing and selling ISAM services. A 2026 study led by Igor Levchenko of the University of Milano-Bicocca in Italy and published in the journal npj Space Exploration agrees. They project ISAM turning into a sustained economic sector by 2030.

The study, however, highlights a gap in the industry. So far, projects have been aimed at servicing large, expensive satellites in geosynchronous orbit whose value justifies the cost. But the region with the most pressing concerns about debris, overcrowding, and atmospheric pollution is low Earth orbit — the domain of small, cheap satellites like SpaceX’s Starlink.

SpaceX has handled its debris problem without much need for ISAM. Only two of the roughly 12,000 launched Starlink satellites have broken apart in orbit, each producing mere tens of tracked debris objects. That debris, says Weeden, will “come down within 20 years.” SpaceX designs Starlink satellites for a five-year lifespan and places them in orbits that decay naturally within five years. This is done in part to comply with a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) rule that mandates operators to deorbit satellites within five years of the end of their mission — a rule intended to keep Earth orbit free of debris. But this same replacement cycle also means burning up satellites every few years, putting more aluminum oxide into the atmosphere.

Some forms of satellite servicing in LEO are well within current technological capabilities. But right now, there’s little incentive. Launching a new Starlink satellite is cheaper than servicing an old one, and no regulations are pushing launch providers to do otherwise.

What’s needed is a change in the rules — but that’s easier said than done. The U.S. accounts for over half of all annual rocket launches, giving U.S. regulators substantial influence over LEO. Yet U.S. regulations have lagged behind a rapidly growing industry, say analysts. U.S. commercial space activity runs through three federal agencies: the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) licenses launches, the FCC licenses the radio spectrum satellites use, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) licenses satellites that gather data about Earth from space.

That framework dates to the 1980s, built around the industry as it existed then. Newly emerging sectors have shaken things up. “Satellite servicing [doesn’t] easily fit into those existing three buckets,” Weeden says. There is no agency explicitly charged with authorizing servicing missions. Lawmakers have been working to update the framework for decades, but progress has been slow. Weeden calls it a wicked problem, a term from public-policy theory for issues with no fixed win condition.

“It’s complex. It’s never-ending,” he says. If left as-is, Weeden warns, the regulatory ambiguity could scare off investors. Made too restrictive, it could delay missions or push companies to relocate.

While U.S. regulations are stalled in the 20th century, other spacefaring nations have taken steps forward. The U.K., Japan, New Zealand, and France have built or are currently building licensing frameworks for servicing missions. If the U.S. were to follow suit and create regulatory clarity for commercial space activity, those new rules could be leveraged toward sustainability efforts — something that’s already happening in Europe. The European Space Agency (ESA) is pushing for an explicit sustainability policy goal — the Zero Debris Approach, which aims to limit new debris in Earth and lunar orbit by 2030.

As a step toward that, ESA has approved Europe’s first debris-removal mission, ClearSpace-1, which is scheduled for a 2029 launch to capture and deorbit a defunct Earth-observation satellite.

But missions like ClearSpace-1 on their own aren’t enough. While deorbiting space junk eases the crowding in LEO, it does so at the atmosphere’s expense. To address the full suite of problems, sustainability experts argue new regulations will have to incentivize an entirely new way of doing business in space.

In space policy and industry circles, people speak of a circular space economy — a concept that reframes spacecraft’s linear life-cycle. “In circular-economy terms,” Bahlmann says, “we … speak of narrowing, slowing, and closing resource loops.” Design satellites to require fewer resources, keep them in service longer, and recover the materials from retired hardware.

The circular space economy is not possible without regulatory reform, Bahlmann says. In his view, outdated regulations, like the FCC’s five-year deorbit rule, reinforce the linear model.

Bahlmann thinks new regulations should incentivize companies for building satellites with standardized interfaces and modular components that make future servicing possible in the first place rather than restricting them or perpetuating the build, use, dispose status-quo.

According to Bahlmann, this also requires clearer international rules covering who can authorize a mission, who’s liable if something goes wrong, who owns a piece of hardware once it’s dead, and who’s allowed to touch it. Without answers to those questions, Bahlmann says, “it will be difficult to develop a circular space economy if technically serviceable hardware cannot legally be touched.”

A 2025 study published in Journal of Spacecraft and Rockets found, using game theory, that removing dangerous debris already saves operators more in avoided collision risk and tracking costs than the cleanup itself costs.

The problem is that remediators bear the entire cost while operators keep the savings. The study proposes a regulatory fix — a third-party body collects fees from the operators who benefit and pays out to the companies doing the cleanup — win-win.

Another possibility is implementing a so-called international “orbital-use fee.” In a 2020 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, economists modeled what happens if operators paid an annual fee for every satellite they keep in orbit. Each satellite poses a threat to other satellites through the potential cost of a collision — the more satellites launched, the higher that collective cost climbs. The orbital-use fee calculates the dollar value of that risk and charges it back to the operator each year, similar to a carbon tax. This lowers collision risk for everyone. And, the researchers found it could more than quadruple the industry’s long-run value, from around $600 billion to $3 trillion. Another win-win.

These kinds of incentives could also open the door to entirely new ISAM markets. One such example comes from Levchenko’s team. They propose something they call small mission extension vehicles, or SMEVs: cheap, universal, mass-produced servicers built to service many satellites through simple, standardized tasks like swapping interchangeable parts.

The technology to build SMEVs exists. The problem is cost. SMEVs only make sense if they’re cheaper than replacing satellites. Bringing down costs and making SMEVs a reality could be incentivized through orbital-use fees or other regulatory changes championed by proponents of the circular space economy.

“My impression is that the industry will continue to grow and that we will launch more, not less, year by year,” Bahlmann says. In fact, new regulations put in place to incentivize servicing over disposal may encourage operators to launch more satellites. Bahlmann offers increases in fuel efficiency as an analogy: “Driving becomes cheaper per kilometer, which can encourage people to drive more and partially offset the expected savings.”

But he believes growth and sustainability can coexist. “The circular space economy is not about degrowth, but about enabling growth in a way that creates economic and social value without compromising the environment,” says Bahlmann. The question, he adds, is what that growth looks like. “Without the right design choices and incentives, more efficient services could simply enable more activity and ultimately add to congestion rather than help us avoid a potentially catastrophic outcome.”

Wicked as the problem may be, something’s got to give. Bahlmann puts it plainly: “For a long time, the linear approach worked well. We did not have to think much about debris. But it is becoming increasingly clear that we cannot continue like this forever.”

#6290. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

This story was updated on November 13, 2026, to correct the spelling of Katy Croff Bell's name, and to correct the location of the corals mentioned in the story from the Indian to the Pacific Ocean.

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6289. ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, said she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”
