#6223. The Best Places to Go in North America and the Caribbean in 2027

How we choose where to travel next can vary greatly. Sometimes it’s a long-held fantasy, originally spurred by a book or a movie; other times, a trusted recommendation from a discerning friend. Increasingly, it’s a single image encountered online—the curve of a sandy cove, the tangled streets of a medieval old town, or a terrace set aglow at golden hour—that prompts us to hit Save. Our annual list of the best places to go takes a more considered approach, pairing the where with the why now. When it comes to the best places to go in North America—a confoundingly diverse set of landscapes that spans 9.5 million square miles—that motivation feels especially relevant: a recognition that the way we travel matters as much as where we go.

Consider Jamaica’s South Coast: In the wake of Hurricane Melissa, you can support communities leading their own recovery, and still enjoy the turquoise waters, farm-to-table dinners, and design-forward boutique stays as rewards along the way. Meanwhile, tiny and culturally rich Curaçao is riding a wave of attention as a FIFA World Cup darling, and new flights and resorts showcase the island’s equally enticing on-the-ground energy. In Canada’s British Columbia, Clayoquot remains a secluded sweep of pristine wilderness. Here a new floating lodge owned by the Ahousaht First Nation is creating novel ways to experience this extraordinary landscape while engaging more deeply with its culture: Walk beneath ancient cedars. Soak in geothermal pools. Listen, learn, and slow down.

Then there are the places revealing new dimensions beyond what first put them on the map. Oregon’s Willamette Valley, beloved by Pinot Noir devotees, is melding a varied and sophisticated food scene with its farm-first, sustainability-minded ethos. In Taos, New Mexico, an arts and cultural renaissance is unfolding against a backdrop of high-altitude adventure, and standout new restaurants will make sure you’re well-fueled for all the wandering.

Each destination on this list comes with expert-backed picks for where to stay, what to eat, and what to do, so you can start planning every aspect of your trip immediately. Follow us into 2027 as we continue to share more about these journeys with on-the-ground reporting and enough inspiration to fill your calendar. See you on the road! —Arati Menon

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: wild coastal landscapes and a groundbreaking new Indigenous-owned luxury lodge

The land and waters of UNESCO-designated biosphere Clayoquot Sound have been stewarded by the First Nations for generations.

Kayaking, whale-watching, and hiking excursions can be coordinated directly through the lodges.

Clayoquot Sound has long drawn adventurous travelers to Vancouver Island’s wild western edge—a maze of forested islands, secluded inlets, and old-growth rainforests. But now, Indigenous-owned hospitality is giving this remote luxury escape a deeper sense of place, shaped by the First Nations that have stewarded its lands and waters for generations.

A UNESCO-designated biosphere region spanning nearly 864,868 acres of land and sea, Clayoquot Sound is already home to the much-lauded Clayoquot Wilderness Lodge. But the July 2026 opening of Wahous Wilderness Lodge in secluded Quait Bay introduces a different kind of high-end stay. Owned and operated by the Ahousaht First Nation, the 16-room floating lodge and four forest cabins were reacquired in 2022 by the Nation’s hereditary chiefs through the Maaqutusiis Hahoulthee Stewardship Society (MHSS). Guests are welcomed into Ahousaht territory with tide-to-table dining, a shoreline spa, and a ceremonial welcome in the cedar longhouse. A stay begins and ends in the longhouse, concluding with a traditional klup-chus-tapčas, or salmon barbecue, in an evening that brings together food, storytelling, and cultural exchange in a final gathering rooted in Ahousaht tradition.

The three-Michelin-key Clayoquot Wilderness Lodge is evolving too. Set on 600 acres at the mouth of the Bedwell River, the off-grid retreat is known for its 25 safari-style canvas tents, cedar-plank boardwalks, and wilderness adventures. Newer experiences in 2026 include after-dark bioluminescence kayaking, a floating sauna, and a guided walk across Flores Island through Ahousaht territory.

New experiences and places to stay aside, Clayoquot Sound remains remote enough to preserve its deep sense of seclusion. This vast coastal labyrinth is best explored by water and on foot: Paddle between forested islands, walk beneath ancient cedars on Meares Island, hike Flores Island’s remote Wildside Trail, or soak in the geothermal pools at Hot Springs Cove. From March to October, join a whale-watching trip to spot orcas, humpbacks, or grey whales. Elsewhere, wildlife may simply find you: Black bears forage along the shoreline at low tide, and sea otters paddle through the inlets. Some excursions can be arranged directly through the lodges, while Tofino-based operators, such as Ahousaht-owned Ahous Adventures or Tofino Water Taxi, make the wider sound accessible. —Ashleigh Stewart

Go for: an island culture bursting with color, rhythm, and Blue Wave energy

Curaçao’s UNESCO-listed capital, Willemstad, is a vibrant blend of European, African, and Caribbean influences.

New nonstop flights from major US airports include American Airlines’ seasonal Chicago O’Hare route from December to April.

In 2026 the tiny Caribbean island of Curaçao made history as the least-populated nation to ever compete in the FIFA World Cup and stole hearts along the way. But the exuberant “Blue Wave” was just a taste of the vibrant energy humming across this 171-square-mile Dutch Caribbean island. In Willemstad, the UNESCO-listed capital, Curaçao’s multicultural spirit—rooted in European, African, and Caribbean influences—is on vivid display. Pastel Dutch colonial buildings house eclectic pubs, boutique galleries, and jazz cafés reverberating with tumba, a blend of Afro-Caribbean and Latin jazz.

By the end of 2026, Curaçao will welcome two new resorts that promise buzzy stays with access to all of the above. The adults-only, 305-key Pyrmont Curaçao, an Autograph Collection All-Inclusive Resort will occupy a beachfront stretch in Willemstad’s bohemian Pietermaai neighborhood, a walkable historic district with a side of nightlife. Here, they will reimagine one 19th-century Neoclassical mansion as a spa, and another as one of six restaurants and bars. In the quieter northwest, which is home to some of the island’s most scenic beaches and national parks, the 297-room Tui Blue Curaçao will feature swim-up suites, six Caribbean restaurants, and a private beach on aquamarine Santa Martha Bay, with daily yoga sessions on the sand. In more good news, the island is also easier to reach than ever before: New nonstop flights from major US airports include American Airlines’ seasonal route that runs from December through April from Chicago O’Hare, launched in late 2025. —Jessica Puckett

Go for: an off-the-beaten-path, community-focused escape—and a chance to support tourism’s recovery after Hurricane Melissa.

South Coast's Treasure Beach has become known for its boutique properties such as Jakes Hotel, founded by local artist Sally Henzell.

This October marks the one-year anniversary of Hurricane Melissa, the strongest and costliest hurricane to ever hit Jamaica. With most of the damage centered in the west and southwest of the island, Jamaica’s South Coast has been at the forefront of recovery efforts—and is now welcoming travelers back with open arms.

Jamaica is so much more than reggae and resorts, and there’s never been a better time for more meaningful travel to one of its most under-the-radar coastal regions. The best-known South Coast area, Treasure Beach, is a mellow seaside town known for its black sand beaches and slow-paced bohemian lifestyle. Every other year, it’s also host to the Calabash International Literary Festival, the largest in the Caribbean (in 2027 it will be held in May). The beaches here are lined with colorful guesthouses and design-forward boutique stays like Jakes Hotel, a beloved family-run establishment founded by local artist Sally Henzell. Further up the coast, Bluefields Bay Villas & Suites is another family-run gem that reopened in February 2026. For a resort stay, Sandals South Coast will reopen in November 2026 following a multimillion-dollar renovation.

It’s also become easier for travelers to pair the beachy South Coast with the lush hills of St. Elizabeth Parish—Jamaica’s breadbasket. The island’s agriculture industry took the biggest hit from the hurricane, prompting Jakes Hotel to double down on its agro-tourism offerings. In March, the hotel launched farm tours and monthly full-moon farm-to-table dinners for guests; its nonprofit arm also provides direct cash grants and equipment vouchers to farmers in the region.

For travelers planning a longer trip, the drive between Negril and Treasure Beach is one of Jamaica’s most scenic. Along the way, stop at the natural swimming pools at YS Falls, sample Jamaican street food beneath the shaded archway of Bamboo Avenue (don’t skip Middle Quarters’ famous peppered shrimp), and take a dip in the turquoise waters of Bluefields Bay. If you have a few days to spare, continue driving east to Kingston, the urban epicenter of Jamaican nightlife and culture. —Hannah Towey

Go for: Tennessee’s other music city whose evolving arts scene is going big

The riverfront Memphis Flyway, an elevated walkway in Tom Lee Park, opened June 2026.

The walkway has become an ideal spot for bird-watchers that intersects with several major migratory routes.

The city of Memphis is best known as a cradle for all things low and slow, from the city’s signature hickory-smoked ribs to the moody numbers emanating from the blues clubs on Beale Street. But the west Tennessean cultural icon also knows how to pick up the tempo, and in 2027 its revitalized arts scene will be in full swing.

As the state’s largest majority-Black city, Memphis is showing off its rich cultural tapestry with the back-and-better-than-ever Memphis Art Museum—the state’s oldest and largest. Facilities reopen in December 2026 at a reimagined three-acre campus located downtown. The new legroom includes a 10,000-square-foot courtyard and a sprawling rooftop sculpture garden. But the real pièce de résistance is what’s on the inside: Inaugural exhibitions revisit and subvert history, from “Rhapsodies in Black,” an examination of the interplay between jazz and Black American abstraction, to “Making Beauty: Hooks Brothers Studio, 1907–1984,” a look back on Hook Brothers, a legendary photography studio that documented Black life in Memphis from 1907 until 1979.

Long-anticipated renovations to the National Civil Rights Museum—including five interactive galleries dedicated to addressing the structural issues of poverty, education, housing, gender equality, and nonviolence—debuted earlier this May. The Metal Museum, one of the few institutions in the world dedicated to the craft, also celebrated a grand reopening in September.

For a breath of fresh air, the riverfront Memphis Flyway, an elevated walkway in Tom Lee Park, opened this June—an ideal spot for bird-watchers that intersects with several major migratory routes. Evenings are well spent at the newest venues in Tennessee’s second music city, like the 4,500-seat Grind City Amp, which opened in April 2026, followed by the intimate vinyl room at Satellite Music Hall in September.

Memphis’s food and hotel scenes also bring high notes to back it all up. Michelin’s inaugural American South edition honored five of the city’s restaurants, including farm-to-table Italian restaurant Hog & Hominy, which nabbed a Bib Gourmand. And when it comes to hospitality, in 2027 Memphis is in with the new thanks to projects like Cooper Hotel, an art-filled boutique set to join the thriving midtown Arts District. —Kat Chen

Go for: a mountain road trip through New England’s wild side

The White Mountains region comprises of nearly 800,000 acres including White Mountain National Forest, which stretches across central and northern New Hampshire and slightly into western Maine.

If you want a New England trip where the scenery does all the talking, look to New Hampshire. The Granite State has long played second fiddle to its more famous neighbors, but that’s part of its appeal: Dense with forests, winding mountain roads, glassy lakes, and small towns, it’s wilder than coastal New England, less manicured than Vermont’s resort towns, and gloriously road-trip friendly. At its heart is the White Mountains, a roughly 800,000-acre region of high peaks, and White Mountain National Forest, which stretches across central and northern New Hampshire and slightly into western Maine.

The region is getting harder to overlook, not least of all because lodgings are getting much more attractive. Under Canvas White Mountains opened on 86 acres in the quaint river town of Dalton in June 2026 with 45 safari-style tents, including stargazer tents with cutouts for gazing up at the night sky. In the scenic Monadnock region, The Inn at Hancock, New Hampshire’s oldest continuously operating inn, has reopened after a three-year restoration with 15 individually designed suites. In Bretton Woods, with grand-hotel history and big mountain views, the iconic Omni Mount Washington Resort completed its major reimagining of its historic rooms and dining in July 2026.

And the food scene has its own unique momentum: Born-and-bred Dover chef Evan Hennessey of Stages became New Hampshire’s first winner of the James Beard Best Chef: Northeast honor in 2026; his newer Topolino brings his Mediterranean-inspired dishes to a more casual setting. Make the trip to Seven Birches Winery in Lincoln for European-style classics and New England ciders enjoyed on a vineyard; it’s located within the recently renovated Riverwalk Resort, tucked away on sprawling Loon Mountain. Add a stately stay at seaside Portsmouth’s new Treadwell Mansion, in a Federal-style brick home, and you have a circuit that makes the Granite State feel both classic and freshly worth discovering. —Jessica Chapel

Go for: world-class wine and a meteorically rising culinary scene with small-town vibes

Restaurants such as Michelin-starred Alea Bakery and Cafe have cemented Willamette Valley's farm-first culinary scene.

South of Portland, Willamette Valley is Oregon's premier wine region—but also a mecca for truffle foraging and coastal pursuits.

Just south of Portland, Oregon’s premier wine region has attracted Pinot Noir devotees since 1985, when the valley’s signature grape beat French Burgundies in a blind tasting and stunned the world. Now winemakers are also earning international acclaim for Chardonnay and dialing in highly regarded traditional-method sparkling wine.

McMinnville is also adding refined lodging to the mix. Piquette, a 17-room boutique hotel, is slated to open on vibrant Alpine Avenue in early 2027. Following will be Marriott’s AC Retreat at Evergreen, which will offer vineyard views, a pool, and a wine bar. In Carlton, Shaughnessy’s team opened Lucky Duck, a two-bedroom rental in the small town’s original bank complete with a Hayward-stocked fridge. The result is an increasingly ambitious and food-focused wine destination that remains refreshingly unpretentious. —Rebecca Toy

Go for: a vibrant culinary scene that puts fresh spins on familiar flavors in a long-loved beach city

Beyond its beaches and robust surf culture, San Diego's restaurants—new and old—are redefining its culinary identity.

Sunny San Diego’s beautiful blue-water beaches have long lured laid-back surfers, while its world-class zoo has created generations of conservation-minded kids. But only recently has America’s Finest City emerged as a culinary mecca where savvy food lovers come in search of their next great meal.

In the seaside community of La Jolla, long home to some of the county’s foundational restaurants, seasoned local chefs and a new guard are making their mark. Consider native chef Travis Swikard of the lauded Cal-Med restaurant Callie, known for dishes like juicy Aleppo chicken and smoky harissa-grilled lamb chops. His sophomore spot, Fleurette, opened at the end of 2025 with a modern French Provençal cuisine that’s built around California ingredients—think Dover sole meunière amandine and buttery soft scrambled duck eggs with San Diego uni. Nearby at Michelin-starred Lucien, in the heart of downtown, a fresh cohort of Per Se alums crafts an intricate tasting menu that celebrates local farms and fishermen. A 20-minute drive north, in Carmel Valley, chef William Bradley’s recently redesigned Addison offers a contemporary Cali tasting menu. The three-Michelin-starred destination, housed in the Fairmont Grand Del Mar, just celebrated its 20th anniversary with the launch of a new champagne lounge—so slip in for a glass before dinner. If fast-fine dining is more your vibe, head to Encinitas, where Chick & Hawk serves spicy fried chicken sandwiches and craft cocktails in a space that pays homage to Southern California’s skate and surf culture of the ’80s and ’90s—which is fitting, given that skateboarding legend Tony Hawk is a partner. For a more intimate, upscale affair, head about 15 minutes up the 101 to idyllic Carlsbad, where the 22-seater Lilo serves a seafood-heavy tasting menu from chef Eric Bost, an LA transplant who has helped shape the city’s dining scene. But it’s not just the flashy new spots that make San Diego’s dining scene great. Barrio Logan’s legendary Las Cuatro Milpas relocated a few blocks away earlier in 2026 after nearly a century in business. While we miss the OG location, we’re happy to report the flour tortillas are still worth the journey.

You’ll need somewhere to rest between all those meals. In Coronado, the historic Hotel del Coronado announced a $550 million restoration in the summer of 2025, while the 31-room Baby Grand is its flashy maximalist foil. And over in Carlsbad the chic new Hotel Solea, Autograph Collection is within walking distance of Legoland. If that’s your draw, know that United Airlines started operating out of its local airport earlier this year. —Omar Mamoon

Go for: pristine blue water, mountains, and a new wave of boutique hotels and world-class restaurants

Despite being a long-beloved weekend getaway in Canada, Simcoe County has flown under the radar for those outside the province seeking a culinary coastal getaway outside of ski season.

New to North America’s 50 Best list, The Pine's husband-and-wife team put a spin on fine dining with dishes like a Shanghai-style lamb schnitzel served with a black-garlic-infused eggplant purée.

Canada will always be associated with natural beauty: the Rocky Mountains of the west, the rugged coastline of the Maritimes, and the otherworldly fjords of Newfoundland. Only recently have people started looking closer to the middle of the country for their dose of outdoor adventure. Ontario, specifically the Simcoe and Grey County regions just a couple of hours northwest of Toronto, has long been a beloved weekend getaway for city folk—but has flown under the radar for those outside the province.

Until recently, you most likely ended up here for a ski trip at Blue Mountain resort or as a guest at a friend’s cottage, as there was little in the way of notable accommodation. But new hotels have popped up in the last few years: starting with the understatedly luxe The Dorchester hotel in 2022, followed by the hip and modern Somewhere Inn Collingwood in 2024, and, most recently, in July 2026, the nine-room Leeward House in the historic town of Thornbury.

The region is anchored by the beauty of Georgian Bay’s Caribbean-like waters and its rugged cliffs—a great place for swimming, boating, and caving in the summer, and complementing Blue Mountain’s Stay and Ski lodging-and-lift-ticket packages in the winter. However, if outdoor adventure isn’t your thing and your palate tends to dictate the itinerary, it has plenty to tempt, with a growing community of globally trained chefs bringing fresh energy to the local dining scene, while championing the producers and purveyors who define the region. Nowhere is this more evident than at The Pine, recently added to North America’s 50 Best list, where husband-and-wife team Jeremy and Cassie Austin are putting their spin on fine dining with a Chinese twist—expect dishes like a Shanghai-style lamb schnitzel served with a black-garlic-infused eggplant purée. They also opened seafood-focused Lore this June, where the menu features gussied-up tuna melts and playful, utterly delicious scallop nuggets. A scenic, 45-minute drive inland takes you to Down Home, where a weekly tasting menu places emphasis on produce from regenerative organic farms. There are plenty of casual but equally delicious options too, like Heart’s Tavern, where chef Teo Paul and partner Luke Wood bring a French bistro sensibility to a 19th-century farmhouse. Even the natural wine scene has found its way here with Chin Chin, a bar from which locals and visitors spill out onto sidewalk benches with glasses of wine and grazing boards stacked with freshly baked baguette and cheese. —Kyle Beechey

Go for: a mountain town meets cultural hotbed

Taos sits at the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo mountains, part of the New Mexico stretch of the Rockies.

Boutique ski resorts famed for deep powder, narrow chutes, and a roster of high-altitude summer thrills. A thousand years of Indigenous arts and culture in one of the West's longest continuously inhabited pueblos. A buzzy contemporary art scene encompassing visual arts, film, music, installation, and craft. These all combine to create a magnetism that has drawn visitors to Taos ever since a ragtag group of creatives descended on the scrappy mountain town to found the Taos Society of Artists in 1915.

The town’s pull is only getting stronger with a series of high-profile openings and reimaginations, from the unveiling of the spiffed-up historic Taos Plaza—its cultural and geographic center—this past summer to the anticipated fall 2027 opening of an ambitious Tribal Heritage Center. Occupying a 14-acre grant returning ancestral lands to the Taos Pueblo, the complex will feature a cultural center, restaurants, galleries, and a pueblo-inspired Marriott TownePlace Suites and Fairfield Inn & Suites. Also next year, the community observatory Cielo Centro, which will house the largest publicly accessible telescope in New Mexico, begins its phased opening with a 1,600-square-foot classroom building, an outdoor amphitheater, and an observation plaza. Recently, too, Hotel Willa, a 52-room motor lodge at the gateway to the Taos Arts District, has been retrofit as adobe-desert chic down to its sun-splashed pool, stargazing deck, gallery, and onsite art programming courtesy of the Paseo Project. Guests can shuttle to nearby ski areas in the hotel’s new electric Volkswagen ID.Buzz.

The best way to appreciate Taos’s role as a base camp for the surrounding Sangre de Cristo mountains is to drive the 84-mile Enchanted Circle Scenic Byway, or head straight for Taos Ski Valley, which debuted a new, modern triple-chairlift last year as part of a multimillion-dollar renovation. Family-friendly resort Angel Fire, which offers snow tubing and the only night-skiing in the state, has vastly expanded access with the high-capacity Angel Express lift, whisking up to 1,800 riders an hour at a speed of 1,000 feet per minute. This upcoming year will see the return of the beloved outdoor Paseo Festival, known for envelope-pushing installations and performance art, which took a pause in 2026 to reboot as a biennial event. The Taos Film Festival, which debuted in 2026, returns April 29 to May 2 at the Taos Center for the Arts.

The little town punches above its culinary weight, too. Make sure to check out the newly opened Dawn Butterfly, the first modern, full-service restaurant inside Taos Pueblo, where local Carpio J. Bernal Jr. serves up indigenous heritage dishes like slow-roasted bison and blue cornmeal with chokecherry sauce. Suchness specializes in unexpected juxtapositions like lamb loin with Moroccan tomato jam and smoked eggplant and rigatoni topped with a smoked carrot Bolognese and vegan ricotta. And for breakfast sample the wood-fired bialy-style bagels topped with wild-caught salmon at Tomorrow and Tomorrow, or indulge in brunch at Juliette in Hotel Willa, where the Dutch pancake is a standout. —Melanie Haiken

Go for: a seafood-forward wine country getaway—with elevated new wellness stays

The weathered granite mountains and rugged terrain of Valle de Guadalupe have greeted a new wave of hospitality offerings such as Mira Earth Studios.

When you come to a stop at the sole traffic light in Mexico’s Valle de Guadalupe, you can see weathered granite mountains and rugged, sun-drenched terrain unfold in every direction. This is the environment that nurtures Mexico’s premier wine region, which might still be young and pliable but produces the mineral Chenin Blanc, the historic misión, unconventional red blends, and the pitch-dark nebbiolo that have drawn savvy oenophiles for years. The region’s culinary offerings are just as compelling: When the Michelin Guide México debuted in 2024, the state of Baja California, anchored by Valle de Guadalupe, emerged as the second-most-decorated region behind Mexico City. All of this awaits less than an hour by car from the closest US–Mexico border crossing point—and it is aging like fine wine.

The 2026 edition of Mexico’s Michelin Guide spotlights several new restaurants, as well as esteemed ones. Damiana, which began as a pop-up and has since found a permanent home in the shade of trees at the Viñedos de la Reina winery, has energized the Valle with chef and co-owner Esteban Luis’s oceanic array of buttery spider crab croquettes, smoked Kumiai oysters, and bluefin tuna dressed with soy sauce then topped with gooseneck barnacle rings. Then there’s Olivea Farm to Table, led by chef Daniel Nates, which dazzles diners on an impressive farm tour that ends in the dining room, where plump mussels are steamed with saffron, and roasted aged duck is balanced by a pair of quenelles in an earthy blackberry sauce. Stalwarts like Animalón, a romantic campestre set under a 200-year-old live oak tree, and Lunario, in an intimate greenhouse-like building, have held on to their Michelin distinctions for innovative tasting menus—anchored in local seafood but also indigenous herbs and seasonal vegetables—that have helped define Baja California’s innovative cuisine.

A new wave of hospitality offerings have quietly opened in recent years to meet this moment. And their flavor here is consistent: sustainable hotels committed to preserving viticulture. The amenity-rich Mira Earth Studios offers a curated selection of local wines, a hot tub, and an infrared sauna in each of its 10 studio suites, which are made of earth and tucked into the hillside. Hike up to the pool for a feast of raw shellfish served with a mosaic of sauces at Mira Fireside by chef José Luis Hinostroza. In like manner, the Banyan Tree Veya, built by renowned Mexican architect Michel Rojkind, features a private plunge pool and 30 villas, each with its own wide terrace, that recede into the landscape. Overlooking the property is Amapola, a showcase restaurant that serves the property’s Pictograma wines and regional ingredients like grilled spot prawns, callo catarina (scallops), and grilled quail over fideos in a minimalist style, courtesy of Baja California chefs Benito Molina and Solange Muris.

There is more to come: Bruma Wine Estate—the hospitality juggernaut that houses iconic restaurants Fauna and Bruma Wine Garden, plus hotels Ático, Casa 8, and Casa Montaña—has a 62-room Montage Hotels and Resorts property targeted for 2028. Valle de Guadalupe has never been loud in its evolution, but with each passing year, it promises a richer experience. —Bill Esparza

#6222. The Sanctuary of a Healing God Was Lost for 1,800 Years. Archaeologists May Have Finally Found It.

A century of digs in Epidaurus reveals a sacred site where pilgrims flocked to honor the son of Apollo.

In the second century C.E., a traveler named Pausanias wrote about an open-air sacred precinct featuring statues of Asclepius—the Greek god of healing and the son of Apollo—and his wife, Epione, near the city center of Epidaurus. The only issue: Nobody knew the location. But now, a scholar at the University of Athens thinks there’s enough evidence to claim we’ve solved the 1,800-year-old mystery.

Vassilis Lambrinoudakis of the Department of History and Archaeology of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens pored over hundreds of years of research and concluded that a site in Epidaurus is the statue-filled spot Pausanias described.

Excavations started in Epidaurus in the early 1900s, and since 1974, hundreds of student archaeologists have painstakingly excavated in and around the city. Lambrinoudakis collated the research, noting that not only has he likely found the mystery location, but that cult worship of Asclepius took place at the site for longer than we knew about.

The oldest religious building in Epidaurus—dated to around 600 B.C.E.—features a structure with an underground chamber cut directly into the bedrock, likely part of early healing traditions. In Greek mythology, Asclepius took over his father Apollo’s role as a healer, and Epione was worshiped for her ability to help soothe pain. The ancient structure has a pebble-lined floor, walls coated in dark red plaster, and a circular basin built into the floor accessible by staircase. The bottoms of four amphorae are embedded in the bedrock floor. In the fourth century B.C.E., crews built a new circular building directly to the west, likely a “deliberate continuity of the same chthonic cult of Asclepius,” the university wrote in a translated statement.

Nearby, the teams found a ground-level altar made of limestone blocks that they believe is older than both buildings. Lambrinoudakis said the combination of the finds shows the cult likely dates to the seventh century B.C.E.

The structure served as a key gathering point in Epidaurus. Excavations revealed walls that created a processional route to and from the building, essentially an uncovered passageway for visitors. A large square in the center of the sanctuary features open space in front of the temple, a key functional element of the site.

“It could accommodate the throngs of pilgrims who arrived at the site to take part in the sacrificial offering to Asclepius, which was accompanied by a festive procession,” the university wrote. To the east, an altar and platforms included seating for prominent families who watched the sacrificial rituals.

Beneath Building K, excavators found an earlier structure from the early third century B.C.E. that sat on an unusually sturdy limestone foundation. The Roman building on top of it, which was rebuilt several times between the second and late fourth centuries C.E., has a central courtyard that probably had colonnades on at least three sides. The courtyard also has a gravel floor and a small basin made from reused marble pieces. In the building’s southwest corner, a large hall with a small basin or bath and a round room resembles spaces in other Epidaurus buildings that have been linked to the worship of Egyptian gods.

In the northwest corner of Building K, on a lower level, sits an unusual, nearly intact crypt that opens to the north. Along its west side, reused column pieces from an unknown earlier building form a three-part niche, and gaps in the wall behind it let sunlight stream in at midday. “The overall character of ‘K’ suggests that it may have been the site of a mystical cult, particularly during the late Roman period,” the university said, adding they were unable to define who—or what—the cult worshipped.

In the agora of ancient Epidaurus, just northwest of the city’s small theater, excavators had already uncovered a monumental fourth-century B.C.E. fountain complex. More recently, they found a large walled enclosure right next to it. Inside were small clay offerings that may once have hung from trees, a piece of a clay heating vessel, and a pottery fragment scratched with part of Asclepius’s name.

At the center of the enclosure, a well fed an underground pointed-arch tunnel that carried water to the fountain. Because water was central to the worship of Asclepius, the university says the offerings, the well, and the fountain together identify the site as the long-lost town sanctuary Pausanias described. Excavators also found a larger-than-life marble statue of a woman in the enclosure. Lambrinoudakis thinks it may be the statue of Epione that Pausanias saw, but without an inscription, he can’t be sure.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6221. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6219. 21 Best Places to Visit in December in the USA

We’ll never forget the first time we visited New York City in December. We’d seen it in movies, but standing there, seeing the Rockefeller Center tree all lit up for the first time, with skaters below and festive music in the air… it was pure magic.

But December travel isn’t just about snow and Santa. We’ve also spent the holidays escaping to the warmth, trading snow boots for flip-flops.

In fact, we’ve been to almost all 50 states and spent a lot of winters trying to find the most fun destinations and best weather. We’ve done so many road trips in the USA and flown almost everywhere, trying to find the best places to either escape the snow or enjoy the winter, you would think we are obsessed. And we want to share all of that knowledge with you.

If you’re looking for the perfect winter getaway, you have a clear choice: either lean into the winter magic or escape it completely. Are you dreaming of a warm-weather escape with sunshine and sand, or a storybook Christmas town that looks like a real-life snow globe?

Based on all those experiences, we’ve put together this list of our favourite places to visit. Whether you’re looking for a festive city, a snowy mountain, or a sunny beach, we’ll help you find the perfect spot.

Here is a quick look at some of the best places for a December getaway in the USA, from festive winter wonderlands to sunny escapes.

December is a month of pure magic and festive energy. It’s the perfect time to use up that last bit of vacation time for the year. The biggest draw is the distinct choice it offers: You can either dive head-first into a winter wonderland, complete with snow and holiday markets, or you can completely escape the cold weather and find yourself on a sunny beach. It’s a month of festive celebrations, incredible decorations, and finding the perfect atmosphere to end the year.

If you’re anything like us, sometimes the best gift in December is a break from the cold. Trust us, we know after living in Toronto, Canada. Those winters are brutal. These are our favourite spots to find sunshine and warm weather, where you can trade your winter coat for a light jacket or even a swimsuit.

We love the laid-back, quirky vibe of Key West, and it’s even more special in December. We have a great memory of biking around the island, seeing the historic inns draped in holiday lights, and then ending the day at Mallory Square for the sunset celebration. It’s a perfect escape from the cold.

Why Visit in December: This is the perfect time to visit. The summer humidity is gone, the weather is sunny and warm (often in the high 70s), and the risk of hurricanes is very low. The whole island is in a festive spirit, with unique events like the “Bight Before Christmas” boat parade.

Where to Stay: We recommend finding a guesthouse or inn in the historic Old Town to be close to the action.

We once went to a holiday luau in Ka’anapali, and it’s an experience we’ll never forget. You’re eating kalua pork and sipping a mai tai, watching a beautiful hula performance… and then Santa Claus arrives on an outrigger canoe. It was the perfect, uniquely Hawaiian way to get into the festive spirit.

Why Visit in December: You get tropical weather, festive holiday luaus, and it’s the official start of the humpback whale watching season. Be aware that this is a popular time, especially around Christmas, so prices can be high and you’ll need to book in advance.

Where to Stay: Look to the resorts in Wailea or Ka’anapali for a classic Maui experience.

We’ll always remember snorkeling the underwater trail at Trunk Bay in St. John. The water was so calm and clear, and seeing all the colourful fish felt a world away from the snow back home. That’s the magic of a Caribbean trip in December, and the USVI makes it so easy for American travelers.

Why Visit in December: It’s the start of the dry season, with fantastic weather and warm, clear water. You get a full-on tropical, warm-weather Christmas experience, all without needing a passport.

Where to Stay: You can choose from large resorts in St. Thomas or more eco-friendly villas and lodges in St. John.

We were not prepared for how magical St. Augustine is in December. We took one of the Old Town trolley tours at night, and seeing the entire historic city, from the old Spanish architecture to the palm trees, draped in millions of white lights… it was breathtaking. It’s a holiday light display unlike any other.

Why Visit in December: The famous “Nights of Lights” festival. The entire city is illuminated, and the mild Florida weather is perfect for walking around and enjoying the atmosphere. It’s one of the most festive and warm places you can visit.

Where to Stay: We recommend a historic inn or bed & breakfast in the downtown district to be within walking distance of all the lights.

While Maui is our go-to for a resort escape, Honolulu is where you go for a vibrant, city-meets-beach holiday. We loved seeing the massive Santa surfing with his reindeer in the fountain at the Iolani Palace. The whole city has this amazing “Mele Kalikimaka” (Merry Christmas) spirit.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect blend of warm beach weather, world-class shopping, and festive displays. It’s also a significant month for history, with the memorial events at Pearl Harbor.

Where to Stay: Waikiki has a huge range of hotels, from historic beachfront properties to modern high-rises.

If your idea of a winter getaway is to truly get away from everything, the crowds, the noise, the stress, then South Padre is a perfect choice. We spent a week there, and our days consisted of long, quiet walks on the beach. It was a total reset and the perfect way to escape the winter blues.

Why Visit in December: The weather is mild, and the crowds are gone. It’s one of the warmest places in Texas and offers a simple, relaxing beach vacation without the high prices or holiday chaos of other destinations.

Where to Stay: You’ll find many beachfront condos and hotels offering great off-season rates.

We thought we knew desert holiday lights, but the “Las Noches de las Luminarias” at the Desert Botanical Garden in Phoenix is on another level. Walking the garden paths lit by thousands of hand-lit luminaria bags, with musicians playing, was a top-tier holiday experience.

Why Visit in December: You get two trips in one: perfect, sunny weather for outdoor adventures like hiking during the day, and stunning, sophisticated holiday light displays at night.

Where to Stay: Choose from upscale resorts in Scottsdale or stylish hotels in downtown Phoenix.

Sometimes, the warm weather destinations just won’t cut it, especially if you are looking for that winter wonderland feel. So, this section is for travellers who want to dive head-first into the holiday spirit. These are the cities and towns that go all-out for December, with millions of lights, Christmas markets, and an atmosphere of pure magic.

We’ve visited NYC many times, but there’s a specific energy in December. We grabbed hot chocolates and walked through the Bryant Park Winter Village, watching the ice skaters zip around the rink under the lights of the surrounding skyscrapers. It felt like being in the opening scene of a holiday movie. There is nothing like New York City at Christmas.

Why Visit in December: It is the quintessential American Christmas destination. From the iconic tree to the world-famous window displays, the entire city is on a different level of festive.

Where to Stay: Midtown is convenient for seeing the main holiday sights, but we also love the West Village for its cosy, neighbourhood feel.

We’d heard Leavenworth was a “Christmas Town,” but we weren’t prepared for the reality. We visited during the Village of Lights festival, and walking through the snow-covered Bavarian-style village while every single building was covered in over half a million lights… it’s not an exaggeration. It’s the closest we’ve ever felt to being inside a real-life snow globe.

Why Visit in December: The entire town transforms into a “Hallmark movie” Christmas village. It’s a full-immersion holiday experience with carolers, festive food, and incredible decorations.

Where to Stay: Book a Bavarian-style lodge or inn right in the village. You must book many months in advance for December.

We love Asheville, but visiting in December is all about the Biltmore Estate. We took the candlelight evening tour, and seeing the main banquet hall with its 35-foot tree, fireplaces roaring, and carolers singing… it felt like we’d stepped back in time into a Gilded Age Christmas party.

Why Visit in December: Christmas at Biltmore is one of the most iconic holiday events in the country. The city itself is a cosy mountain retreat, and the Blue Ridge Mountains are just beautiful with a dusting of snow.

Where to Stay: You can stay on the Biltmore Estate for the full experience or choose a boutique hotel downtown.

Here are the remaining destinations for the “Best Christmas Towns & Festive Cities” section, all written with unique, December-focused content.

We’ve visited a lot of Christmas markets, but visiting the one in Bethlehem, known as “Christmas City USA”, just felt right. We sipped hot cider and browsed the stalls in the old quarter, and you can feel the city’s 250+ years of Christmas tradition. The whole place is lit by the glow of a giant Moravian star on the hillside.

Why Visit in December: This is Christmas City USA. It was nicknamed this on Christmas Eve, 1741. It offers one of the most authentic and historic holiday experiences in the country, blending its Moravian heritage with a European-style Christkindlmarkt.

Where to Stay: Look for a hotel or inn in the historic downtown area to be close to the festivities.

Walking into Solvang in December felt like we’d been transported to a Danish village during its Julefest celebration. We spent the day exploring the half-timbered buildings, windmills, and bakeries, all decorated for the holidays. It’s such a unique and charming way to experience a winter getaway in the middle of California.

Why Visit in December: The town’s month-long “Julefest” (Yule-fest) celebration is in full swing. It’s a one-of-a-kind Danish-style Christmas with parades, markets, and, of course, delicious European pastries.

Where to Stay: Choose one of the charming Danish-themed inns right in the village to be in the middle of the Julefest activities.

We had to see the “Christmas Capital of Texas” for ourselves, and it did not disappoint. The entire historic Main Street is transformed. We loved seeing the vintage railroad, which becomes the “North Pole Express” for the month. They take the “Christmas Capital” title seriously; there are over 1,400 events in 40 days.

Why Visit in December: It is the officially designated “Christmas Capital of Texas”. The sheer number of festive events, light displays, and activities is staggering, making it a top-tier destination for families and holiday lovers.

Where to Stay: The Gaylord Texan Resort is an attraction in itself, or you can stay near the Historic Main Street to be close to the events.

A New Orleans Christmas is an experience all its own. We did a “Reveillon Dinner,” a modern take on a Creole holiday tradition, and it was one of the most memorable meals we’ve ever had. Afterwards, we walked to Jackson Square to see the St. Louis Cathedral all lit up while carolers sang.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience unique Creole Christmas traditions you won’t find anywhere else. The weather is mild, the food is incredible, and the city’s lobbies (like at The Roosevelt) have some of the most elegant decorations we’ve seen.

Where to Stay: We recommend a hotel in the French Quarter to be in the middle of the action and see the decorated lobbies.

We went to Natchitoches (pronounced Nak-a-tish) specifically for its Christmas Festival, and it was a total joy. It’s one of the oldest and biggest in the country. The whole city, which is the oldest in Louisiana, lights up with over 300,000 lights along the Cane River, and the weekly fireworks shows are fantastic.

Why Visit in December: It hosts one of the oldest and most celebrated holiday festivals in the US, running for six weeks. It’s a classic, Southern Christmas experience in a beautiful historic district.

Where to Stay: Book a room at a historic bed & breakfast in the downtown area.

Visiting Colonial Williamsburg in December felt like walking through a living history Christmas card. We joined a candlelight tour, and seeing the historic buildings lit by real candles in the windows, with carolers in period costumes and the smell of woodsmoke in the air… it was absolutely magical.

Why Visit in December: You get to experience a traditional, 18th-century “Colonial Christmas”. The decorations are all-natural (no plastic lights), and the atmosphere is incredibly authentic and charming.

Where to Stay: Stay in one of the historic Colonial Houses or a tavern right in the restored area for the full immersive experience.

Here is the final category of destinations. This section is all about embracing the snow and finding that perfect winter wonderland.

For many, holiday season travel is all about finding that perfect, snowy scene. These are the places to go for world-class skiing, cosy lodges, and that magical feeling of a true winter escape.

We’ll always remember our first “après-ski” in Aspen. We had spent the day on the mountain hitting fresh powder whenever we got the chance, and as the sun went down, the sky lit up with this incredible pink and orange light they call “Aspenglow.” Sitting by a fire, enjoying a glass of Christmas cheer, and watching the snow fall on the historic town, it just felt like the peak of a luxury winter trip.

Why Visit in December: It’s one of the world’s most famous upscale ski destinations, and the town is just as much an attraction as the mountains. The festive atmosphere, high-end shops, and restaurants are all decked out for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Aspen is known for its luxury hotels and ski-in/ski-out resorts.

One of our favourite things about Park City is its history. We loved skiing down to the historic Main Street, popping off our skis, and walking straight into a saloon that’s been there since the silver mining days. It feels like a real Western town, not just a ski resort.

Why Visit in December: It’s a historic mountain town with two world-class ski resorts (Park City and Deer Valley). The historic Main Street is incredibly charming, and the “Snow Globe Stroll” features life-sized snow globes you can walk through.

Where to Stay: You can find ski-in/ski-out hotels or stay at an inn on the historic Main Street.

Jackson Hole in December is just dramatic. We took a sleigh ride through the National Elk Refuge, and seeing thousands of elk gathered against the backdrop of the snow-covered Teton mountains… it was a powerful and wild winter experience we’ve never forgotten.

Why Visit in December: It’s the perfect mix of rugged “cowboy Christmas” charm and some of the most challenging ski terrain in North America. The town square, with its famous antler arches, is beautifully lit for the holidays.

Where to Stay: Stay at a slopeside resort in Teton Village or in a hotel in the town of Jackson.

We love Whitefish because it feels like a real, down-to-earth ski town. We spent a day snowshoeing in nearby Glacier National Park, enjoying the total silence and incredible snowy landscapes, and then came back to town for a casual dinner. It’s all the beauty, without the glitz. Just what we were looking for in a winter vacation.

Why Visit in December: It’s a laid-back, charming mountain town with a top-rated ski resort and stunning scenery. It’s also right next to Glacier National Park, which is a spectacular place to explore in the winter.

Where to Stay: You can find lodges on the mountain or stay in one of the friendly inns in downtown Whitefish.

This was a trip purely for the fun of it, and it was 100% worth it. You drive down streets named “Santa Claus Lane” and “St. Nicholas Drive,” the streetlights are shaped like candy canes, and you can visit the Santa Claus House and see his reindeer. It’s a surreal and joyful experience.

Why Visit in December: It’s the ultimate Christmas fantasy come to life. The entire town is Christmas-themed, 365 days a year, but it’s most magical in December with real snow on the ground and the added bonus of possibly seeing the Northern Lights.

Where to Stay: North Pole is very small; most visitors stay in the nearby city of Fairbanks, which has a wide range of hotels.

For the best warm weather, your top choices are Southern Florida (like Key West), Hawaii (like Maui and Honolulu), and the desert Southwest (like Phoenix and Palm Springs). The U.S. Virgin Islands are also a fantastic passport-free tropical option.

Leavenworth, Washington, is often considered the ultimate “Christmas town” as it looks just like a Bavarian snow globe. Other top choices include Bethlehem, PA (known as “Christmas City USA”), Solvang, CA (for a Danish-style Julefest), and Grapevine, TX (the “Christmas Capital of Texas”).

Yes, but it depends on the park. It’s the perfect time to visit desert parks like Death Valley, Everglades, and Big Bend, where summer heat is unbearable. However, many mountain parks like Glacier, Yellowstone, and parts of Yosemite are mostly inaccessible due to heavy snow and road closures.

You are almost guaranteed to find snow in the mountain towns of the Rockies, like Aspen, CO, Park City, UT, and Jackson Hole, WY. You’ll also find snow in the Cascade Mountains (like Leavenworth, WA), Alaska, and the mountains around Lake Tahoe.

December is a magical month to travel. Whether you’re chasing the sun, seeking out that perfect snowy scene, or looking for a town that’s full of holiday magic, the US has the perfect spot for you.

We hope this list, based on our own winter travels, helps you plan your next getaway. Save this on Pinterest for your holiday planning! Where is your favourite place to go in December?

#6218. Walking the Peaks of the Balkans, a Trekking Route With Community At Its Core

I'm awoken by the sound of cowbells clanging outside my bare-boned wood cabin in Dobërdol, a high mountain settlement in northern Albania. Through the window, slightly fogged from the chilly morning air at 5,700 feet, I see the culprits: five chestnut-colored cows munching on grass just feet from my bedside, their bells and tails swinging away.

The Albanian Alps are one of our Best Places to Go in 2027.

I make the short and frigid walk across the guesthouse lawn to the breakfast room, maneuvering around a dozen or so hikers' tents pitched in the grass. Yesterday’s 10-mile trek from Çerem to Dobërdol is still fresh in my mind: dusty dirt trails edged with wild blueberries I couldn’t resist picking and patches of willow gentian, their petals so intensely purple they matched the berry stains on my fingers. The forests of pine, beech, and spruce in these parts are thick enough that the daylight dims inside of them; the valleys dizzyingly deep as they fold in on themselves.

The Peaks of the Balkans trek is a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro.

Local-owned guesthouses welcome trekkers with included meals, like fresh vegetables, homemade dairy, and cured sausages and meats.

It’s mid-September, and only 7 a.m., but breakfast is already in full swing, not an empty seat left at the tables squeezed into the cozy timber-framed room. The Kurmekaj brothers, our hosts, are frantically grabbing four plates apiece from the kitchen, loaded with fried eggs, sausage, fresh sheep cheese, and cucumber-and-tomato salad, a fixture on the Balkan plate. I do my best to duck out of their way as the door behind me swings open and more trekkers pile in.

This is my fourth day of ten on the Peaks of the Balkans trek, a 119-mile inn-to-inn circular trail across the long-disputed borderlands of Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro, through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask. Conceived in the early 2010s as a cross-border peace and tourism project, this trail was meant to reconnect mountain communities that had been splintered by war, create livelihoods, and give residents a reason to remain—or return—to villages hollowed out by conflict and emigration.

The Peaks of the Balkans trail offers both busy sections and quiet side trails where your only companions may be a single hiker or group of grazing cattle.

By those measures, it has been remarkably successful. A late 2025 study published in the Journal of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism estimated that roughly 43,000 hikers now walk the trail each year—up from regional estimates of roughly 20,000 in the pre-pandemic era—injecting more than €25 million ($27.7 million USD) annually into mountain regions where family homes, shepherd settlements, and seasonal villages have increasingly become guesthouses for trekkers. But that success is also beginning to crowd some of the places that the trail was created to support, as a growing number of travelers takes interest.

Ricardo Fahrig of the Albania-based adventure travel company Zbulo, which has been running Peaks trips since the trail’s early years, helped me piece together my own self-guided route on these trails. He says the contrast between busy Dobërdol and the quieter terrain I’m soon to enter after breakfast gets to the heart of the issue. “It’s not the number of travelers on the Peaks of the Balkans trail,” he tells me, “but rather the distribution. Some sections remain sparsely visited, while others, like Dobërdol, struggle with volume during a relatively short season”, a period from roughly June through September, with some hikers continuing into early October.

After breakfast, just a few steps down the trail from the guesthouse in Dobërdol, the clatter and congestion of the morning fade immediately. So do the other trekkers, flowing like a stream up the steep green lip of the expansive bowl-shaped valley we all woke up in, then onward to Milishevc, Montenegro, the usual stop after Dobërdol.

Stepping off the primary Peak of the Balkans trail—which the writer did with a self-guided itinerary from Zbulo—allows for quieter moments and a greater sense of solitude.

All except two. Stef Van Dam, a seasoned Dutch thru-hiker I’d met on my second day on the trail, falls into step beside me on the cattle-worn traces of the route we've chosen to take instead. He, too, is detouring off the official trail. Whereas I’m headed for the heart-shaped lake below Gjeravica, Kosovo’s highest peak, he will peel off later to summit it—“the peak of the Peaks of the Balkans,” he calls the mountain.

At the empty pass marking the Albania-Kosovo border, 1,600 feet of ascent later, we collapse onto the same rock—for all we know, Van Dam is munching his apple in Albania while I air my blisters in Kosovo just next to him. From up here, this border is steeped in irony—a line so invisible we have to guess at where exactly it’s drawn, yet a matter that has been fought over, fortified, closed, and redrawn for more than a century.

Ahead, a narrow dirt track just below the Kosovo side of the pass continues along the contour line, snaking through the treeless and boulder-strewn landscape. To our left and many mountain miles away, we spot the village of Junik where we’re both planning to sleep that night, me in a gueshouse and Van Dam in his tent somewhere nearby. As if marking the spot, a golden eagle circles in the unblemished autumn sky above it.

“This is exactly what I came to this trail to find,” Van Dam says, the first to interrupt the silence. “I wanted something quiet, more remote than other trails in Europe. I’ve found it here.”

Having myself walked a few of the more notably crowded European trails, including the Camino de Santiago, I know what he means. Besides the two of us and the eagle riding the thermals overhead, there isn’t another soul in sight.

Along the route, small guesthouses warmly welcome trekkers, who have created a reason to stay—or return—to communities once disrupted by conflict and emagration.

By late afternoon, after Van Dam and I part ways below Gjeravica. What appeared as a scattering of rooftops no bigger than a thumbnail now reveals itself in the distinct forms of summer homes and traditional katuns, seasonal shepherd settlements composed of simple huts and stone-walled livestock pens.

The family has only recently begun welcoming trekkers into their home, and they radiate the kind of excitement that comes from still being delighted by every single arrival. Renaja leads me to my room for the night, tucked on the third floor beneath the A-frame eaves. Downstairs, pizza bakes in an old wood-burning stove while Renaja's mother and grandmother set a long table for the dozen or so guests still dribbling in.

The old highland idea of besa—that a house belongs not only to its owner, but to God and to the guest—is coming to life before my eyes. Or, as Fahrig, who first came to these mountains in 2012, later puts it: bukë, kripë, zemër, an Albanian expression meaning “bread, salt, and heart.” “The material offering may be simple,” he says. “The welcome is what makes it memorable.”

The following morning, I continue deeper into Kosovo, eventually rejoining the main Peaks of the Balkans route. Now, it’s Montenegro on the other side of the invisible line I keep crossing. Over the coming days, the trail shifts between empty mountain passes and occasional stretches of asphalt—the latter one being a reason, Fahrig says, that many trekkers truncate this section entirely. He estimates that places such as the Rugova Gorge—a river-carved passage whose 2-3,000-foot-deep limestone walls bear stone-blasted tunnels, a frothy emerald river, and viewpoints at every turn—currently receive around 30 percent or less of the traffic funneled through Dobërdol.

The Peaks of the Balkans stitches together sections that include dirt paths, country roads, and sometimes asphalt—but even the less photogenic portions lead to impactful destinations.

In Drelaj, where this dramatic gorge opens into a wider pastoral valley, skipping Kosovo begins to feel like missing the point. This quiet highland hamlet is embraced on all sides by forested mountains. Across its green curves and garden plots are chalet-like summer homes built out of wood and stone, each boasting a balcony or porch turned toward the mountains and the mosque whose slender minaret rises at the center of it all.

After a day of sharing the trail with more cows than people, passing by deserted villages, and hugging a gully’s edge on a heavily eroded and unpaved fire road, I eventually spill out of the forest onto asphalt that ends in Drelaj. My guesthouse, Konaku i Malsorit, is tucked just to the right of the minaret. An Albanian flag (this part of Kosovo is majority ethnic Albanian) whips in the breeze above the two-story home and its garden, ripe with peppers, tomatoes, onions, and maize.

Minarets dot the skyline in even small villages in Kosovo and Albania.

My host Blendi Lajqi tells me his family fled Drelaj during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War after their home was burned by Yugoslav and Serbian forces. He was six years old. After the war, the family moved to Peja, the nearest major city, and for around two decades, he says, the house and the land they left behind here were “dead, no longer a home.” The creation of the trail gave his family—and others in the village—a reason to return and reinvest in what they left behind. Looking around at it now, “dead” is hard to imagine.

The room I’m sleeping in, now completely redone into what could easily be a fully functioning apartment, once served as a makeshift hospital for the Kosovo Liberation Army (UÇK), the ethnic Albanian guerrilla force that fought the Yugoslav and Serbian forces during the war. Here, he tells me, Lajqi’s mother and aunt cared for the wounded.

Many hikers arrive knowing almost nothing about what happened here, he says. But for those who make a point to learn about it, the history of this region gives different weight to this trail—and the intention behind it. The guesthouses along the Peaks aren’t simply infrastructure for hikers. “It’s brought life back to the land and the house where my family lived until the beginning of the war,” Lajqi tells me. “When we opened the guesthouse, our home became a place where people from all over the world could come, stay, eat, talk with us, and experience our way of life. For me, there’s something special about that.”

Trails in this region include a great deal of altitude change—and the views that come with that.

The writer gathers around the dinner table with fellow trekkers at a local guesthouse.

Few people, however, have watched tourism reshape these mountains as long as Skender Selimaj of Hotel Rezidenca Quku i Valbones in Valbona, Albania. When he and his brother Alfred returned from the United Kingdom in the early 2000s, after leaving Albania during the period of communism, the high-walled valley hemmed in by jagged limestone peaks still revolved largely around subsistence farming. In 2004, they opened Restaurant Rilindja—meaning “rebirth” in Albanian—without knowing whether enough travelers would come to sustain it. Then, in 2009, Selimaj helped clear the passes toward Theth and Çerem and carried some of the first wooden trail signs into the mountains himself.

As in many locations along the Peaks of the Balkans route, the influx of tourism has since reshaped the Valbona Valley. The single-day hike over Valbona Pass to Theth has become one of Albania’s most popular mountain routes, which is also why my self-guided Zbulo itinerary intentionally bypassed it. Even with the trade-offs, Valbona has benefited. Farmers can now sell cheese, meat, eggs, and milk locally at better prices. Families have new income, while local children, Selimaj says, sometimes grow up speaking English simply from meeting travelers from around the world.

Selimaj, who spent years working as a mountain guide and in mountain rescue, still spends his free time exploring the terrain he grew up in, though he’s faced the fact that solitude is increasingly difficult to find. Where he once expected wild goats and empty mountains, “everywhere you go, you see somebody,” he says. He doesn’t wish tourism away; he has seen too clearly what it has done for local livelihoods. What he does want is a Valbona that remains clean, green, and recognizably local, where old stone houses and family-run businesses aren’t crowded out by large-scale outside development.

The Peaks of the Balkans trail passes through what’s called the Accursed Mountains—a name whose ominous origins supposedly lie either with the devil, war, or travelers cursing the range’s unforgiving terrain, depending on who you ask.

For Fahrig of Zbulo, the answer to the newfound business isn’t necessarily fewer trekkers. What he hopes to preserve on this trail are “living communities rather than places shaped entirely around visitors.” Doing that, he argues, means spreading trekkers more evenly: encouraging hikers to continue through Kosovo, directing some traffic toward quieter alternatives just beyond the busiest passes, and steering repeat or more adventurous trekkers toward newer alternative long-distance routes like the 225-mile High Scardus Trail that traverses the remote and mountainous borderlands of North Macedonia, Kosovo, and Albania.

In Kosovo, some of that work is already underway. Lajqi is part of a volunteer effort with other guesthouse owners and tourism businesses to create more natural alternatives around paved sections of the original route without cutting the villages themselves out of the trail—the other risk of making changes. “The best solution is not to completely change the original trail,” Lajqi says, “but to offer more choices, preserving the connection between the villages while also giving hikers the kind of mountain experience they came for.”

Over the days that follow, I keep moving west, circling back towards Theth. Each day brings with it another 3,000-foot pass to scale, another cucumber-and-tomato sandwich to enjoy once I get there, along with a steady mix of surprise, (some) stress, and plenty of solitude. Occasionally, I get lost when my GPS stops working or the orange dots and red-and-white striped trail markers disappear, and yet I always find my way. I walk, at times, with no one, and in other moments with dozens of travelers. Sometimes, it's just me and cowbell-clanging bovine. I keep going like this, collecting these little moments and memories, until, on the 10th day, I pass a bunker, the crumbling Cold War-era concrete mushrooms built by communist dictator Enver Hoxha, and realize I must be back in Albania.

By the time I approach Theth—the end of my route—I feel like I’ve walked through both versions of the Peaks: the one overwhelmed by its own success and the quieter version still there available alongside it.

The guesthouses along the Peaks aren’t simply infrastructure for hikers. “It’s brought life back to the land and the house where my family lived until the beginning of the war,” Blendi Lajqi of Konaku i Malsorit says.

For my final night on the trails, I hike into Bujtina Kometa, a guesthouse in the quiet hamlet of Okol situated roughly a mile-and-a-half from central Theth. A mezze spread of marinated chicken, seasoned potatoes, olives, tomatoes, soft cheese, and tzatziki for dipping lands on the table, all prepared by our host Ermira and her family. The thing about these trails is that even if you go your own way by day, you'll find yourself breaking bread with familiar faces by night. Every person around the table, I realize, is someone I've met somewhere along the trail—people I’ve shared miles with over the last 10 days as our paths kept crossing.

Ermira’s father tops up our water and hints at honey-soaked fruit for dessert; woodsmoke from a neighbor distilling homemade raki drifts through the low-lit dining room. Van Dam, seated across the table from me now, reaches for another forkful of potato dripping with tzatziki. The busy center of Theth, with its tour buses and day-trippers, still feels worlds away.

For one more night, these Accursed Mountains and all they carry—the besa, the borders, the beauty, and the stories etched into them—envelop us, proving that wide-open spaces and quiet still have their place in these mountains.

Most hikers spend about 10 to 13 days completing the full Peaks of the Balkans route.

The complete Peaks of the Balkans circuit covers roughly 119 miles (192 km) across Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro. Most hikers spend about 10 to 13 days completing the full route, though shorter itineraries of 5 to 8 days often cut or bypass certain stages. Most routes involve 5 to 8 hours of hiking per day, typically covering 8 to 17 miles with significant elevation gain and loss.

Getting there: Fly into Podgorica in Montenegro or Tirana in Albania, transferring via shuttle or 4x4 to trailheads in Theth, Valbona, or Plav.

When to go: The core trekking season runs from June through September, but is increasingly stretching into October. Late June through August generally offers more reliable pass conditions, though the trail can get busy. Early June can still mean snow lingering on the highest passes, while September is the sweet spot for favorable hiking weather (peak traffic proves that everyone knows this). Early-to-mid October can be beautiful for experienced hikers willing to gamble on shorter days, colder nights, and the occasional burst of snow; later in the month, high-altitude guesthouses begin winding down, and do not reopen again until early May or June.

Who to go with: Albania-based Zbulo offers guided and self-guided trips (with logistics arranged, but no guide) ranging from 8 to 12 days. These include cross-border permits, guesthouse reservations, meals, luggage transfers, and route planning. If you're traveling independently, be sure to secure your date-locked cross-border permits at least two weeks before hiking, or have an agency like Zbulo secure them for you.

Where to stay: Accommodation ranges from family-run guesthouses and homestays to simple mountain huts, cabins, and small hotels. In remote sections, expect basic rooms—sometimes shared—along with hearty home-cooked dinners, breakfasts, and often a packed lunch for the following day. Budget roughly $25-55 USD per person per night depending on the room and whether meals are included. Book ahead in high season, and carry plenty of cash in Albanian lek or Euros in small denominations; card payments and ATMs are scarce in the mountains. In May and other shoulder-season periods, it is possible to arrange rooms on the fly, but from June through September—especially in bottlenecks like Dobërdol and popular stops such as Theth and Valbona—it’s smarter to book several weeks ahead. Camping is also possible on parts of the route, including at some guesthouses that allow trekkers to pitch a tent for a small fee and use facilities or buy meals. You can arrange your accommodations directly with hosts over WhatsApp using contacts found through Google Maps, social media, or the official Peaks of the Balkans App; many are now available on platforms like Booking.com as well.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.
