#6168. 26 Dreamy Caribbean Hotels to Escape to This Winter

Nowhere evokes the images of white sand, turquoise water, and warm hospitality quite like the Caribbean. There are over 7,000 islands in the region, and the best Caribbean hotels can be found on just a small clutch of them. This is the ultimate place to vacation. The sunsets seem to stretch for hours and are best enjoyed with bare feet, salty sea hair, and a rum punch in hand. When it comes to choosing where to visit, it's hard to go wrong, but each spot has its own unique charm, quirks, and list of beautiful places to stay. Whether you're looking for a luxury resort with glossy interiors in the Bahamas or a boutique bolthole run by a local family in Barbados, there's an address for you on the list below. Consider this your definitive guide to the best hotels in the Caribbean.

Descending a steep hillside into a 100-acre estate is a momentous entrance anywhere, let alone one stretched out between the iconic peaks of Petit and Gros Piton, after a winding journey up and up and up the mountainside. It’s worth the climb. In bouncy Soufrière, Sugar Beach's 130 bright white villas gleam between the thick foliage and fan out over the hillsides until they reach St. Lucia’s prettiest white-sand beach. Between the chocolate, the cocktails, the sunsets, and the salt in your hair, a stay here is a full sensory experience, which continues in the evenings as the whistling frogs' calls ring out into the balmy night, echoing across the mountaintops. —Charley Ward

This namesake hillside resort set above Toiny Bay gives “wild” an unexpected new meaning when it comes to sceney St. Barts. On the scrubby southeastern point of the island, this unfussy haven is where an in-the-know social set heads to find serenity, whether via an early morning surf lesson or at the wave-lapped beach club. Rugged shoreline views and cacti-dotted greenery imbue a sense of calm from the second you’re greeted with a glass of Champagne at check-in.

Secluded infinity-pool decks boast far-flung views of the azure sea and surfers paddling out to the white caps consistently churning up on this side of the island. The suites and villas here were redesigned in 2024 by Osborn Interiors to swap in more modern touches. If St. Barts’s reputation for heaving parties and see-and-be-seen celebrities might have you thinking the Champagne-drenched French Caribbean island isn’t for you, Le Toiny probably is—and anyone else who wants the serenity of a wild coastline at their fingertips. —Shannon McMahon

This resort is a true slice of paradise, and the kind of place you'll be itching to return to the moment you leave. Expect utter peacefulness, relaxing accommodations, excellent food, and water activities galore. The spacious, contemporary cottages—30, in all—were recently redesigned to be brighter and airier, swapping out dark wood for light and granting unobstructed ocean views via large sliding glass doors. The decks are nearly as large as the bedrooms, with lounge chairs, daybeds, and private plunge pools to dip into. For those up on the hill, staff is on standby to ferry guests up and down in golf carts. As an all-inclusive property, your meals, afternoon snacks, and fresh sushi are covered, as are cocktails and beverages, like the juice of the day served at breakfast. You're here to rest and delight in the calm waters of the cove—swim, snorkel, paddleboard, or head out on a sunset cruise or deep-sea fishing trip aboard one of the property's three boats. —Madison Flager

There’s an irresistible sweetness to the rainbow skies, lush palms, and bone-white Moorish architecture of Cap Juluca, a premier luxury experience unrivaled in the Caribbean, as expected from an LVMH brand. Go for an enchanting, Caribbean-spirited, never-lift-a-finger luxury experience of textbook island bliss. Lose yourself in the tranquility and contentment of the Guerlain spa, eat at some of the premier dining spots on Anguilla, and find out how beautiful life can be at the bottom of a rum punch before being lulled into a deep sleep by the spellbinding sound of lapping waves off a humid ocean breeze—from the inside of your own villa, of course. It's an experience so good, your palate for a luxury vacation will have a new standard. —Bridget Knowles

On a hilltop overlooking turquoise Castle Harbour, Rosewood is the epitome of extravagance, from its whitewashed marble corridors right down to its powdery beach. When this swank resort first opened as Rosewood Tucker’s Point in 2009, it ushered in a new level of luxury in Bermuda. Nearly 10 years later, the bar was raised yet again with a $25 million renovation of the guest rooms and public spaces. It's now got a handsome look, a handful of additions, and a bevy of resort-wide upgrades. Expect all the bells and whistles of a full-service luxury stay: A Robert Rulewich–designed, championship-caliber golf course; several swimming pools (some adults-only, others just for kids); a state-of-the-art fitness center; a full-service Sense Spa; tennis courts; a kids club; and a private beach that will keep you drooling for days. —David LaHuta

Anguilla is a small-but-mighty island packed with luxury properties, dining options, and outstanding beaches. Barnes Bay and Meads Bay surround the Four Seasons on both sides, with waters that are occasionally rough but known to be swimmable at other times of the year. Regardless of the conditions, white beach chairs line the sand in pristine formations each morning, and three large pool areas—two kid-friendly, one adults-only—provide plenty of swimming options when the ocean is unavailable. The property stretches across the shore, which means each room provides a unique view of some combination of beachfront, ocean, palm trees, or garden. In my oceanview one-bedroom suite, we overlooked the modernist pool deck as well as the distant ocean, with a plunge pool on the balcony and ample outdoor space for afternoon lounging. The bathroom was equipped with two sinks, a large tub, and a marble walk-in shower. —Emily Adler

In a hidden corner of St. Barts, down a steep and winding road, you come to a Gauguin-like canopy of lush green vegetation, beyond which the half-moon sandy perfection of Flamands Beach reveals itself and the Cheval Blanc reigns supreme. Low-built and quietly sprawling, the property was elegantly renovated following Hurricane Irma by Parisian design supremo Jacques Grange, whose interiors speak to a chic European aesthetic of quiet indulgences. The atmosphere is almost Parisian (there’s a Guerlain spa on the premises) but with a devil-may-care attitude.

Young French culinary star Jean Imbert’s Creole-inspired menu at La Case is light but gastronomic, and the cocktails are sublime. I spent my lunches with feet in the sand at the La Cabane beach restaurant, watching a parade of Birkin bag–carrying ladies power-walking along the beach, moguls on their phones doing business, and boho French girls running into the waves in tiny Eres bikinis. It reminded me of St. Tropez’s Plage Pampelonne, but a lot less frenetic, and with an ambience that’s both relaxed and indulgent. My assigned butler would WhatsApp me when my room was done, or a spa appointment was due. But it was my private yoga sessions in the garden’s pagoda that I won’t forget in a hurry. —Vassi Chamberlain

Book a stay to experience Six Senses’s hallmark approach to barefoot luxury and a warm, welcoming vibe that befits the Spice Isle and its people. The hotel’s 71 rooms, suites, and villas are built into the slopes around the lagoon and across a bluff. In the thatched beachfront suites, each room (including the bathroom) is designed to offer direct access to a private pool and the ocean shore. Grenada is ever so tiny—12 miles by 21 miles long. Still, the resort is set away from the bustle of Grenada’s capital, St. George's, the popular beaches of Grand Anse and BBC, and treks into the rainforests—getting to any of these takes about 30 minutes by car. Out of 200 employees here, 180 have been hired locally—in many cases, hyper-locally, from the parish of St. David. This is part of the Six Senses commitment to integrate with local communities across its global footprint. The result is a resort that mimics the friendliness and easy hospitality of Grenada’s people, and the best way to enjoy this is to slip right into an island state of mind with them. —Arati Menon

Travelers who want to feel like they’re summering at a friend’s beachfront estate will thoroughly appreciate the laid-back vibe of the Potlatch Club on the isle of Eleuthera. The lush property has only 11 keys on 12 acres, a seamless service team that's worked together for more than 20 years at other hotels, and a cluster of storied structures, some of which date back to 1923. In the 1950s, after the property was purchased by a trio of socialites, it became a private hideaway for celebrities like Paul McCartney, who honeymooned here with his late wife Linda in 1969.

Current owners Bruce Loshusan and his business partner Hans Febles began work on the resort in 2016; Loshusan recruited Nassau-based interior designer Amanda Lindroth to help produce the dreamy, relaxed atmosphere that encompasses what people find enchanting about island life: white shiplap ceilings, pink coral stone floors that extend to the bathrooms, and cozy wooden porches with rattan daybeds and chairs. —Alexandra Sanidad

From the moment the resort’s yacht glides into the serene waters of Yacht Harbor in Sprat Bay, the transition from passenger to prized guest is practically instantaneous. Peter Island is the largest private island in the British Virgin Islands, yet the resort has managed to capture an utterly intimate vibe. The resort strives to be as sustainable as possible; it has a reverse osmosis water purification plant and two wind turbines that can generate up to 75% of the island's power. And yet Peter Island still doesn't mess with what works, and leans into a familial flavor of hospitality that feels like you’re at your favorite aunt and uncle’s for the holidays. —Kat Chen

Images of Rockhouse’s thatch-roof stone villas and bright red ladders dropping into the sea have come to represent a certain brand of Jamaican cool. The property, currently celebrating its 50th anniversary, isn’t shy about honoring its place in pop culture history: Bob Marley and the Rolling Stones once jumped off its iconic cliffs, and reggae and dancehall ephemera line the walls. Rooms are simple but still retain an essence of the sleepy 1970s Negril that originally defined the property: Four-poster beds are draped with mosquito nets and decorated with locally sourced quilts; in the villa rooms, palm-fringed outdoor showers mean morning routines are accompanied by birdsong; and the cool, simple stone floors keep you feeling in tune with island life. Meanwhile, food here is a primer in Jamaican classics, especially at jerk spot Pushcart, where DJs take over the sound systems for regular dance parties. The Rockhouse crowd knows how to have a good time. —Lale Arikoglu

Cap Cana is chock-full of resorts to get away from it all, but tastemakers, design lovers, and those looking to instill envy in their followers will want to head straight to St. Regis’s first foray into the Dominican Republic. While you can expect the same high-end amenities of the brand—butlers on call to arrange excursions, seafood towers, Champagne, a luxe spa—what sets this hotel apart are the details grounded in Dominican culture. Set on 16 acres of beachfront property, the rambling, indoor-outdoor resort with 200 rooms, including 36 suites, features tropical plants, patterned brickwork, and curved ceilings adorned with wickerwork. Artworks by Dominican artists are peppered throughout the building, lending a gallery-like vibe.

As for local flavors, dine at Cassava for breakfast, lunch, or dinner, and head to the Amber Room for a cigar and two fingers of rum. In between, you can play at the Jack Nicklaus Signature Punta Espada golf course, which abuts the property; indulge in services at the salon and the spa; or just unwind on the beach or by the pool (try to score one of the private cabanas). Whatever you decide, as you languorously wander from bed to breakfast, from beach to pool, from lunch to cocktails to dinner, you can relax knowing that everything will be taken care of. —Damian Fallon

You can become a little numb to beauty in St. Barts, but even after having been on the island for days, I think I squealed when I pulled into Eden Rock. It’s just so perfect—so chic, so glamorous, but in this easy, island-appropriate way. It’s the type of place that just being there makes you feel like the most glam, sun-kissed version of yourself. The hotel is almost entirely surrounded by calm, gin-bottle- blue water that’s heavenly for a swim. There’s a diving platform a little ways out; you can take out rafts and paddle around the point, and there’s a reef if you want to snorkel. The rooms are lovely and elegant, with a subtle Carib-meets-nautical vibe, at once bright and airy.

When it comes to the food, rockstar chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten is in charge of the menu at the main restaurant, and the resort’s breakfast spread is wild in scope and quality; don’t miss it. Sure, you could have a delightful breakfast by your private pool, but the people-watching here is too good—you’d be missing an opportunity if you stayed in. It’s a pretty diverse crowd in some ways, but the common denominator, to tell it straight, is money. This place is not cheap, but it’s one of the rare hotels that is absolutely worth it. The setting is unparalleled, and the food, service, and design are top of the top. There is no way you’ll go and not dream (maybe nightly) about going back—it’s that special. —Rebecca Misner

As COMO’s sole property in the Americas, Parrot Cay's renowned luxury experience makes it an unrivaled property in Turks and Caicos. The pinnacle of bespoke solitude, it's located on a private island enmeshed in the wilderness. You arrive after a 15-minute chauffeured drive from Providenciales International Airport, then a 20-minute panoramic boat ride through cays and turquoise waves hugged by mangroves. It’s primeval in nature and worlds away, despite its ease of access from the main island. The private, white-sand beach—with miles of clear-water sandbars inviting you to walk across, float around, and laze about for ages—is the main reason why the property has been dubbed by locals as "the Maldives of the Americas," despite being entirely singular in the impression it makes. If you’re seeking a romantic getaway inspired by an itch for an immersive nature escape, this is the place to go—and I recommend booking a private beach house with your own plunge pool for the full, immersive experience. —B.K.

Step onto the grounds of Coral Reef Club, and you would be forgiven for feeling like you’ve been transported back 50 years to a bygone era of old-school glamour. Families frolic by the ocean on chic sun loungers, while glamorous older couples are served sherries by attentive waiters in immaculately pressed uniforms. The 88 suites and cottages with plunge pools or wraparound balconies are intertwined among 12 acres of lush gardens, rooms merging classic Bajan style (think colorful art and cane furnishings) with English touches such as pretty verandas with wooden railings and old-fashioned outdoor lampshades.

Breakfast is an elaborate affair with both a large buffet offering everything from Bajan fish cakes to fresh pancakes and a made-to-order menu. Those with space left over for lunch can enjoy anything from local roti to juicy Cajun shrimp tacos over views of the crashing waves. But dinner is where it really gets glamorous, where stone pillars and the most attentive waiters you may ever come across serve a classic European menu infused with Caribbean touches to the sounds of a live singer. –Jessica Rach

Though it's just 21 miles long, Grenada packs a punch: You will find lush rainforests, nature reserves, spice plantations, the charming town of St. George’s, and beaches so perfect that they look photoshopped. For those seeking a serene island escape, the 28-room Silversands Beach House is the place. Time seems to stop here, a feeling that begins the moment you drive up the entrance and the turquoise waters of Portici Beach come into view.

The rooms and suites are so lovely—private terraces, floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the sea, calming shades of cream and light wood—that you may never want to leave; but the dreamy infinity pool and sandy beach just a few steps away make a great case for venturing out. The food at the upscale Mediterranean-inspired Azzurro restaurant is another highlight: Pasta is made in-house, seafood is locally sourced, and the roasted vegetable pizza is the perfect finale to a day spent on the water. There’s also plenty to experience nearby, and the staff will gladly guide you through activities, whether it’s touring the beautiful island or a rum tasting. The vibes are unhurried, gracious, and sweet, and you’ll feel yourself slipping into island time along with everyone else. —Pallavi Kumar

There are Caribbean beach resorts, and then there is Little Dix Bay, which was completely rebuilt after being decimated by hurricanes in 2017, celebrating its 60th anniversary in 2024. It’s undoubtedly got the bells and whistles—a truly transcendent spa, one of the best rum collections in the Caribbean, and so forth—but what sets Little Dix Bay apart is its staff, some of whom have worked here for over 30 years.

There are 42 guestrooms, 35 suites, two beach houses, and two hillside villas with a contemporary-yet-textured aesthetic. With sleek furniture juxtaposed against stone walls (a reference to the island’s iconic boulders), a minibar station that feels homey and not like an afterthought, and comfortable beds perfect for pressing snooze on your alarm clock, there isn’t a bad room in the house here. It’s the kind of place where guests at checkout will turn to their butler and ask, “Same time next year?” —Todd Plummer

It’s easy to imagine that very little has changed at this 1950s-era resort since John F. Kennedy absconded to Cottage 25 to chip away at his inaugural address and Oscar Hammerstein wrote The Sound of Music while taking in the killer ocean views. The green-striped awnings shading vast terraces and the interiors’ cream-colored paneling offset by dark wood, along with the tea and sandwiches served at four sharp every afternoon, enhance that caught-in-time feeling. That Ralph Lauren has had a major hand in the design in recent years is a delightful non-surprise, with playful preppiness on display at every turn, like the bar with its deep booth benches upholstered in navy-and-white stripes and photos of bygone guests, like Warren Beatty, covering the walls. —Charlie Hobbs

Built in 1970 and family-run ever since, The Sandpiper’s original charm remains, and despite being renovated (the suites are particularly modern), a thread of tradition runs through this property and nods to its history. Fifty rooms—some with their own plunge pools—span two-story, pavilion-style houses surrounded by lush vegetation. Four contemporary suites with direct beach access and ocean views sit separately in the hotel’s tropical gardens and offer modern comforts like a complimentary bar, White Company amenities, and even a personally appointed butler.

As one of the world’s most desirable winter destinations, the Caribbean has an abundance of resort options based on a familiar model. These are the expansive beachfront properties with grand entries, cavernous lobbies, and ostentatious styling featuring a plethora of palm trees, pools, and piña coladas. I’m not suggesting this can’t make for a fantastic getaway—but if this is what you desire, Rock House is not for you. Located in tropical Turks and Caicos but taking its inspiration from the Mediterranean, Rock House offers guests something refreshingly different.

Opened in 2022 as an addition to the renowned Grace Bay Resorts brand, Rock House synthesizes 30 years of luxury resort expertise into a modern European-style experience that satisfies the senses and nourishes the soul. Every detail, from the painstaking dedication to preserving the native ecology surrounding it to the in-house phone app that enables you to effortlessly communicate with the guest experience team without leaving the beach or your private infinity pool, has been thoughtfully considered. Families are welcome, but Rock House may appeal most to lovers and those seeking a truly tranquil environment to relax and recharge. —Caryn B. Davis

Bermuda is generally divided into two parts, east and west, with the capital of Hamilton somewhat in the middle. Most luxury resorts reside in Hamilton or on the east end, but one historic hotel is found on the quieter west end. The resort’s iconic pink cottages, four bars and restaurants, two-tiered pool, and expansive grounds that include four private beaches have been brought into the 21st century after a refresh—no small feat since some architectural details date back to the 1600s.

The 86 cottages are chic, with a tropical-inspired color palette, dark wood statement beds, quirky rattan chairs, and boldly patterned textiles. Vintage-inspired pastel-colored scalloped umbrellas and cushy lounge chairs populate the refurbished pool area and its accompanying bar and restaurant, which also sports a magnificently detailed shell-encrusted back bar. A highlight is the Sunken Harbor Club (an outpost of the same-named Brooklyn bar), which is decorated with shipwreck treasures rescued by the late Bermudian diving legend Teddy Tucker. Bermudian-rooted cuisine is on offer, with dishes like miso-marinated black cod complementing classic island cocktails and new creations by barmaster St. John Frizell. —Devorah Lev-Tov

Combining sustainability best practices with true luxury, this sleek eco-resort is a model for Dominica and the wider Caribbean, demonstrating that you needn’t sacrifice creature comforts to have a green vacation. Coulibri Ridge was built with environmental consciousness at its core—a construction process that took the Canadian-Dominican owners a whopping 15 years to complete. Now, what was once a colonial-era citrus plantation has been transformed into a hillside retreat that aims to be self-sufficient. The 285-acre property is completely powered by the sun via 225 solar panels and 288 recyclable non-lithium batteries; two communal pools are solar-heated and kept clean not with chlorine, but by using a copper ionizer. But if you think the resort is more functional than fancy, think again. Guests are treated to modern studios, lofts, and penthouses with sweeping views of the water, tropical and bountiful breakfasts (included in the rate), and a spa with open-air treatment rooms. —C.D.

This family-owned boutique hotel’s trump card, besides the photogenic striped pink scalloped umbrellas, is its quarter-mile of powder-soft beach in a sleepy cove. Pastel-hued suites are dotted around tropical gardens festooned with palms and banana leaves and a terra-cotta pool terrace, which feels suspended over views of the bay. Tastefully dressed in subdued fabric of hand-printed corals, whitewashed rattan, and bamboo, rooms spill onto terraces framed by bougainvillea, inhaling the salty breeze. The main spaces read like a British country estate, with a drawing room and cavernous hall, just with exotic pinks and greens and plantation shutters—a blend that reflects the island's rich (and often checkered) history.

Mornings at Cobblers Cove recall country clubs of yore, where a genteel breakfast is occasionally interrupted by the pop of a tennis serve or a Champagne cork. Afternoons typically slump between lounge chairs and the balmy sea, where guests can paddle out in search of turtles or gently part the calm, glassy water on a paddleboard. When not leaning into the hotel’s afternoon tea tradition or its phenomenal spa, sailing and water skiing sessions take place every day, and guests can join local fishermen on “catch of the day” adventures. The on-site restaurant preserves its status as one of the island’s top eateries, while weekly buffets and barbecues show off local dishes in a more buttoned-down setting. —Rosalyn Wikeley

Far from the tourist hustle and bustle of the northwestern coast, Jamaica’s chicest and arguably most famous address is located on the northeastern coastline of Oracabessa—a jewel of about 5,000 people, with a thriving community of creatives. Writer Ian Fleming became so enamoured with Oracabessa while on assignment with the British Navy during World War II that he returned to buy a property, building GoldenEye, where he would go on to write all 13 James Bond novels during his winter stays. In 1976, Bob Marley became the owner, later selling it to Chris Blackwell—founder of Island Records, who expanded the property to include a range of private huts, cottages, and villas dotted around the tropical 40-acre grounds. The beachside hideaway is home to four restaurants and bars, including the laid-back bamboo bar which serves Jamaican jerk barbecue right on the sandy Low Cay beachfront. —Ruth C. White

Colorful is the best adjective for Jumby Bay. Emerald-green lizards dart up whitewashed walls, iridescent hummingbirds hover over pink Mexican creepers, and yellow-chested bananaquits search for crumbs on breakfast tables. There are blindingly white sands to cross and turquoise waters to slip into for a world of plump orange starfish, yellow-tailed snappers, and blue tang. Beneath all this shifting color is the lush, 300-acre private island that remains one of the most exclusive in the Caribbean. Its “no cars, no keys” policy brings a feeling of intimacy to the three restaurants, spa, 40 rooms and suites, and 14 villas that make up the hotel, all of which offer luxury as dazzling as the island’s colors.

The generously sized suites come with a little entrance courtyard where wicker chairs swing in the warm breeze. Terraces overlook the sea or are inset with a pool. Some bathrooms spill outside with vast tubs waiting under palm fronds. Step outside your room to enjoy Taittinger on tap (part of the inclusive rates, which also offer limitless water sports) or sip daiquiris made with local black pineapple. Food served at the Estate House, once part of the original sugar plantation, brims with a sense of place. But the best experience has to be a rum tasting with the barman, which leads to serious Caribbean contentment. A stand-out amenity: access to The Hut, the hotel's private island beach club. —Mary Lussiana

How we choose the best hotels in the Caribbean

Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

#6167. Flight Disruptions Ease; DOT Lays Blame for ATC Outage

Air travel in the U.S. was returning to normal Monday, even as the backlog from Friday’s massive air traffic control outage remained evident.

Flights across the country were taking off regularly, and the long lines seen at airports such as Atlanta and New York-JFK over the weekend were easing. Some travelers are still waiting on rescheduled flights, however, and there will likely be several hundred flight cancellations and thousands of delays as the day goes on.

According to FlightAware, there were around 300 cancellations in the U.S. as of 9 a.m., which is already above average for an entire day of operations. There were about 1,270 delays.

Dallas/Fort Worth, Chicago O’Hare, Charlotte, North Carolina, and Reagan National reported the highest number of cancellations and delays Monday morning.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said over the weekend that operations should be close to normal by Monday evening.

According to the DOT and FAA, the outage was caused by a router installed during an upgrade of ATC communications systems.

The contractor that performed that upgrade, Duffy said Saturday, is L3Harris, a legacy technology provider for the FAA.

Either because of an installation mistake or a problem with the router itself, the router began “flooding” other routers in the system, the secretary said, leading to the outage.

The FAA has not made a final determination about the cause, but in either case, “we’re going to hold people accountable,” Duffy said.

“This was an FAA system that didn’t meet the moment,” he added. “A contractor didn’t meet the moment, or the equipment didn’t meet the moment.”

Duffy also noted that L3Harris actually owns the ATC communications network.

“I can’t go somewhere else, they own it,” he said.

Clearly frustrated with the situation, Duffy broadened his criticism to other private companies performing work for the DOT.

“Many of our contractors, many of our partners, they take our money and they provide really poor service to us,” he said. “Full stop. And we have demanded more.”

“L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA,” the company said in a statement released Saturday. “With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines, and air traffic operations seriously.”

The outage has also rekindled a months-long debate over funding for the DOT’s ongoing ATC modernization program. Duffy said Friday night that the FAA’s initial $30 billion target is no longer enough, and he now wants $50 billion.

#6166. Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

That majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

Colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

“I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”

Still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

#6165. Lufthansa Unveils Spacious Business Class Seats And Starlink For Select A320 Flights

Lufthansa is finally adding proper business class recliners to a small portion of its Airbus A320 fleet. The new seats will cost extra, even for passengers already booked in business class, but I welcome the option. After years of selling an economy seat with a blocked middle as business class, this is an upgrade worth getting excited about. It is a welcome change for an airline more accustomed to following competitors than setting the standard.

Lufthansa has opened bookings for its new “Premium Business Seat,” which will initially be installed on six Airbus A320ceo aircraft.

Each aircraft will receive eight recliners in the first two rows, arranged 2-2. Features include:

The six aircraft will also receive Starlink Wi-Fi during the retrofit.

These are recliners rather than flat beds, but they will represent a substantial improvement over the standard European business class seat, particularly on longer flights, which for those unaware is simply a regular economy class seat with the adjacent seat blocked.

The first modified aircraft is scheduled to enter service on December 16, 2026, initially operating various routes.

Dedicated deployment begins in February 2027, with seat reservations now available for flights from March 1, 2027:

Look for the Premium Business Seat designation when booking:

Lufthansa is retaining its standard business class offering behind the recliners. Business class passengers can select the larger seat during booking or subsequently through seat reservations, subject to the buy-up price: buying business class will not automatically get you a business class recliner on these routes.

I can already hear the objections: passengers are paying a premium for business class and then being asked to pay again for a better seat. But this is quite different than what intra-Europe business class has been for as long as I can remember on Lufthansa (except for the old A300s) and I would still rather have this option than continue with the blocked-middle arrangement as the only choice.

Lufthansa calls this a “commercial test.” Demand and the response to its booking options will determine whether the concept expands, but I think this concept is going to do great.

I wrote about the Eurowings Premium BIZ concept when it was announced last year. It was rather amusing that the budget carrier would introduce proper narrowbody business class seating before its “full service” Lufthansa Group siblings.

That project was intended to test the concept for other airlines within the group. Now we are seeing a similar approach at Lufthansa itself. The conventional European model has an operational advantage: airlines can move the curtain to adjust the size of business class. Dedicated recliners make that space less flexible.

Installing a small permanent cabin while retaining conventional business class behind it strikes me as a reasonable compromise. Lufthansa can sell the larger seats to passengers willing to pay for them and still expand the rest of business class when demand warrants. I would particularly like to see this spread to longer routes across the group. An empty middle seat is welcome, but it becomes a rather thin comfort proposition when you are spending several hours onboard, especially with those uncomfortable Recaro slimline seats.

One Mile At A Time suggests that Air France should introduce proper business class seats throughout its Airbus A220 fleet. I love that idea…SWISS should do the same.

The A220 offers an especially compelling opportunity because its economy cabin is arranged 2-3. With adjacent seats blocked in business class, Air France sells only three seats per row.

A proper 2-2 business class cabin would allow it to sell four seats across while giving passengers a wider seat. Additional legroom would consume more cabin length, of course, so the calculation is not quite as simple as adding another paying passenger in every existing row, but I think the math would work.

For illustration, replacing three conventional business class rows with two recliner rows would reduce capacity from nine passengers to eight. That is a modest reduction in exchange for a much better product, though the actual economics would depend on the seat dimensions and final layout.

I have already experienced what this could look like on my Bulgaria Air A220-300 flight from Sofia to Amsterdam. The airline offered proper recliners in a 2-2 layout, with leg rests and power outlets. I found it an excellent way to spend three hours flying within Europe.

Air France and SWISS have invested heavily in its premium reputation. A small recliner cabin on the A220 would extend that investment to the European flights that often begin or end a longhaul business class journey.

We do not need a flat bed from Paris to Amsterdam or Zurich to London, but on longer European routes, a comfortable recliner would give me another reason to choose one carrier over another.

Lufthansa will install eight Premium Business Seats on each of six Airbus A320s, with bookings now open for select Frankfurt flights to Athens, Nice, and Cairo from March 2027.

The surcharge will bother some passengers, understandably, but I think it makes sense and am pleased to see Lufthansa offer a better seat and hope the test succeeds.

Eurowings demonstrated a willingness to try something different. Lufthansa is following. Perhaps Air France, SWISS, and others will see an opportunity too. European business class has room to improve, and a seat that is actually different from economy is a very good place to start.

#6164. Trump Blames Buttigieg For FAA Meltdown While Elon Musk Blames Sean Duffy

President Donald Trump blames Pete Buttigieg for the nationwide FAA meltdown. Elon Musk, meanwhile, is pointing at the tTransportation Secretary Trump appointed, claiming Sean Duffy rejected an offer of free Starlink service. The finger-pointing continues, but neither accusation tells stranded passengers exactly why a router installation brought the system down.

Speaking to reporters on November 16, Trump singled out his predecessor’s transportation secretary for the failure that halted departures across the United States:

“Buttigieg ruined the system. He totally ruined it.”

When asked what personal responsibility he accepted, Trump responded:

He also praised Duffy and attributed the disruption to aging equipment. I have already addressed the problem with blaming the previous administration. America’s air traffic control infrastructure has suffered from decades of deferred investment. That includes the Biden administration, but also Trump’s first term and the administrations before it.

Friday’s failure, however, occurred during work performed under the current administration. An explanation of what Buttigieg allegedly did wrong would be useful, but of course Buttigieg is just the whipping boy for an administration that shows no personal responsibly for any of its deleterious actions.

Musk has offered a different accusation. In a post on X, he wrote:

“Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were.”

Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were. https://t.co/OZwDeiXOAr

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 16, 2026

That is a pointed criticism of the same official Trump says handled the situation well, but Musk does not explain when the offer was made, what equipment or service was included, where it would have been deployed, or how it would have prevented this particular failure…what a surprise.

I would like Duffy to answer the allegation directly. Was there an offer? What did it cover? Why was it declined? If the proposal was unsuitable, explain why.

Musk should also substantiate his assertion that the service would have been needed here. Being able to offer satellite internet does not establish that his proposed “gift” would have kept this particular network operating.

I love Starlink as an airline passenger. It is easily the best inflight internet service available now, and it increasingly influences which flights I book. But that does not mean it is or would have been a solution to an air traffic control network failure.

According to the FAA’s explanation, excessive connection attempts flooded its telecommunications network, destabilizing aircraft communications and radar feeds. Investigators identified sites in El Dorado, Arkansas, and Amarillo, Texas. L3Harris had been working at El Dorado, including installing a new router. Blocking those locations apparently stabilized the network. The broadcasting function on the new routers was also disabled as a precaution.

To support Musk’s claim, we would need to know whether his proposed Starlink connections would have bypassed the affected equipment and preserved the necessary communications.  Perhaps Starlink could have provided useful redundancy…but maybe the proposed installation would have had no bearing on this failure.

Buttigieg has defended his record, pointing to improvements in controller staffing, runway safety, and flight cancellations during his tenure.

He also says he launched the communications modernization project that the current administration is continuing. His response asks for an accounting of the money already authorized and an explanation of why the execution of that work triggered such a widespread failure.

As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived. We reversed a decade of decline in air traffic controller staffing, drove down runway safety incidents, and when I left office we were experiencing the lowest flight cancellation rates in… https://t.co/68KleIhFEc

— Pete Buttigieg (@PeteButtigieg) November 16, 2026

They do not mean Buttigieg’s tenure should escape scrutiny. The January 2023 nationwide ground stop occurred on his watch, and the system still required enormous investment when he left office while his boss prioritized student loan forgiveness and federal mask mandates instead of accelerating infrastructure programs like Air Traffic Control modernization.

But acknowledging those shortcomings does not relieve the current administration of responsibility for its own decisions. Duffy has been Transportation Secretary for nearly two years. He oversees the department responsible for explaining this failure and should be held accountable for the actions under his watch.

There is an obvious temptation to enjoy the spectacle: Trump blames Buttigieg while Musk suggests Trump’s own transportation secretary rejected help. I find the contradiction revealing, but passengers deserve something more useful than competing accusations.

The investigation must establish what changed in the network, why that change caused such a widespread disruption, and whether the safeguards surrounding the work were adequate. Congress should examine the Starlink allegation too, if Musk can provide a concrete proposal and evidence supporting his account.

Duffy may have had reasonable grounds to decline whatever Musk offered, but he should be able to articulate them. Likewise, Musk may have identified a missed opportunity, but he should be able to demonstrate his rather glaring accusation.

And Trump should stop treating an investigation as unnecessary because he has already identified a political opponent to blame. The age of the equipment was known. The difficult task was upgrading it while maintaining reliable service. That is the work his administration undertook, and that is the work it must explain to a weary public.

Trump says Buttigieg ruined the system and accepts no personal responsibility. Musk says Duffy rejected free Starlink service that was needed. Both claims deserve scrutiny and neither establishes the technical cause of Friday’s meltdown.

I would be far more receptive to an administration that acknowledged a failure during a difficult modernization project and explained how it would improve the process. Instead, we keep receiving accusations, praise for the response, and demands for more money.

The passengers who lost days getting home deserve a candid explanation of what went wrong. So do the taxpayers being asked to fund the repair. Is this really a political issue that should divide us?

#6161. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in new Congress

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, said on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

“Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his new White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

“Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat said. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” said Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”

Despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

“Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he said Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”

Members of House Republicans’ new leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader shows that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up."

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, said Republicans should heed one big takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”

#6160. Review: Park Hyatt Vienna, My Favorite Hotel In The Austrian Capital

The Park Hyatt Vienna is not only my favorite hotels in Vienna, but one of my favorite Hyatt properties in the world. With excellent service, nice amenities, delicious breakfast, and central location, our latest stay was another great reminder of what a superb property this is.

Although we could have connected directly to Zürich after landing in Vienna, I was able to force a 23.5-hour layover into the itinerary, which gave us a chance to stay to the Park Hyatt Vienna, a hotel I’ve enjoyed many times over the years but it was the first time my children had come along.

I booked this for 35,000 World of Hyatt points (versus a cash rate of over €700) and applied a “Guest of Honor” to the reservation, which essentially marks me as “Globalist” in the system.

Our Austrian flight landed at 11:30 am into VIE and I had emailed the hotel requesting an early check-in, specifically noting that we would be happy to forgo an upgrade in order to access our room a few hours early. Our request was honored.

The Park Hyatt Vienna is ideally located on Am Hof in the heart of the old town, an easy walk from St. Stephen’s Cathedral and many of the places I most enjoy visiting in Vienna.

Checking in, I was welcomed back to the hotel and the amenities were explained, including breakfast and pool hours (most important to my kids!).

We were assigned room 331, a standard room with two twins beds. While not an upgrade, the room was spacious enough and quite comfortable with a desk, round table, chair, and the two beds.

My daughter jumped right into bed to go to sleep (it was, after all, about 3:15 am in Los Angeles), but I pulled her out: no napping today would hopefully mean no jet lag tomorrow.

The bathroom featured really beautiful stonework behind the bathtub and included two sinks, a separate water closet, and walk-in shower.

The room had a wardrobe that included a coffee machine, hot water kettle, and mini-bar including snacks and drinks.

A welcome amenity was also waiting for us including various chocolates and candies.

The room had plenty of 220-volt outlets and also a safe to lock valuables. Unfortunately, the room did not have any USB-C ports or wireless chargers.

A primary reason I booked this hotel was for the pool and wellness. My kids love to swim and I can’t think of a better hotel pool than this one: we spent a lot of time here in the afternoon and evening.

The entire pool and spa area is posh, with a full-range of treatments available but nice say chairs with fresh peaches and plums, a locker room, and a wellness area with a sauna and steam room available to all guests.

Side note: the hotel has a cryogenic machine in the spa that will let you stand in -110ºC temperatures for three minutes…I was tempted and probably would have tried it had I been alone.

Thankfully, there was no drama this time in the sauna!

> Read More: Accused Of Being A Child Predator at Park Hyatt Vienna!

The fitness center is located in the spa area on the lower level, but accessible 24/7 with your room card and includes TechnoGym equipment. I awoke an hour before the kids and went down to workout…a nice way to start the day and fight jet lag.

You mustn’t skip breakfast here, for it is truly a treat.

The Bank is the most beautiful part of the hotel: an ornate dining room that was once the grand lobby when this hotel was still a bank. Breakfast is served from 7:00 am each morning until 10:30 am (11:00 am on weekends) and includes a delicious buffet plus an additional a la carte menu. If breakfast isn’t clouded in your rate, it is €58 each, which while steep is really worthwhile considering all you get with it.

There’s a bar section in The Bank that includes alcohol, including a large cocktail menu, and lighter food. It’s open from 9:00 am to 1:00 am on Monday – Wednesday, till 2:00 am on Thursday – Saturday, and from 5:00 pm to 1:00 pm on Sunday (good luck finding anything open on Sunday in Vienna…).

The hotel’s Viennese café includes cakes, coffee and chocolates, as well as alcoholic drinks and snacks, with an outdoor terrace. Open each day from 9:00 am to 8:00 pm.

Open from 9:00 am to 6:00 pm daily, the Lounge offers a more informal dining experience where you can enjoy hot and cold drinks plus a variety of food. Menu here.

Finally, 24/7 room service is available. Menu here.

There used to be really posh cigar lounge in this hotel, but now it is a beauty salon (Vienna has banned indoor smoking after being a smoker’s haven for so many years).

Our entire say was marked by one pleasant service encounter after another. I had a nice extended conversation with teh doorman and another great conversation with the agent who checked me in. We had a nice chat with our waitress in The Bank and the spa staff was also very friendly. I do speak German, albeit with an American accent, and appreciated that the staff was willing to engage in my less-than-perfect German as opposed to switching to English.

This was another wonderful stay at the Park Hyatt Vienna and I’ll sum it up by saying simply that I cannot wait to return.

My original review is below, dating all the way back to August 2014. Heidi and I went for my birthday just weeks after we got married…the hotel had recently opened and we had a great stay. It’s nice to see this hotel age so gracefully and what a joy it is to share this property and the lovely city of Vienna with my children.

Vienna is a stately city rich with majestic architecture, an erudite culture, and a regal sense of style. In the center of the old city, replete with cobblestone walkways, horse drawn carriages, and glistening statues of historical luminaries, a new Park Hyatt hotel has opened on the site of a former monarchical bank. My wife and I celebrated my birthday in Vienna last weekend and stayed for two nights at Park Hyatt’s newest property.

A historic property located on Am Hof 2 in the heart of the First District of Vienna, a UNESCO World Heritage site, the hotel’s location cannot be beat. Within a few paces is the Goldenes Quartier shopping district, St. Stephan’s Cathedral, Hofburg Palace, Spanish Riding School, and many museums.

We began the day in Frankfurt with an early flight on Austrian Airlines to Vienna. I sent a note to the main hotel e-mail, park.vienna@hyatt.com, just before takeoff requesting an early check-in and had a response waiting when I landed in Vienna – the room was ready.

From Vienna Airport you have two public transportation options for getting into the city – the City Airport Train (CAT) which travels non-stop to the heart of Vienna or a suburban train (S-Bahn) which calls at several stations on the way into town, taking about 15 minutes longer than the direct service. The CAT is 14EUR one-way while the S-Bahn is 4.40EUR. We took the S-Bahn into town, then connected on the underground train (U-Bahn) to Herrengasse Station, which is just a short walk from the hotel.

A smiling porter greeted us outside the door and took our luggage. Inside, a friendly young man checked us in, speaking first in English when he noticed my American passport but then switching to German upon the request of my wife that I practice my Deutsch! He escorted us upstairs and demonstrated the hi-tech features of our room. Like many Park Hyatt properties, lighting and draperies are electronically controlled by a central push-button unit.

I loved the room – a spacious standard room with tremendous natural light, a great view, and functionality. The room featured copious electrical outlets – an essential amenity when taking my business on the road, as I did here even on my birthday weekend. The layout of the couch in front of the bed in front of the desk nicely utilized the space in the room and the separate entry hall insulated the room from outside noise.

Two doors decorated in geometric art-deco style, closed off the bathroom and entry hall from the bedroom. The bathroom was very large (and well-placed mirrors made it appear even larger) and featured a sizeable bathtub, walk-in rain shower, two sinks, and a separate water closet.

A minibar featured an Illy coffee machine with several packets of complimentary espresso and snack and drink for purchase. The refrigerator did make a rather loud humming sound that could be heard even when the bedroom door was closed. I am a heavy sleeper, but my wife woke me up one night to “turn the climate off” yet it was not the air conditioning, it was the refrigerator! It was not terrible, just noticeable.

It was warm outside and we had a problem getting the air conditioning to activate. Turns out one of the windows was open just ajar – just make sure all your windows are tightly shut and your room key is in the slot by the door or else your air conditioning will not function. Once on, the room cooled down rapidly. Vienna boasts exceptional weather so most of the year there is no need for a/c anyway.

The hotel offers three dining options in addition to 24-hour room service; The Bank, Pearl, and The Lobby Lounge. Pearl bar features an outdoor terrace in addition to a contemporary indoor seating area and specializes in cocktails. A tapas menu is available with food as substantial as Wiener Schnitzel also available.

The Lobby Lounge offers drinks and light meals and sits next to the Living Room, a cigar and whiskey lounge that is one of the hotel’s best features. Admittedly, I see little value in setting fire to and then inhaling a plant that is linked to lung cancer but many of my friends and my brother hold a different opinion, so I find myself in cigar bars quite often. If you are a conneousier of cigars or just enjoy an opulent room to enjoy a drink in with friends, this bar is not to be missed. With plush couches and rich wooden paneling on the walls, I felt like I was part of the gentry mulling over world affairs in the cigar and brandy room onboard the Titanic.

Finally, The Bank is the hotel’s most opulent restaurant and central to the character of the property. Here, on the site of the former cashier’s hall, we had breakfast each morning. Breakfast was 33EUR and the buffet was expansive with all that you would expect in a comprehensive breakfast—fresh squeezed juices, cereals, fruits, breads, cold-cuts, cheeses, breakfast meats, and eggs. Coffee (it was tremendous) as well as pancakes, waffles, French Toast, and eggs are included in the buffet and can be ordered from your server.

We spent hours in here each morning enjoying a leisurely breakfast (breakfast ends at 10:30a during the week and 11:00a on weekends) and found the service to be warm, personal, and punctual. I thought everything was great – my wife had a problem with her eggs on the first morning (soft boiled eggs came out hard-boiled, then an omelet ordered with no cheese was delivered with cheese) but the issues were quickly remedied and did not reoccur the next morning. The juices were remarkably tasty (apple, orange, and even grapefruit were exceptional) and my favorite part of the breakfast was the cheese-covered cooked tomatoes.

Lunch and dinner are also offered each night in The Bank and you will find no menu posted online because the menu, sourced with local ingredients, changes often. Prices were moderate and I was prepared to dine at the restaurant for my birthday, but when mentioning that I was especially looking for fish, the concierge directed me to a restaurant called Kornat about 15 minutes away by foot, which specializes in fish and seafood.

So I missed trying out The Bank for an evening meal, but I did appreciate the restaurant recommendation for the food was amazing and we enjoyed a prime outdoor table thanks to a call ahead from the concierge.

I do have one gripe and only one true gripe about the property: the in-room wireless internet speed was unreliable. The Park Hyatt Vienna offers complimentary wired and wi-fi internet, which is a nice feature, but I found myself on multiple occasions banging my hand on the desk with disgust as poor connectivity led to unacceptably long page load times and the inability to make internet-based telephone calls. Other times, though, the interent worked perfectly well with pages loading fast and no issue with Skype calls or viewing YouTube videos. Admittedly, I did not not bring my ethernet cable converter for my MacBook Air so I was unable to test the wired internet speed.

A large fitness studio with state-of-the-art, brand new equipment was much appreciated. Several bikes, treadmills, and ellipticals filled one side of the room while strength training equipment and free weights filled out the other. The room itself, with brass candelabras and wooden floors was an elegant place to work out and apples, bottled water, refrigerated towels, newspapers, and magazines were available.

The gym overlooks the swimming pool below, which sits on the site of the former bank vault. With an ornate frieze relief and elongated white leather couches, it offers a refreshing antidote to the hot afternoon sun (or cold). Adjacent to the pool is a lounge with chairs to relax and also steam room and sauna facilities. My one regret is that we did not spend an extra day in Vienna just to lounge around the spa. Certainly, seeing Vienna is the priority if your time is limited, but this is a great complimentary benefit of the hotel that seems to go unutilized, as I saw many hotel guests and no one using the pool or spa lounge. Full spa services are available here in the Arany Spa and you can even see the original 3-ton bank vault door.

This hotel is a category six property, meaning it is 25,000 Hyatt Gold Passport points per night or 12,500 points plus a $150 co-pay (my preferred method of payment to help stretch out my points). The daily rate during the summer is about 375EUR or $500. Gold Passport availblity is good.

I can’t tell you how much I enjoyed the city of Vienna and both my wife (who is not usually a city person) and I wish to return soon. When we do, we will definitely choose the Park Hyatt again, allowing an extra day for the spa and enjoying at a more leisurely pace one of Europe’s greatest capital cities.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Vienna is such a great city, and this hotel definitely seems to suit the historic feel of the place well.

#6159. 11 Best Vacation Rentals in Riviera Maya for Beach Access, Private Pools, and Jungle Views

From the bustling city of Cancún to the somewhat more tranquil bohemian beach town of Tulum, the Riviera Maya is home to some of Mexico’s most idyllic beaches along the Caribbean. Featuring turquoise waters, windswept bays, and wide swaths of verdant jungle harboring hidden cenotes, this region of the Yucatán Peninsula delivers equal parts serenity and adventure. After living in Mexico for over 10 years, I’ve stayed in and driven through many of the towns and beaches that make up this region, and it's hard to choose a favorite.

As wonderful as the beachfront views, jungle tranquility, and local activities are here, the vacation rentals in the Riviera Maya are equally as impressive. They have a way of making the surrounding nature feel even more pristine. Whether you’re venturing to the region solo or traveling with friends and family, there are gorgeous options for nearly every type of traveler, each offering a personalized way to visit this corner of the Caribbean. Read on for my favorite vacation rentals in the Riviera Maya, from city escapes in Cancún to beachy stays in Tulum and everything in between.

#6158. United CEO Still Keen on Merger Prospects

Months after American Airlines rejected his pitch for a merger, United CEO Scott Kirby remains convinced that U.S. carriers will have to consolidate to thrive.

“I think the biggest impediment is having a willing partner,” Kirby said at the Yahoo Finance Invest conference on Nov. 12. “I am more convinced today than I was when I wrote my note six months ago that it could get approval. It could get approval because it is good for customers.”

Kirby’s original pitch to American shocked the aviation industry, as it would have brought together two of the country’s largest commercial airlines and given the combined company a market share of just over 34%, a level of dominance not seen by any U.S. carrier in years. Analysts predicated that the Justice Department would reject the tie-up as anticompetitive, citing regulators’ decisions on much smaller attempted mergers over the past several years.

The speculation ended when American released a public statement saying it had no interest in a merger, and would stick to its existing turnaround plan.

But Kirby has continued to defend his proposal and the logic behind it, arguing that a consolidated United-American would deliver a better experience for customers, create more high-paying unionized jobs, and make the U.S. more competitive in international travel.

The CEO acknowledged Thursday that such a large deal would face obstacles but insisted they could be overcome.

“It wouldn’t be easy,” he said. “We’d have to do some divestitures, but I 100% think it could get approved.”

Airlines around the world are facing new pressure to cut costs or consolidate as jet fuel prices rise. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in April that he believes there is “room for some mergers” in the airline industry, but did not mention United or American by name.

Neither the Justice Department nor the Transportation Department ever formally weighed in on the potential United-American merger, as a final deal was never filed. President Donald Trump said he would not support it, and cited competition and consumer prices as the reason.

#6156. Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

“Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, said that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”

Ors said he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.
