As someone who will log over 200,000 miles in the air this year, my travel strategy centers on maximizing value with minimal effort, especially when flying United. Even though I’ve earned their invite-only Global Services status, pairing that status with a United credit card unlocks even more value.

While United has several different credit card offerings, the United Club℠ Business Card is the clear choice for me.

The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

United Airlines offers discounted award pricing to elite members and cardholders. These discounts stack with each other to yield bigger savings on flights. The minimum discounts don’t necessarily sound substantial. Cardholders receive at least a 10% discount on United-operated award flights, while elite members get a minimum discount of 15%.

And while those are impressive, we’ve actually found much bigger discounts than that, sometimes exceeding 100,000 miles per ticket. We've even seen one-way international business-class awards drop from over 300,000 miles to under 100,000 miles.

A recent real-world example just came up on my podcast. My co-host had just opened a United credit card and was looking at a flight home from Europe for his family of four. Award tickets in business class were 80,000 miles one-way, per passenger (plus taxes and fees).

As soon as the new United credit card was linked to his profile, he saw a 15% discount, or 12,000 fewer miles per award ticket. So, less than a week after signing up for the card, he had already saved 48,000 United miles.

United recently changed how members earn miles on paid flights. Now, members without a United credit card earn significantly fewer miles than they used to. The good news is that adding a United credit card to your wallet can now boost your earnings by 30% to 50%.

For a top-tier 1K or Global Services member, that’s an extra three miles per dollar on every eligible ticket. For a road warrior taking two $450 round trips monthly, that could mean more than 30,000 extra miles earned per year.

United also changed access to United Club lounges. Its All Access membership, which includes guest privileges, can cost as much as $1,400, depending on your elite status

However, the United Club Business Card gives you two ways to significantly reduce your out-of-pocket costs for the All Access membership: Spend $50,000 on the card in a calendar year, or hold Premier Gold status or higher. With a $695 annual fee, the card can be a much cheaper way to bring guests into United Clubs.

I don’t spend much time in lounges when traveling for work, preferring to arrive as close to departure as possible. But family travel moves at a slower pace, making lounge access a welcome respite, especially with United's recent upgrades.

Access for the family used to be a “nice” plus. With the new and refreshed clubs United has opened recently, the lounge game has stepped up more than a notch.

It started with a beautiful refresh of the West United Club in Denver a few years ago. This was an existing club that shut down for a massive refresh, which gave us a peek into what the future holds for club design. Denver also debuted United’s new “grab and go” concept, United Club Fly.

Fast forward to 2026 and the airline has made two massive improvements on the United Club front. United recently opened a new, 800-seat club at George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) in Houston with an outdoor terrace. It also just opened a brand new club in the new E terminal at Washington-Dulles International Airport (IAD).

Not every club is as stellar as these new gems, but United is clearly upping its game.

United's recent changes make a compelling case for pairing elite status with a credit card. For business travelers, the United Club Business Credit Card offers more miles, cheaper awards and maybe even a quiet place to sit with the family on your next vacation.

#6139. Why Qantas Picked A 'Proven' Rolls-Royce Engine Over A Theoretically Better One For Project Sunrise

Ultra-long-haul flights have exploded in popularity over the past decade, largely because the current generation of long-range widebodies is exceptionally fuel-efficient. Recent advances in efficiency and capability are now allowing Qantas to launch Project Sunrise, two ultra-long-haul nonstop routes that will both be longer than today's longest flights (Singapore to New York JFK and Newark) by a wide margin.

The longest of these, Sydney to London Heathrow, will last over 20 hours. Qantas placed its official order for the Project Sunrise aircraft in 2022, selecting the Airbus A350-1000ULR after an intense competition between the A350 and the Boeing 777X.

What's unusual is that the 777X has been relatively popular while being equipped with the world's most advanced jet engines. However, Qantas still selected the older A350-1000 to operate the world's longest flights, a move that solidifies the Airbus A350's position as the world's ultimate long-range airliner.

The core of Project Sunrise is the launch of new ultra-long-haul nonstop flights connecting Sydney to London Heathrow and New York JFK. The longer of the two, Sydney to London Heathrow, will be 9,188 NM (17,016 km), and will also be the first Project Sunrise route to launch in October 2027.

The first A350-1000ULR will arrive in April and will operate short-haul crew familiarization flights, while the London route will launch once Qantas has three examples to hand. Sydney to New York will be the second route to launch, and Qantas will subsequently place the A350-1000ULR throughout its current route network, mainly displacing Boeing 787s to launch new routes.

While Qantas has previously stated that it will also connect Melbourne to London and New York, these routes appear to be less of a priority based on Qantas's most recent announcements. They may only come with the final A350-1000ULR deliveries as the carrier increases its focus on Sydney. Flight times from Sydney to London will last over 20 hours, or about two hours longer than the Singapore-JFK service.

Some have expressed skepticism over whether passengers would prefer a 20-hour nonstop over a 24-hour one-stop route. However, there was similar skepticism a decade ago about the commercial viability of 17 to 18-hour flights, like Singapore-JFK or Qantas's own Perth-London route. By and large, these routes have proven popular with passengers and have become quite lucrative.

Technically, the Airbus A350-900ULR could likely operate the Project Sunrise routes, but Qantas desired more capability. The A350-900ULR is a fairly minimal modification to the A350-900, featuring weight reductions and software changes to enable more fuel to be carried in the plane's center tank. With a deactivated forward cargo hold, it essentially trades payload for fuel.

Qantas desired a larger aircraft that could carry significantly more payload than the A350-900ULR. Airbus offered the A350-1000ULR, while Boeing offered the 777X. Initial discussions centered around an optimized version of the smaller 777-8. It's unclear what exactly Boeing planned for the 777-8, but as delays with the program continued, the 777-9 also came into the picture.

While the plane's current brochure range is too short for Project Sunrise, the 777-9 could have received a higher gross weight and auxiliary fuel tanks to make the route, albeit with a reduced capacity. It's generally believed that this was offered as an interim solution until the 777-8 was ready, and it was even reported that Boeing also offered the 777-200LR as another alternative solution.

Ultimately, Qantas announced the A350 as the preferred choice for Project Sunrise in 2019 for flights to commence in 2023, and then placed its official order in 2022 (the order was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic). The timeline is crucial because the 777X is one of the most delayed aircraft programs in recent history.

At 10,573 miles (17,015 km), the journey is no mean feat.

The Boeing 777X will be exclusively powered by the General Electric GE9X. While the Rolls-Royce Trent XWB on the A350 is a remarkable engine, the GE9X will be unrivaled in terms of thermal efficiency, in large part due to the extensive use of advanced materials like ceramic matrix composites. It can almost be considered half a generation ahead of the Trent XWB/Trent 1000/General Electric GEnx.

However, the GE9X and the 777X are also unproven. Qantas's desired timeline for Project Sunrise would have made it one of the first operators of the 777X. While General Electric has a proven track record in delivering dependable large turbofan engines, any new engine experiences teething issues upon introduction, which can be problematic to deal with.

What's more, early production of the GE9X and the 777X will be limited (as is the case with any new aircraft), resulting in slow deliveries during the 777X's first few years. In comparison, the Trent XWB is a proven engine that has been remarkably trouble-free, while the A350 is an established type.

While deliveries of the A350 have currently been slow due to supply-chain constraints, this has been affecting the entire airline industry and is hardly unique to the A350. As a whole, it's less risky to go with the aircraft and engine type that has been in service for nearly a decade compared to the brand-new plane/engine.

The GE9X will be an excellent engine once it enters service, but this doesn't mean that the 777X will burn less fuel than the A350-1000. The aircraft still retains a heavy-metal fuselage, while also featuring massive wings. It's a fundamentally larger, heavier plane that will be significantly thirstier than the A350-1000, and the 777-9 addresses this through its massive capacity, giving it competitive per-seat economics.

The 777-8, however, is smaller than either, while costing almost the same to operate as the 777-9, making it an uneconomical aircraft. The advantage of the 777-8 is its field performance and range, but for Project Sunrise, the A350-1000 is more than capable with the ULR improvements.

As a whole, the 777-8 has been an extremely slow seller due to these issues. In addition, the 777X's delays were also very problematic. In 2019 (the same year as when Qantas publicly selected the A350), Boeing planned to start delivering the 777-9 in 2021, while the 777-8 was delayed to 2023, the same year that Qantas intended to start Project Sunrise flights at the time. At the time, there were already concerns about whether the timeline would stick.

These concerns have proven valid, as the 777-9's entry into service is now set for 2027. Meanwhile, development of the 777-8 has been paused due to a lack of demand, with Boeing instead focusing on the 777-9 and then the 777-8F, as these models are more popular. For Qantas, relying on the 777-8 would have been significantly riskier than going with a derivative of the in-service A350-1000.

A key factor the airline can capitalize on is that Qantas will be the only carrier to offer non-stop services on these competitive routes.

While it has the same 'ULR' designation as the A350-900ULR, the engineering to create the A350-1000ULR is closer to how Airbus created the A321XLR. Key to the plane's range is the addition of a new 20,000-liter integrated Rear Centre Tank, derived from the design of the RCT on the A321XLR. In addition, the A350-1000ULR features a higher Maximum Takeoff Weight of 322 tons.

This will be available on all future A350-1000s. However, Qantas has an exclusivity deal on the A350-1000ULR variant specifically. To further extend the plane's range, Qantas is installing just 238 seats, making it the lowest-capacity A350-1000 configuration in the world. There will be six first class suites built by Safran, 52 business class seats based on the Safran Unity, 40 premium economy seats based on the Safran Z535i, and just 140 economy seats based on the Recaro R3.

In addition, the A350-1000ULR will also come with a new crew rest facility for the pilots, of which there will be four on each flight. Some have questioned Qantas's decision to install economy seats on the A350-1000ULR, considering that Singapore Airlines' A350-900ULRs lack this cabin.

However, Qantas is catering to a much larger leisure and visiting friends/relatives market than Singapore Airlines, and it specifically bought the A350-1000ULR for its size as well as its payload capacity. Economy was always part of the plan, and Qantas will be configuring the economy seats with more legroom while also offering an onboard 'Wellness Zone.'

Thank you for subscribing to our newsletter,

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6138. Delta’s Amazon Leo Wi-Fi Plans Face Uncertainty After Rocket Failure

Inflight Wi-Fi is currently undergoing quite the glow-up, thanks to the widespread rollout of Starlink Wi-Fi. Not only are most airlines offering this service for free, but it also represents a massive upgrade in terms of speeds.

While carriers like United, American, Southwest, and Alaska, are all rolling out Starlink Wi-Fi, Delta is countering the trend, and went with Amazon Leo, which is Amazon’s competitor to Starlink. This has of course made quite some headlines, due to Elon Musk’s public ridicule of Delta, plus what Delta CEO Ed Bastian reportedly said behind closed doors. Along those lines, there’s some potentially bad news for Delta.

On Sunday, November 15, 2026, a Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance (ULA), a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed about 10 minutes after lifting off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. This was the first mission failure in ULA’s roughly 20-year history, and the company has issued the following statement in response to this:

Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.

Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today.

ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us. That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.

We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible.

ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action.

We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.

BREAKING: The Vulcan Rocket of United Launch Alliance (Lockheed Martin and Boeing) suffered total mission failure minutes after launchAll 40 Amazon Leo satellites onboard were destroyed pic.twitter.com/NskOOy8uAW

This isn’t about the loss of 40 satellites as such, as that’s only a tiny percentage of the satellites that were supposed to be deployed as part of Amazon Leo, across dozens of missions. Instead, the issue is that this will now delay future launches, while an investigation is performed, improvements are made, etc.

Prior to this, 398 satellites had already been deployed for Amazon Leo, across 14 launches, making up around 12% of the 3,236 satellites that are needed for global coverage.

This rocket failure is absolutely a setback for the rollout of Amazon Leo, though it remains to be seen just how much of a delay it represents. Amazon has released a statement saying it remains confident that ULA will learn from the mission and deliver on their long term plans.

We know that Amazon Leo was targeted for an initial service rollout before the end of 2026 in select regions, with a more widespread introduction in the months that follow.

Rockets are far from my area of expertise, but based on my understanding from those who know more than I do, it seems that this likely represents a delay of several months to the program, at an absolute minimum, if not more. As you’d expect, a thorough investigation needs to be performed, any learnings need to be implemented, etc.

Keep in mind that JetBlue was supposed to introduce Amazon Leo as of 2027, and Delta was supposed to introduce Amazon Leo as of 2028. I think it’s safe to say that the timeline looks worse today than it did 24 hours ago.

One of the risks with picking a service that’s still in development is that the timeline is really quite fluid, and this is an example of that. Delta has of course made quite the headlines over its lack of selecting Starlink, and I imagine this will only make matters worse for the airline.

United expects to have Starlink on all planes by the end of 2027, while Delta was only going to start introducing Amazon Leo on less than half of its planes as of 2028. So the airline was already at a disadvantage there, and that disadvantage has just grown even bigger.

A Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered a failure on Sunday, as it was on a mission to deploy dozens of Amazon Leo satellites. While this was only a small part of the overall rollout of this, the failure will absolutely delay additional rocket launches, which are needed to get this network functioning. This was the first mission failure in ULA’s roughly 20-year history.

It’s anyone’s guess how much of a delay it will cause for the introduction of Amazon Leo, and what impact that will have on Delta and JetBlue. It’s absolutely certain that the timeline looks worse now than 24 hours ago, though we don’t know much more as of now.

Getting a great deal on a cruise is getting harder. Strong demand for cruises allows cruise lines to raise fares significantly and cut back on last-minute discounts to fill unsold cabins.

As a result, the fares you’ll find for cruises can sometimes be much higher — by 20% or more — than what you were expecting.

So, how do you get the best cruise deal if you’re trying to book a cruise for this year and beyond? To start: Don’t panic. Even if fares seem high, you can find ways to save when booking a vacation at sea.

Below, we’ve assembled 10 of our top tips for finding a bargain on a cruise. These are travel hacks that can work any time — not just when fares are rising. Combine a few of these strategies, and you are sure to find the best cruise deals available on your next sailing.

As is the case for resorts on land, floating resorts (i.e., cruise ships) can be significantly less expensive during the “offseason” travel months of September, October and November.

These are months when kids are typically back in school and family travel drops off, resulting in diminished demand for many types of travel, including cruises.

These months also fall during the Caribbean's hurricane season, which keeps some people away from land resorts and cruise ships in the region.

Related: Cruising during hurricane season: What to know — and should you go?

In addition to the fall months, the offseason period for cruising generally includes parts of January and February, but it varies by region.

Traditionally, the summer months of June, July and August have been high season in many cruise destinations like the Caribbean, Europe and Alaska. The periods around major holidays — such as Easter, Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day — also are considered the busy season for cruising and bring higher prices.

It’s a growing truism of the cruise world: The earlier you book, the better price you’ll get.

Cruise lines often open departures for bookings with the lowest prices at which they want to sell the trips. Then, as the departures start filling up, they slowly raise prices on the remaining inventory.

To get the best price on any particular sailing, your best bet, in many cases, is to book right when the sailing opens for sale. This means planning way in advance. Many cruise lines open their reservations for sailings two or even three years before departure.

Booking far in advance can pay off in more ways than one. One big advantage to booking ahead of time is that you’re far more likely to get the exact cabin type you want. On many ships, the least expensive cabins and most expensive suites often sell out first and quickly.

Related: A beginners guide to picking a cruise line

Worried you might miss out on a deal by booking a cruise super far in advance? Here’s the good news: If, for some reason, the cost of your cruise drops at a later date, you often can get your fare reduced to match the lower price (see, Monitor Your Fare, below).

As noted above, cruise lines typically offer their lowest fare for any given sailing just after it opens for booking — often two or even three years before it’s scheduled to begin.

Generally, the fare will only go up as the sailing date approaches, but, in some cases, cruise lines will drop the price of a cruise significantly at the last minute. This can happen when the line finds itself with a lot of unsold cabins for a voyage.

If you’re flexible and can travel on short notice, you can sometimes find a last-minute deal for a cruise where the line is scrambling to fill berths just before a departure.

A key thing to know here is that last-minute discounting isn’t as common as it used to be. Like airlines, cruise lines have become much more savvy about revenue management over the years, and it’s rarer that they find themselves with a lot of unsold inventory on sailings just before departure.

You’ll also have to be flexible to take advantage of these deals. If you have a specific cabin type on a specific sailing on a specific ship that you’re eyeing for a vacation, you can’t count on it being available — especially not at a rock-bottom rate.

Also, don’t forget that you may pay a lot more for flights to a cruise and a precruise hotel if you wait until the last minute to book them. Last-minute cruise deals often work best for travelers who live near a departure port that they can reach easily by car, avoiding the cost of last-minute flights and hotels.

Booking early doesn't mean you've locked in the lowest fare. Cruise lines use dynamic pricing. Fares can rise or fall even after you book, so it pays to keep an eye on prices.

If the fare drops for the same sailing and cabin category, you may be able to get the lower price.

This is often the case until the last few months before the sailing begins, when the cruise enters what’s known as the final payment window. At that point, the fare you’ve paid is locked in.

Cruise lines won't necessarily adjust your booking automatically — you'll need to ask. Policies vary by line. Many of the big lines — including Royal Caribbean, Carnival, Norwegian and Princess — have some form of price-protection or “best price guarantee” program.

Most times, you can reprice your booking at the lower fare before making your final payment. After final payment, your options narrow. Some lines will offer an upgrade, onboard credit or a future cruise credit equal to the difference, rather than cash.

To request a price adjustment, contact the cruise line or your travel agent with your booking number and details of the lower fare. Make sure you're comparing the same sailing and cabin category, and note that not all fare types allow for changes to the fare you’ve paid after booking.

Read the fine print, too. Repricing can mean giving up promotions tied to your original booking, such as onboard credit —  and some lines exclude shorter sailings.

Some cruise-specialist travel agents will monitor your fare for you. You can also set up fare alerts that will send you an email if the price has dropped.

At many big lines, you’ll find that the newest, most amenity-filled cruise ships sell at a premium price. Older ships come with a discount.

The older ships are, of course, older, and they sometimes don’t have quite as much to offer on board as the newer ships. But if you’re looking for a deal, they can bring great value.

If you're not fussy about where you sleep, there's another way to trim your fare. That's booking a guarantee cabin.

A guarantee fare lets you choose the category — inside, oceanview, balcony or suite — but not the specific cabin. The line assigns your room later, sometimes just days before sailing. What you're guaranteed is a cabin in the category you paid for, or a better one.

In return for that flexibility, lines often price guarantee cabins below the cheapest cabin you can pick yourself in the same category. The savings vary by line, sailing and category, but can run from roughly $50 to $200 or more per person.

That's the trade-off: You give up control over deck and location. You could land near the elevators or a noisy venue. If you need a specific spot — close to the dining room for mobility reasons, adjoining cabins for a family or midship if you're prone to seasickness — book a cabin you choose yourself.

Occasionally, when a ship is full in your category, a guarantee passenger sometimes gets bumped up to a better one. This is the exception, rather than the rule. Plenty of guarantee bookings end up in the least desirable cabin in the category.

Are you a plan-it-yourself type of traveler? We get it. Many of TPG’s staffers are that way, too.

But even if you book all your land trips on your own, you might want to use a travel agent who is a cruise specialist to book your next voyage.

One big reason is that cruise-selling travel agents often have access to lower bulk fares for sailings that aren’t available to the general public. Big travel agencies will block out large chunks of cabins on ships soon after they open for booking to lock in such group fares, then sell them over the coming months.

When you book through cruise travel agents, you can sometimes receive lower fares and extra perks like onboard credit or amenities.

Travel agents specializing in cruising will also be able to guide you through the many types of cabin categories on some cruise ships and steer you away from cabins to avoid. Plus, they’ll be there for you when things go wrong on a cruise.

You don't have to be planning an extended family reunion or large event to get a group deal. Most cruise lines treat a booking of several cabins as a group — and they reward it.

The threshold varies by line; eight cabins is common, though some lines start lower. Perks can include a discounted group fare, onboard credit and, for the person who organizes the booking, a free berth. That's essentially one free fare, not including taxes and fees. The bigger the group, the bigger the perks.

Even if you aren't traveling with a crowd, it's possible to build one. Cruise forums and social media groups often organize sailing-specific meetups where strangers pool cabins under a single group booking to reach the threshold. Each cabin typically pays its own fare, and some organizers pass part of the savings along to the group.

Group bookings can come with their own payment schedules and change or cancellation rules, so read the terms before you commit. These bookings usually run through a cruise-specialist travel agent or the line's group desk.

Some of the best bargains in the cruise world are the voyages that cruise ships make as they reposition from one part of the world to another.

This is because cruise lines often have trouble selling these trips. They typically have oddball itineraries with very few port calls and lots of sea days — something that doesn’t appeal to many cruisers. Repositioning cruises also tend to be considerably longer than standard weekend getaways or weeklong voyages — a turnoff to the many travelers who have limited vacation days.

To sell them, cruise lines often have to reduce their per-day prices sharply, making them a bargain.

Among the most common repositioning cruises are sailings between the Caribbean and Europe in the spring as lines move ships to Europe for the summer. Similarly, there’s a wave of repositioning cruises between Europe and the Caribbean in the fall.

You’ll also find some repositioning cruises every year between the Caribbean and Alaska and between the West Coast and Asia or Australia.

Some cruise lines offer reduced fares or special perks to special groups, these include military members and veterans, teachers, seniors and residents of particular states or regions.

Terms vary widely. Eligibility for spouses, age cutoffs and whether the discount can be combined with other promotions all differ by line, so ask when you book and have your documentation ready.

#6136. Condor Asks Passengers To Share Magazines To Save On Fuel Costs

It’s obviously a tough time for many airlines around the globe, given the impact that higher jet fuel prices are having on economics, in an industry with razor thin margins. Along those lines, German airline Condor is looking for all kinds of way to save on fuel costs… including reducing the number of inflight magazines onboard!

aeroTELEGRAPH flags how as of November 1, 2026, German airline Condor has slashed the number of inflight shopping magazines it has onboard flights. Instead of each passenger having their own inflight shopping magazine:

The airline has confirmed that the goal is “to reduce the weight on board and thus fuel consumption,” and it’s pointed out how the inflight shopping magazine is also available digitally, via the inflight entertainment system. These inflight shopping magazines have both the food & drinks available for purchase, as well as duty free items.

Initially this is being viewed as a trial, and after winter, the airline will decide whether or not to continue with this policy.

Over the years, we’ve seen a good number of airlines eliminate duty free sales and inflight magazines, with the primary motivation being to reduce the weight of the aircraft. However, it’s definitely a bit unusual to see an airline put a magazine at some seats, but not others. After all, some people may prefer a physical magazine, so are you supposed to ask your seat mate if you can borrow it, or how does that work?!

I am curious if this leads to a reduction in onboard sales. After all, passengers onboard flights are a pretty captive audience, and might browse a magazine out of boredom. I mean, just look at SkyMall, in all of its former glory. Did anyone really need the world’s largest wine glass, or a bigfoot garden statue? Nope! But if you’re bored enough, you might be convinced of some pretty wild things!

Condor isn’t stopping at inflight magazines when it comes to trying to find ways to reduce the weight of aircraft. This is part of a larger project at the airline, with the goal of operating flights as efficiently as possible, with as much resource conservation as possible.

In order to find additional cost saving measures, the airline is undergoing a cabin clearing process, as it’s described. This involves removing all movable items from the aircraft, inspecting them, and then deciding if they’re needed anymore. Of course safety equipment is the one exception.

Realistically, I can’t imagine there’s all that much that can be removed anymore, without cutting some very basic amenities on long haul flights. After all, it’s not the 1970s, and it’s not like there are endless amenities onboard for passengers.

German airline Condor is asking passengers to share inflight shopping magazines, as part of an initiative intended to reduce the weight of aircraft. While it goes without saying that a single magazine doesn’t lead to a huge increase in fuel burn, when you multiply it by the number of magazines, the number of flights an aircraft makes, and the number of aircraft in the fleet, it sure can add up.

While eliminating things like seat back magazines is nothing new, the concept of sharing magazines is a new one for me. Obviously Condor wants it both ways — it still wants to be able to make money selling things, but doesn’t want the weight of one magazine per person.

I am curious if this test proves successful, or if this leads to a material reduction in sales.

What’s your take on Condor’s cost saving initiative?

#6135. Starlux Adds First Route to Australia, New Zealand

Taiwanese carrier Starlux is branching out to Australia and New Zealand with a new, one-stop connection.

Starting March 23, 2027, the airline will fly from Taipei to Sydney to Auckland. Flights will initially operate four times weekly, then switch to daily on May 1. Starlux will operate the route using Airbus A330-900 aircraft.

Taipei-Sydney-Auckland will be the airline’s first one-stop or through route; all other flights are nonstop from Taiwan. Officials said the one-stop approach will give travelers access to “two incredible destinations in one journey.”

Starlux said it is working with Qantas to arrange connecting flights to other destinations in Australia, New Zealand, and Fiji.

Starlux is headquartered in Taipei and mainly flies within East and Southeast Asia, though it also offers service to North America and Europe. In the U.S., it serves Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Phoenix, and Ontario, California.

#6134. Democrats mulling Iran war funding cutoff strategy

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

“I know it’s going to be my main push,” he said. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”

Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators said. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”

While ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the new Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how quickly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, said that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”

Democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

"I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries said.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro said earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

The administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks said. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#6133. 28 Seats: European Carrier Reveals First-Ever Premium Economy Cabin For US Routes

Irish flag carrier Aer Lingus has become the latest airline to join the premium economy revolution, with the airline having just unveiled its new product offering ahead of its launch next October. It plans to fit 28 spacious recliner seats on ten of its Airbus A330 widebody twinjets. This will represent the bulk of its twin-aisle fleet, with ch-aviation showing that it currently has two Airbus A330-200s and 12 A330-300s.

While the introduction of premium economy for the first time in the Irish flag carrier's history is the main headline, Aer Lingus will also use this refurbishment as an opportunity for a nose-to-tail reimagining of its A330 interiors, with business and economy class also changing. Passengers flying on Aer Lingus' US routes will be the first to benefit from the update, with Dublin to New York JFK being the first route.

Aer Lingus has chosen the RECARO R4 seat for its new premium economy cabin on the Airbus A330, which will be able to accommodate 28 passengers in four seven-abreast (2-3-2) rows. These flyers will be able to look forward to an increased seat pitch of 38 inches, with the seats measuring 18-19 inches in width. They will also offer guests a greater deal of recline, at eight inches. The soft product is strong too.

On this front, Aer Lingus says that its premium economy passengers can expect, among other things, "an upgraded three-course dining experience, complimentary drinks throughout the flight, comfortable bedding, an amenity kit and noise-reducing headphones." All the while, Starlink WiFi will help them to stay more connected inflight than ever before. Lynne Embleton, the CEO of Aer Lingus, said that:

"Our ambition here is simple. We want to give our customers greater choice, comfort, and connectivity, while creating an experience that feels unmistakably Aer Lingus."

It is no secret in the world of modern commercial aviation that the transatlantic market between Europe and North America is one of the most lucrative corridors around. As such, premium demand is often high, and Aer Lingus is set to tap into this trend by launching its newly fitted A330s on the long-haul route from Dublin (DUB) to New York (JFK). These flights will begin in just under a year, on October 1, 2027.

Initially, Aer Lingus plans to deploy its premium economy-equipped A330s on the EI104/105 rotation. These flights are operated today by the A330-300, which is the larger and more numerous of Aer Lingus' two variants of the Airbus A330. At the time of writing, these widebody twinjet aircraft feature a two-class configuration with 30 business class flatbeds and either 283 or 287 economy class seats on board.

As more and more of Aer Lingus' Airbus A330s are retrofitted with the new cabins, the carrier will be able to roll the product out on a growing variety of, as it puts it, "additional North American routes." According to Cirium, an aviation analytics company, its present A330 services across the pond from Dublin serve Boston, Chicago, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Miami, New York, Orlando, and San Francisco.

The 8-hour flight rule explains when Premium Economy beats Business Class on price, comfort, sleep, and corporate travel value.

With ten of Aer Lingus' A330s being taken out of service for the premium economy refit, this presents an opportunity for the Irish flag carrier to undertake a nose-to-tail reimagining of its widebody twinjet fleet. This is exactly what it plans to do, hence the aforementioned addition of Starlink WiFi. This will also see it refit its business class cabins with 28 Collins Elevation suites in a four-abreast 1-2-1 layout.

The carrier is also reimagining its business class catering offering and fitting its A330s with a snack bar. As for economy class, Aer Lingus promises "ergonomic seating, six-way adjustable leather headrests, [and] refreshed dining options."

#6132. Welcome To One Mile At A Time, Daniel Ross! Here’s What’s Going On…

It’s a big day here at OMAAT, as I’m delighted to welcome our first full time contributor in the site’s nearly 19-year history. Let me start with a little bit of background, and then I’ll talk about Daniel Ross, who is joining the team. As a creature of habit, this feels like a whole new frontier, but I’m excited!

I’m incredibly fortunate that I’ve never had a “traditional” job — I started OMAAT my freshmen year of college as a hobby (after having been passionate about miles & points in my teens), and nearly 19 years later, that’s still what I get to do full time.

I’m blessed that I can wake up every day and cover an industry that I love. While OMAAT is a business that pays my bills, it has never been exclusively about maximizing profitability, coming up with some five-year business plan, or seeing what opportunities there are to sell. It’s also my hobby.

Now, the downside to this — at least if you ask my family — is that I also “work” seven days per week, 365 days per year. Other sites in the space that are this size might have one or two dozen contributors, but for me, that has never sounded very appealing. My passion is actually getting to cover the industry, rather than managing a huge group of people.

Let me be clear, I don’t do this alone, as I have two great people who do a ton of to work to handle everything in the background, much of which readers don’t see — Jeremy oversees business development (basically anything having to do with the business side of things), and Howie manages things related to credit cards and tech (which largely helps pay the bills!). I’m incredibly grateful for their contributions, because it allows me to focus on content.

In the past, I’ve had some part time contributors, and I also very much appreciate the contributions they’ve made. However, given the volume of content at OMAAT, it’s hard for that to make a meaningful difference in terms of workload, etc.

Recently I finally accepted the fact that it’s time to add a full time contributor. That’s not because I want to meaningfully change anything about the site in terms of the content mix, or because I want to step back from things. Quite to the contrary, it’s because I want to do the best possible job I can.

As many people can surely attest to, if you take pride in what you do (rather than just turning your site into an AI slop machine), it just takes a lot more effort than in the past to accomplish the same results, given how everything on the internet has shifted. Aside from spending time with family, this site and industry is basically my entire life — it’s not a means to an end, but the passion as such is the “end.”

So my hope is that by having someone join the team full time on the content front, I can actually put more time into the areas that I’d like to improve — engaging with the community, responding to comments and emails, etc. These are all things I’ve gotten very bad at, not due to a lack of caring, but due to a lack of hours in the day, especially as someone who has two small kids.

For that matter, I’m planning on imminently launching a new video series (which I wrote about over the summer), not to replace written content, but to complement it, as I think we have a unique angle for it. I just couldn’t carve out the time for that without getting some more help. So I’m finally no longer putting this off, and I’m ripping the band aid-off.

Let me emphasize that the goal here is to genuinely do a better job of providing useful and interesting content to community members, rather than anything else. This isn’t a “we’re cutting free food & drinks in economy due to customer feedback, it’s an enhancement” situation!

I’d like to welcome Daniel Ross to OMAAT, as he’s joining full time as of today! Daniel isn’t new to the miles & points world, as has he contributed to many sites over the years (The Points Guy, Business Insider, Upgraded Points, etc.), so odds are good that you may be familiar with him (and you can follow him at cometravelwithdan on Instagram).

Shortly Daniel will be publishing his first post introducing himself, but let me provide a little background on how this came to be, and how I envision this evolving.

I’ve actually never met Daniel before in person. I’ve always had respect for his work and think he has done a great job with writing, social media, video content, etc. We hadn’t connected until not that long ago, and hit it off.

When it comes to working with people, and especially adding them to the OMAAT team, I try to follow my gut, and I think Daniel will be a good fit. I know OMAAT readers value opinions, analysis, and someone with interesting takes, and I think Daniel checks all those boxes. For example, he was just telling me about Aerolineas Argentinas’ quirky baggage allowance, so I’m excited for the expanded content coverage, as that’s something I would’ve never written about (I’m more into covering Air Côte d’Ivoire’s insane first class carry-on allowance).

One of the specific reasons I don’t want a dozen contributors is because I think it’s important for people to have a unique voice, and for readers to get to know that, and I think people will enjoy hearing Daniel’s takes on things.

Daniel also does a great job with social media and video content, which is something that I’ve historically struggled with. My general philosophy is that if I can’t do something right, I won’t do it at all, and that basically sums up the OMAAT strategy for social media up until now. 😉 I think Daniel strikes the unique balance of being interesting without being obnoxious and clickbaity, and I appreciate that.

So, what exactly will Daniel be doing at OMAAT? This is very much a “we’re going to evolve together on this” situation, given the initiatives I’ve had in mind for some time:

Transparency is important to me, and Daniel is someone who understands how “particular” the OMAAT community is. 😉 Obviously the OMAAT community is very much about written content, so that’s why I think it’s important that this is where he focuses to begin with, since that’s the medium people are most familiar with. Then we’ll see where things go from there…

It’s an exciting (scary?) day here at OMAAT, as Daniel Ross is joining the team, as the first full time contributor of the site in its nearly 19 year history. I’m excited, and the goal is to add someone with a unique and interesting voice, to expand coverage on things, etc.

My hope is also that it frees up a little more time for me, so I can focus a bit more on the community aspect of things. In the long run, you can also expect a bit more of a focus on video and social media, but we’re starting with what we know here!

I’m excited about this, and Daniel will have a post soon introducing himself. Thanks to everyone for their patience, and stay tuned!

PS: For those wondering about the British Airways 747 featured image, it’s because I noticed Daniel had that as his model plane in the background behind his desk during our video calls, so we’ll throw him that Easter egg. 😉

#6131. How Are Hotels Paid When You Redeem Points, And For Elite Perks?

There’s a real thrill to redeeming points for stays at luxury properties, and getting outsized value. I’m sure many people have wondered about the economics of that. How much is the hotel getting reimbursed for your stay? Who is paying for any elite perks that you receive? Does the hotel care if you redeemed points or not? Let’s talk about those various points in this post…

The major global hotel groups (Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, Marriott, etc.) don’t own a vast majority of their properties. Instead, the companies have an asset light strategy, and have management or franchise contracts for the individual properties.

In some cases, large investment firms own hotels, and they may have properties belonging to all kinds of brands. In other cases, a hotel may even be family owned.

The way the major hotel groups make money is primarily through fees (they’re also increasingly directly monetizing their loyalty programs, but that’s a whole different topic). There’s typically an initial fee to open the hotel, and then on top of that, there are fees on ongoing revenue. The ongoing fees typically fall into one of two categories (and they’re typically a percentage of revenue):

Then any upside (or downside) typically falls with the hotel owner. So the major hotel groups are making money, regardless of whether a hotel is raking in the cash or hemorrhaging money.

Now, one of the reasons that consumers flock to certain hotel groups is because of their loyalty programs, which are massive marketing machines. A big part of the value proposition of these loyalty programs is the ability to redeem points.

As you’d expect, those points are redeemed centrally through the program, and then the loyalty program has to “buy” that room from the hotel. After all, the hotel owner wants to be compensated for each head in a bed, especially since they’re already paying a system fund fee, to fund these perks. That brings us to the question of how hotels are reimbursed…

As you’d expect, hotel groups don’t publicly disclose how they reimburse their properties when members redeem points. However, over the years we’ve been able to get some insights into this.

Sometimes guests are given folios that are actually intended for the loyalty program, while in other cases the reimbursement rates showed up online when they weren’t supposed to.

While the exact reimbursement policies differ by program, here’s the general concept:

So I’m totally making this up here, but if a hotel is charging $400 on a particular night, maybe the loyalty program would pay $80 for that room if occupancy is under 90%, while it might be paying $350 if occupancy is over 90%.

Note that the number of points you redeem for a stay doesn’t directly determine reimbursement for a hotel. In other words, a hotel doesn’t get paid X amount per redeemed point. Similarly, if a program offers a fifth night free on award redemptions, the hotel is getting reimbursed for all five nights, as it’s the loyalty program incurring the cost there.

Instead, points redemption rates are set by the loyalty program, and are intended to reflect the cost incurred by the program. That’s why in many cases you’ll find that redemption rates don’t correlate directly to how much a property would cost in cash, but rather also factor in average occupancy at a property.

A hotel loyalty program would probably rather you redeem your points at a $1,000 per night hotel that’s 50% full, rather than a $500 per night hotel that’s 95% full, because the latter redemption will cost the program more. Hotel loyalty programs use historical data to determine points pricing, and the costs they incur.

Let me actually give a real example from a recent stay. I recently redeemed points for a two night stay at a Wyndham Rewards property, at the cost of 30,000 points per night. The folio I was sent accidentally had the amount Wyndham had to pay, rather than the amount I had to pay.

Even though I was paying the same number of points both nights, the hotel was being reimbursed around $87 for one night, and $184 for the next night. Funny enough, while sitting in the lobby working the first morning, I overheard one front desk agent tell the other that they were fully sold out the following night, so that tracks. The first night was being reimbursed at a reduced rate, while the second night was being reimbursed based on something closer to the average daily rate.

If you have elite status with a hotel loyalty program, how does taking advantage of elite perks factor into this when redeeming points? Who pays for breakfast? Who pays for suite upgrades? Who pays for waived destination fees and parking?

The answer is that “it depends,” though here are a few general considerations:

As you can see, funding elite benefits is a combined effort between the loyalty program and hotels.

For those curious, generally individual hotels don’t know how you earned your elite status. So it doesn’t matter to them if you earned it through actual hotel stays, or just by holding onto a credit card. Presumably a front desk agent could look at your stay history, but they typically wouldn’t have any reason to do so, in this context.

This is a loaded question, and there’s obviously no single right or wrong answers. A few thoughts, though.

Hotel staff are trained by corporate to treat guests redeeming points the same way as those paying cash. Many hotel groups even train front desk staff to thank people for redeeming their points, since it reflects engagement in the program. Officially, you should expect exactly the same treatment as if you paid cash, and you absolutely shouldn’t feel sheepish about the fact that you didn’t pay cash for your stay.

Now, in practice that might not always be how things play out. There’s sometimes a back and forth between hotel owners and hotel groups. Hotel owners often want it both ways — they want the power of the major hotel group distribution channels and loyalty programs, without actually incurring the costs associated with it, whether it’s complimentary upgrades, points redemptions, or a decent breakfast.

Will you sometimes find a hotel that’s perhaps a bit condescending if you redeem points and have an issue? Absolutely, but it’s not how it should be, and it’s the exception rather than the norm. Some may remember my stay at the Aegon Mykonos, at the time a Marriott Autograph Collection property (the hotel has since… mysteriously disappeared?).

Long story short, I was downgraded despite using a confirmed upgrade, and the manager was completely unapologetic about it, and was unwilling to do anything meaningful. One of his defenses was that I was staying “complimentary,” and therefore shouldn’t be complaining.

The hotel industry is complex, given the various parties involved, from the hotel group to the individual hotel owners. Hopefully the above is a useful rundown of how reimbursement works when redeeming points. The important thing to understand is that hotels get paid a lot more when you’re redeeming points if the property is full.

When redeeming points, you definitely shouldn’t feel sheepish about it. You earned your stay, and the reason hotels belonging to major loyalty programs are able to command a revenue premium is because of the points and loyalty perks they offer.

What’s your take on how hotels are reimbursed for award stays? And do you feel like you’ve ever been treated differently when redeeming points?

#6130. Van Hollen announces bid for majority leader, but Schumer says he has the votes

Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday night that he would run for Senate majority leader, launching a challenge to Sen. Charles E. Schumer of New York, the current Democratic leader.

Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat first elected to the Senate in 2016, served in leadership in the House and has been chairman of both the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. He has said since the midterm elections he was listening to fellow Senate Democrats about the possibility of a run for the top job.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”

Schumer has already said he has the votes needed to continue serving as the leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people,” Schumer said in a statement.

Schumer's supporters were quick to highlight the success at the ballot box in 2026, with the Democratic caucus potentially growing to 56 seats if former Rep. Mary Peltola prevails in Alaska.

“Chuck has outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with the Democrats, said in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”

In keeping with the World Series theme, Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., echoed King with her own statement of support for Schumer.

“The Brewers just had a record season, and next year is not the time to change our management," Baldwin said. "The same is true in the Senate.”

In an interview with MS NOW about his run, Van Hollen conceded that Schumer would be the favorite in the secret-ballot contest, which will take place in December.

“Am I the underdog? Yes,” Van Hollen said. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”

Van Hollen outlined legislative priorities including restoring Medicaid funding that Republicans cut in last year's budget reconciliation law and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits. But he suggested Democrats need to go further.

"We need to extend tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, but we can’t stop there, right? We have a completely broken health care system. It’s become profits, not people. And so my view is, we also need in the first 100 days to make health care more affordable for tens of millions of people," Van Hollen said. "We need to immediately make it clear that nobody’s going to pay one penny to subsidize data centers. ... We need to make sure that we have a livable minimum wage."

He also said he would not take sides in contested Democratic primaries, and he would make sure the DSCC did not take money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.

Van Hollen's early backers include progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who emerged from a hotly contested Democratic primary in Michigan while the Senate Democratic political apparatus was backing Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich.

“In April, I was the first candidate in the country to call on Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats, and I am proud to stand with him in his bid to become Senate Majority Leader,” El-Sayed said in a statement. “Michiganders demand money out of politics, money in pockets, and Medicare for All. Sen. Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus. It’s why he has my full support to lead our caucus.”

#6129. The Hub Delta Air Lines Threw Away After Merging With Northwest

photosounds | Shutterstock | Simple Flying

The 2008 merger between Delta Air Lines and Northwest Airlines was the first to create one of the US's current 'mega legacy carriers.' Delta Air Lines and its contemporaries today have hubs spanning the entire country while operating over 1,000 mainline aircraft each.

The main benefits of these mergers were scale, including network size, and all three legacy carriers have largely used the hubs that they inherited from their mergers to their advantage, enabling further growth and boosting relevance in more markets. One of the biggest exceptions, however, came with Northwest's hub at Tokyo Narita International Airport.

Northwest had traditionally been heavily focused on its Asia network, competing primarily against United Airlines to be the dominant US airline across the Pacific. Ever since the merger, Delta has attempted to still be competitive in this market space, but has moved away from the Narita hub, slowly de-prioritizing it and then pulling out of Narita entirely in 2020.

Going into the merger, Atlanta-based Delta had hubs in Atlanta, New York, Cincinnati, Salt Lake City, and Los Angeles, while Northwest Airlines brought hubs in Memphis, Detroit, Minneapolis, and Narita. In addition, the carrier often labeled Amsterdam and Paris as hubs, but these were joint venture hubs dominated by joint venture partners KLM and Air France.

Narita, on the other hand, was a fully Northwest operation with a large number of US-bound flights and intra-Asia routes. Memphis was dehubbed after the merger due to the decline of the city's economy as well as its proximity to Atlanta, while Cincinnati was also eventually dehubbed in favor of Detroit. After the merger, Delta also began pursuing hubs in Boston and Seattle, with some success.

As a whole, Delta's network changes were primarily from growth and rationalizing some elements of the hub structure to remove redundancy, but the Narita hub was different because, to an extent, the carrier still has not added back the lost capacity. At the time of the merger, Northwest served 19 cities from Narita, but in the 2010s, Delta slowly cut away at the hub until pulling out of Narita entirely.

The US routes were mainly replaced by services to Tokyo Haneda Airport, but Delta also cut services to many Asia-Pacific destinations. This includes Beijing, Guangzhou, Busan, Guam, Palau, Manila (which will be returning in 2027 from Los Angeles), Saipan, Singapore, and Bangkok. As of 2026, Delta still does not fly to most of these cities.

The Narita hub made sense in the 20th century, when the longest-ranged Boeing 747-200s couldn't reliably fly routes longer than New York to Tokyo. Northwest would have all of its US services stop in Narita, and passengers would then transfer to flights bound for other Asian destinations.

However, aircraft like the Boeing 747-400 and 777, along with the later Airbus A350 and 787, could fly nonstop from the US to most cities in Asia, making the stop in Narita redundant. While this helped fill the intra-Asia flights, the US hubs had much greater connecting feed as well. Delta had already operated a hub in Los Angeles, which has a strong local market for Asia travel, but also heavy competition.

Delta Air Lines Long-Haul Destinations Served From Seattle In 2026

Seoul Incheon International Airport (ICN)

Josep Tarradellas Barcelona–El Prat Airport (BCN)

Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG)

Taipei Taoyuan International Airport (TPE)

Rome Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO)

In 2012, it elected to begin building Seattle as its primary hub for transpacific flights, inheriting former Northwest services to Narita, launching Beijing (previously announced by Northwest), while later adding Osaka, Shanghai, Haneda, Seoul, Hong Kong, and most recently, Taipei. Not all of these services stuck around, but Delta committed to Seattle for transpacific flights, while also growing its domestic and European network from its new hub. Operating smaller widebodies nonstop from Seattle to Asia proved more lucrative.

As such, Delta quickly built a much larger domestic network in Seattle compared to the US network out of Narita. In recent years, Delta has experienced difficulties competing with Alaska Airlines and foreign carriers out of Seattle, and is therefore planning to grow its transpacific network out of Los Angeles as well. It's already added Hong Kong, and Manila will be coming in 2027, while Singapore is also rumored to be returning as a nonstop.

Delta has replaced its intra-Asia operations out of Narita with nonstops from the US, but there's still a large number of Asian cities that have lost service on Delta metal. The reason for this is that, for all intents and purposes, Delta has replaced its Narita hub with a hub in Seoul, except that the intra-Asia flights are now operated by fellow SkyTeam member, Korean Air, rather than using widebodies with the Delta livery.

This is possible due to the metal-neutral joint venture that became effective in 2018. As part of their joint venture, Delta and Korean Air coordinate schedules, pricing, and codeshare on each other's flights, while also sharing revenue. They essentially act as one airline across the Pacific.

Seoul Incheon International Airport (ICN)

Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW)

Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL)

Minneapolis-St Paul International Airport (MSP)

Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC)

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA)

Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG)

Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW)

Seattle Tacoma International Airport (SEA)

Taipei Taoyuan International Airport (TPE)

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA)

Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW)

Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL)

Honolulu Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL)

Minneapolis-St Paul International Airport (MSP)

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA)

This allows Delta to still sell one-stop tickets to destinations like Singapore or Bangkok, but with a layover in Seoul and a segment operated by Korean Air. To the carrier, it makes essentially no difference whether the second leg is flown by a Delta or Korean Air jet, except that codesharing with a partner costs less money. In recent years, Delta has been practically allergic to adding new long-haul and ultra-long-haul routes if a destination can be conveniently served by partner airlines.

However, customers in the US are increasingly seeking out nonstops to major international destinations, while the carrier's latest contract with its pilots mandates a one-for-one increase in widebody flying relative to any capacity growth by foreign partners. As such, the airline is increasing its US-to-Asia nonstops, with the Seoul hub filling in the gaps that were previously served by Narita.

In short, Delta was able to fully replicate its intra-Asia network out of Narita with Korean Air's operations out of Seoul after their joint venture agreement went into effect, and Delta also benefited from not having to operate these flights with its own metal. The cities with the highest demand got their own nonstops from the US.

The 2018 joint venture agreement officially rendered Narita redundant within Delta's network, relegating it to just a spoke airport. However, Delta also had a better airport with which to serve Tokyo directly. Upon Narita's opening in 1978, the Japanese government moved all international flights away from the older Haneda Airport, but in 2010, it began permitting foreign carriers to serve Haneda again on a limited scale.

Haneda is closer to the city center than Narita, making it more desirable, but it's also a slot-controlled airport. As such, Delta had to build up its Haneda operations slowly, as it had to wait for the Japanese government to release and award slots, while rivals American Airlines and United Airlines still serve both airports. Today, Delta serves Haneda from Atlanta, Detroit, Honolulu, Los Angeles, Minneapolis, and Seattle.

While its Tokyo network is smaller than rivals, it lacks a major Japanese partner, which makes Tokyo less important to Delta than American and United. Delta has recently announced that it will be returning to Narita in 2027 with a single daily flight from Seattle, but in all likelihood, this is due to a lack of slots at Haneda. If Delta could, it almost certainly would have added a second daily flight to Haneda, but has to return to Narita instead.

There's no mid-market cabin class on Alaska Airlines' Dreamliners.

Similar to Northwest, United Airlines also formerly had a significant intra-Asia operation out of Narita due to aircraft range limitations. These routes went away as the carrier began taking new Boeing 787s that could serve destinations like Singapore nonstop, but United still serves Narita nonstop from the US alongside its newer Haneda routes due to its joint venture with All Nippon Airways.

Haneda is primarily for origin & destination traffic, whereas Narita is for additional Asia-Pacific connections. Within the past few years, however, United has begun adding new flights within Asia out of Narita again, using Boeing 737s to serve Cebu, Kaohsiung, Koror, Saipan, and Ulaanbaatar.

Naturally, these are destinations that can't be economically served nonstop from the US with a widebody, but the major reason why United has begun these routes is due to issues with its Guam hub. Travel demand to Guam remains significantly down from pre-COVID levels, while United operates crew bases and specially configured 737s out of this hub located thousands of miles away from the mainland.

Rather than operate half-empty 737s out of Guam or move planes and crews to the mainland US, United has instead opted to move some of its 737s to Narita. It's notably operating routes that are not currently served by All Nippon Airways (ANA) , and it's also allowed the carrier to operate direct flights to destinations not served by any other US airline. United still relies on nonstop flights from the US to serve Asia, while the Narita operations today are mainly a creative use of assets.
