#6128. Is The Amex Gold Card Worth It? 4x Points & $424 In Credits Justify The $325 Fee

The American Express® Gold Card has a $325 annual fee (Rates & Fees), which is obviously on the steep side. While I’ve published a full Amex Gold Card review, in this post I’d like to talk more broadly about whether the Amex Gold Card is worth it, with my firsthand experience.

The Amex Gold Card is an absolute powerhouse for dining purchases, whether you spend money at restaurants or supermarkets, so those are bonus categories that have real value for people. However, when it comes to making the math on the card work, it’s all about how much of the $400+ in annual credits that you can take advantage of, to help offset the fee.

So rather than just summarizing the Amex Gold benefits, I’d like to take a first-person look at how I get value from this card, to account for the points I’m earning and redeeming, and how much of the credits I’m easily able to take advantage of. After all, we shouldn’t judge cards by their published perks, but instead, by our actual use.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

Before getting into individual categories and credits on the Amex Gold Card, here’s where I am on the math over the past year, at the time of this post:

Quite honestly, the math on this card has worked out quite well for me. I don’t want to say I’m coming out ahead on the Amex Gold Card purely in terms of the card’s credits, but they greatly help offset the annual fee, and then the 4x points is what makes the card worthwhile for me. If I could just remember to be a little more consistent with using the dining credits or using the Dunkin’ credits at all, I’d be coming out even further ahead with this product.

The Amex Gold Card has an improved welcome offer where you can earn a bonus as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $8,000 within the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, those 100,000 points are worth $1,700 (assuming that’s what you’re eligible for).

With a full six months to hit the spending requirement — a little over $1,300 per month — this should be easy enough for many people to complete (and if not, there are always creative ways to complete minimum spending). Thanks to Amex’s “apply with confidence” feature, there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

When I applied for the card, the welcome offer was “only” 60,000 points, so this is quite a bit better. I received instant approval on the card. I should also emphasize that the product isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past.

On top of that, you may not be eligible for the welcome offer on this card if you have or have had American Express Platinum Card® (learn more). That’s why I always recommend applying for the Amex Gold before the Amex Platinum, since that will allow you to eventually earn the welcome offer on both cards. As I see it, you get the Amex Gold for the return on spending, and the Amex Platinum for the perks. In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention that if you have some Chase cards you’re considering applying for, perhaps get those first, given the limitations of the Chase 5/24 rule.

I’ve of course already redeemed a lot of the points earned from the welcome offer on the card, including for a flight in All Nippon Airways first class, which I booked with Air Canada Aeroplan points (moved over from Amex).

This is where the Amex Gold Card really becomes exciting, and where the personal version of the card is nicely differentiated from the business version of the card — the bonus categories are broad, everyday, and hard not to use. The Amex Gold offers:

Based on my valuations, that’s like an 8.5% return on prepaid hotel stays, a 6.8% return at restaurants and at U.S. supermarkets, and a 5.1% return on eligible flights. The 4x points on dining and 4x points on supermarket categories are the two that matter for most people, and they’re genuinely best-in-class.

I’ve just gone over how much spending I’ve put on the card over the past year, and it’s not pretty… yow, food is expensive, especially when you add two little kids to the equation! I’ll simply say that I’ve earned six figures worth of points from the 4x points categories on this card.

I’m not a huge fan of doing math this way, but just to do the breakeven math on the Amex Gold annual fee, based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, spending just under $4,800 per year (just under $400 per month) in the 4x points categories would earn you enough points to help offset the annual fee, not even factoring in any of the other benefits.

I do want to add two caveats to the Amex Gold earning structure, just to balance things:

Eligibility is always determined by how the merchant is categorized, so some places you’d consider a restaurant or grocery store may not code that way, and that’s something to be aware of. It’s certainly an issue I’ve faced a few times with the card, where it didn’t code exactly as I expected.

For example, you typically expect a coffee shop to code as a restaurant for these purposes, but I’ve had a few that didn’t code that way. Fortunately I’m not spending a fortune at coffee shops, so it’s not a huge deal.

Here’s the heart of the “worth it” question, as I see it. The Amex Gold Card offers statement credits that could save you up to $424 per year, more than offsetting the annual fee (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

But they’re fragmented across several buckets, most of them monthly use-it-or-lose-it, so the advertised number and the amount you’re actually able to use can be very different. Here’s how each Amex Gold credit has worked for me, ranked from easiest to hardest to redeem. But first, below is a chart summarizing the basics of the Amex Gold credits (Enrollment is required for select benefits)..

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a $10 Uber Cash credit every calendar month, valid toward Uber and Uber Eats purchases in the United States An Amex Card must be selected as the payment method for your Uber or Uber Eats transaction to redeem the Amex Uber Cash benefit. In order to use this, you need to pay for your purchase with an Amex card, and the Uber Cash can only be deposited in a single account.

This is the Amex Gold credit I maximize most reliably, because it’s effectively cash toward something almost everyone uses — a ride or food delivery. Even if you don’t take Ubers, the credit works on Uber Eats.

Personally, I generally use Lyft for rideshare and Uber Eats for food delivery, so I easily get the full value of this credit each month on food orders alone. I wish I didn’t use Uber Eats so much that I consider it to be “good as cash,” but that’s the current reality.

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a semi-annual Resy credit — a $50 credit in January through June, and a $50 credit in July through December — valid at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants, Resy.com, and in the mobile Resy app. There’s no need to even make a reservation, as long as you pay at an eligible restaurant.

Because it’s semi-annual rather than monthly, it’s lower maintenance, but it requires you to actually dine at a Resy restaurant in each half of the year — which is easy in a major city and harder elsewhere.

As someone who lives in Miami, there’s absolutely no shortage of Resy restaurants, so I get full value out of this with minimal effort. Fortunately whatever part of the meal isn’t covered by the credit still earns 4x points. So over the past year, I’ve gotten the full value out of this… yay! But if you live in a more rural area, you may not have any Resy restaurants near you, and the credit may not be worth much unless you’re traveling.

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a $10 monthly dining credit, for a total of up to $120 each year, valid for purchases with Grubhub (including Seamless), Buffalo Wild Wings, Five Guys, The Cheesecake Factory, and Wonder. Only purchases in the United States qualify, and you’re limited to a single credit no matter how many authorized users you have.

The catch is that it’s tied to a specific list of merchants, so it’s only “easy” if one of those fits your routine. Grubhub is the flexible one for most people.

It goes without saying we all have different spending patterns. Personally, I sort of struggle with the credit. I don’t remember the last time I went to a Buffalo Wild Wings, Five Guys, or The Cheesecake Factory (nothing against them, I sort of love the SkinnyLicious menu, but they’re just not near me), and I don’t even know what Wonder is. So that leaves Grubhub.

I try to use the dining credit on Grubhub whenever I can, but to be honest, many months I forget. That’s because Uber Eats and DoorDash are the primary delivery apps I use. The $10 isn’t necessarily that huge of an incentive to remember, which is why it sometimes slips my mind.

Amex Gold cardmembers receive a $7 monthly Dunkin’ credit, earned after using your enrolled card to pay at more than 9,000 Dunkin’ locations nationwide.

This is the most polarizing credit on the card. If there’s a Dunkin’ on your commute and you actually like Dunkin’, enjoy some coffee on Amex. If there isn’t, you may forfeit $84 of the headline credit total — and it’s worth subtracting from the card’s advertised value when you do your own math. Keep in mind that there aren’t even Dunkin’ locations in some states, like Oregon and Washington.

I have read that a $ 7-per-month reload would trigger the credit as well, so you could accrue it. I probably should’ve been taking advantage of that all along, but this is also where “credit card fatigue” kicks in, and I just forget to even focus on this.

After all, on some level this credit card game is supposed to be fun, rather than just spending every month chasing dozens and dozens of credits. Or maybe I just have too many cards? 😉 So yeah, unfortunately I’ve been losing $84 per year in value with this credit by not taking advantage of it.

Two more perks on the Amex Gold Card are worth a brief mention, because they round out the card without being the reason to get it.

First, Amex Offers. One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which provides savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. The more Amex cards you have, the more offers you’ll have access to, and they could save you hundreds of dollars per year.

For example, I recently had an Amex Offers deal for 1,200 bonus points when spending $150 with Amazon, and that could be used up to three times. Since I shop on Amazon all the time, that’s an easy bonus of 3,600 points as I see it.

Second, The Hotel Collection. For staying two or more nights at select luxury hotels, you can receive extra benefits through The Hotel Collection, including a $100 hotel credit and a room upgrade if available. This is different than Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, which requires having the Amex Platinum. I can’t say that I’ve used this, because when it comes to Amex’s hotel programs, I typically gravitate toward FHR.

Lastly, while I wouldn’t consider it to be particularly valuable either, I should also mention that the Amex Gold offers Hertz Five Star status, which is at least worth being aware of (Enrollment is required for select benefits). This gets you an upgrade to a higher car class on rentals when available as well as a 25% bonus on all Hertz rentals.

The Amex Gold Card has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use it for purchases globally — and because the 4x dining category applies at restaurants worldwide, this is genuinely one of the better cards to carry abroad for meals. Just remember the 4x supermarket category is U.S.-only, so that bonus doesn’t follow you overseas.

I use this card all the time for dining abroad, and it’s a good way to maximize rewards. For example, on my summer trip to the Dolomites, I used the Amex Gold Card for all my dining outside hotels, which included some great meals.

I should acknowledge that Amex doesn’t quite have the global acceptance of Mastercard or Visa, for example, though the gap is much smaller than in the past.

I think the Amex Gold Card is a product that has bonus categories that are about as well rounded as one could imagine, in terms of appealing to the average consumer. Everyone eats, and this card is great for those people, whether you get your food at restaurants or supermarkets.

I will say, the math on this card may break down for you if you fall into one of the following two categories:

Personally, the math on this card is working great for me. I do wish I more consistently maximized the credits, as I do a pretty good job, but not a great job. Based on my own usage patterns, I basically view this as a card costing me well under $100 per year (after subtracting the value of the credits), and then I get a very well balanced return in some bonus categories for that. I guess I just need to do a better job of actually using those Dunkin’ credits, and at least reloading my account.

I also think it’s worth emphasizing that the Amex Gold might not be the right style of card for some people, depending on your consumer preferences:

For me, the Amex Gold Card is proving to be a keeper, and I plan to renew on my account anniversary, while paying the annual fee. The rewards structure on this card is excellent and simple, while the credits help make this an affordable card to hold onto. So if you ask me, the card is a clear “yes” if:

If you’d forfeit two or more of the credits, do the math on the credits you’ll actually take advantage of before counting the full $424 — the card can still win on dining and supermarket earning alone, but the real math is different than the marketed amount.

The other nice thing is that if you get the Amex Gold and decide after a year or more that the card is no longer a good fit for you, you can typically product change it to another card. This allows you to preserve the rewards, credit history, etc.

The Amex Gold Card is one of American Express’ best rewards cards for earning points, with 4x points on dining and U.S. supermarkets, which is hard for any other card to beat. The earning side is the easy part — almost everyone can use it.

Whether the card is worth its $325 annual fee on an ongoing basis comes down to one honest question: how many of the up to $424 in annual credits will you actually capture? The credit is real — up to $120 for dining, up to $120 in Uber Cash, up to $100 with Resy, and up to $84 with Dunkin’ — but it’s fragmented, and the gap between the headline and your real capture rate is the whole decision.

It’s easiest to make the math work if you actually spend a substantial amount on the 4x points categories, since the value of that will quickly make a material difference to your points earning.

What’s your take on the value proposition of the Amex Gold Card? Which credits do you actually capture each year, and which ones do you forfeit?

#6127. Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill.

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech company and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”

“The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we're going to work to make sure that happens.”

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar said. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

“We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”

Also late Thursday, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott, R-S.C.,  sent a letter to Huang calling on him to appear at a Dec. 3 committee hearing and another letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify at a Dec. 10 hearing "regarding recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate's fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

“There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

Mast said the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don't let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don't get sold to them, even though it's the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can't access it remotely.”

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you're going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

In a statement Thursday, Warren said that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an update on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.
